questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 6-month-old boy was brought to the casualty with seizures. The pediatrician tries to do CSF sampling. What are the structures punctured by the pediatrician while piercing through the marked structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Scalp, dura, arachnoid

The given image shows the skull of an infant and the arrow points towards the anterior fontanelle. The procedure of collecting CSF from the anterior fontanelle is called ventricular tapping. The various structures pierced are the scalp, dura, and arachnoid.

Fontanelle tap/ Percutaneous ventricular puncture:

A fontanelle tap or percutaneous ventricular puncture is performed in infants without access to a VP shunt, who require urgent ventricular decompression and have an open anterior fontanelle. The infants’ open fontanelle is directly punctured with a butterfly needle to enter the lateral ventricle to collect CSF samples or release the pressure or place a drain/catheter.

A 25-gauge butterfly needle is inserted through the anterolateral aspect of the anterior fontanelle (away from the midline, avoiding the superior sagittal sinus).

The image below shows the various fontanelles.

The scalp is a soft tissue that covers the calvaria of the skull. It consists of five layers (Mnemonic: SCALP). Below the scalp and the calvaria lie the meningeal layers, namely, pachymeninges [arachnoid + dura mater (P-AD)] and leptomeninges [arachnoid + pia mater (L-AP)]. One must reach the subarachnoid space below the arachnoid layer to collect or tap CSF. So, the layers pierced in the order are as follows:

1. Skin
2. Connective tissue (superficial fascia) with blood vessels and nerves
3. Aponeurosis (galea aponeurotica) with occipitofrontalis muscle
4. Loose areolar (subaponeurotic) tissue
5. Pericranium
6. Dura mater
7. Arachnoid membrane

The given images show the various layers that are pierced.
questions.learning: Scalp, dura, arachnoid — The given image shows the skull of an infant and the arrow points towards the anterior fontanelle. The procedure of collecting CSF from the anterior fontanelle is called ventricular tapping.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Identify the genetic disorder mentioned below:
questions.explanation: The image summarizes the classic clinical features of Turner's syndrome (Option C), a chromosomal disorder in females typically characterized by a 45,X karyotype. Key manifestations shown include short stature (the most common feature), webbing of the neck (pterygium colli), and a "shield-shaped" broad chest with widely spaced nipples. Internal findings include "streak ovaries" due to accelerated oocyte loss, which results in primary amenorrhea and infertility. Congenital heart defects, specifically coarctation of the aorta (Option C), are also frequent. Cubitus valgus (an increased carrying angle of the elbow) is another classic sign. Klinefelter syndrome (Option D) occurs in males (47,XXY) and presents with tall stature and gynecomastia. Kallmann syndrome (Option B) involves delayed puberty and anosmia. Testicular feminizing syndrome (Option A) involves an XY karyotype with female external genitalia. The visual triad of webbed neck, short stature, and streak ovaries is pathognomonic for Turner’s
questions.learning: The image summarizes the classic clinical features of Turner's syndrome (Option C), a chromosomal disorder in females typically characterized by a 45,X karyotype.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the probable diagnosis from the given clinical image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Uterocervical prolapse

In the provided image, it is evident that both anterior and posterior vaginal walls protrude completely outside the vaginal orifice, and the entire uterus is positioned below this level, indicating a case of procidentia/ grade IV utero-cervical prolapse.

Utero-cervical prolapse is commonly seen in the elderly age group due to weak pelvic muscles.

Differential diagnoses of genital prolapse include:

• Vulval cyst and Gartner cyst.
• Cyst of the anterior vaginal wall - tense with well-defined margins and cannot be reduced with pressure.
• Urethral diverticula - small and located low in the anterior vaginal wall. Urethroscopy aids in diagnosis.
• Congenital elongation of the cervix - vaginal portion of the cervix is elongated without accompanying vaginal wall prolapse. The fornices are deep.
• Cervical fibroid polyps - cervix is located high up and a rim of the cervix is felt above the pedicle of the cervical polyp.
• Chronic inversion of the uterus- identified by the higher position of the cervix and the inability to define the uterus on palpation. Diagnosis is confirmed by the use of a uterine sound and further examination with ultrasound and laparoscopy, which reveal a depression at the fundus and an absence of the uterine fundus in the pelvis.
• Rectal prolapse.

The image below depicts the various degrees of genital organ prolapse:

Other options:

Option A: Cervical carcinoma

It commonly presents with post-coital bleeding or postmenopausal bleeding. When they present as CIN lesions, they can be identified by colposcopy but mass lesions will present with fungating, cauliflower, or punctate hemorrhagic lesions.

The provided image shows a normal transition zone, in the given setting without VIA or colposcopy it is difficult to diagnose the lesion as CA cervix.

The image below shows characteristic hemorrhagic and cauliflower lesions seen in the CA cervix:

Option B: Uterine inversion:

Acute uterine inversion is a rare and life-threatening post-partum complication. Uterine inversion is associated with primiparity, the use of oxytocin, macrosomia, and fundal insertion of the placenta. Premature traction on the umbilical cord and fundal pressure before placental separation are the usual direct causes. During per abdomen examination fundus of the uterus is felt to be absent. Care for acute uterine inversion involves pain management, resuscitation, and replacement of the inverted uterus before edema sets in by the O'Sullivan method.

The image below image shows uterine inversion which can be identified by a completely inverted uterus.

Option D: Fibroid polyp

They are leiomyomas that present as polyps. A fibroid polyp is generally firm, permanent, paler than a mucus polyp, and is of various sizes. Sonosalpingography is also a very good technique for detecting submucous fibroid polyp.

Note:

Cervical fibroid polyps can be easily identified as the cervix is high up in its normal anatomical position unlike in the given image. The image attached below shows degenerated fibroid polyps.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: An elderly woman presents with mptoms of confusion, intense thirst, abdominal discomfort, a pale complexion, and sensitivity in her thoracic spine. Her lab results show signincant findings: 1. Hemoglobin (Hb) : 6.9 g/ dL 2. White Blood Cell count : rBq c m 40 0 3 ο , 3. With a normal differential 4. Serum calcium: 13 mg/dL 5. Creatinine: 2.3 mg/dl 6. Albumin: 2.4 g/dl 7. Urinalysis: Positive for Bence-lones proteins 8. A skull X-ray indicates lytic lesions. Based on 9. These findings, what is the most likely diaglosis?
questions.explanation: The provided image and clinical triad are pathognomonic for Multiple Myeloma (Option B). This is a plasma cell malignancy characterized by the "CRAB" features: Calcium elevation (13 mg/dL), Renal insufficiency (Creatinine 2.3), Anemia (Hb 6.9), and Bone lesions. The presence of Bence-Jones proteins (monoclonal light chains) in the urine is a specific diagnostic hallmark. The skull X-ray provides definitive visual confirmation, showing multiple, small, well-defined "punched-out" lytic lesions. Metastatic breast cancer (Option A) can cause lytic lesions but would not show Bence-Jones proteins. Primary hyperparathyroidism (Option C) causes hypercalcemia and a "salt and pepper" skull but lacks monoclonal proteins. Milk-alkali syndrome (Option D) involves hypercalcemia without skeletal destruction. Therefore, the combination of specific laboratory markers and pathognomonic radiographic findings confirms Multiple Myeloma as the definitive diagnosis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old patient sustains a fall from the 2nd floor of a building and is brought to the emergency department. Which of the following is not an adjunct to the primary survey?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. CT abdomen and pelvis

CT abdomen and pelvis are not an adjunct to the primary survey. CT scan is a part of a secondary survey.

The primary survey identifies and manages the most immediately life-threatening pathologies first.

The secondary survey includes investigations that help identify all other injuries, excluding the apparent ones. This includes X-rays of the spine and extremities(limbs) and a CT of the abdomen, head, chest, pelvis and spine.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A male patient presents to the emergency department after a car crash. On examination, his BP was 80/40mmHg and pulses were feeble, neck veins distended, and heart sounds were muffled. Which of the following changes will you expect in the jvp of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Absent Y descent

The given clinical scenario with hypotension, muffled heart sounds, and distended neck vein suggests a diagnosis of cardiac tamponade. The JVP finding most likely to be seen is absent y descent.

Cardiac tamponade is the accumulation of fluid in the pericardial space. It results in the obstruction of the blood flow into the ventricles.

This manifests as Beck's triad which consists of the following:

* Distended neck veins (due to decreased venous return)

* Muffled heart sounds (fluid accumulation in the pericardial space)

* Hypotension

The physical examination findings in a patient with cardiac tamponade are:

* Tachycardia

* Hypotension

* Elevated JVP

* Pulsus paradoxus

JVP will have a prominent x (early systolic) descent but an absent y (early diastolic) descent because of the limited or absent early diastolic filling of the ventricle. There may be reductions in the amplitude of the QRS complexes, and electrical alternans of the P, QRS, or T waves in cardiac tamponade.

An eFAST is reliable and will show fluid in the pericardial space. A chest X-ray will show an enlarged heart shadow.

Cardiac tamponade can also be treated with open surgery procedures like sternotomy or left thoracotomy. This also allows for the heart to be repaired during the procedure.
questions.learning: Absent Y descent — The given clinical scenario with hypotension, muffled heart sounds, and distended neck vein suggests a diagnosis of cardiac tamponade.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are correct in respect of Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS)? 1. It is caused by the release of lipopolysaccharide endotoxin from dying E. coli bacteria. 2. It is same as bacteraemia. 3. It results in Multiple Organ Dysfunction Syndrome (MODS). 4. White cell counts of more than 12 × 10⁹/L are present. Select the answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 3 and 4

Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS) is a clinical syndrome of generalized inflammatory response that can be triggered by infectious or non-infectious insults such as trauma, burns, pancreatitis, or sepsis. If uncontrolled, SIRS may progress to Multiple Organ Dysfunction Syndrome (MODS).

• 1. It is caused by the release of lipopolysaccharide endotoxin from dying E. coli bacteria. ✓

• Gram-negative endotoxins (lipopolysaccharides) are potent triggers of SIRS by stimulating massive cytokine release. Although SIRS can occur due to many infectious and non-infectious causes, this statement is correct.

• 2. It is same as bacteraemia. ✗

• Bacteremia refers to the presence of bacteria in the bloodstream, whereas SIRS is a systemic inflammatory response that may occur with or without infection.

• 3. It results in Multiple Organ Dysfunction Syndrome (MODS). ✓

• Persistent or severe SIRS can progress to MODS, characterized by dysfunction of two or more organ systems.

• 4. White cell counts of more than 12 × 10⁹/L are present. ✓

• One of the diagnostic criteria for SIRS is WBC >12,000/mm³ (12 × 10⁹/L), <4,000/mm³, or >10% immature (band) forms.
questions.learning: 1, 3 and 4 Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS) is a clinical syndrome of generalized inflammatory response that can be triggered by infectious or non-infectious insults such as trauma, burns, pancreatitis, or sepsis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient underwent lipoma excision 5 weeks ago and now presents with a scar confined to the original incision site. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A thickened, raised scar that remains confined within the boundaries of the original incision is definitively a Hypertrophic scar (Option C) . These typically develop within weeks of a surgical procedure or injury and may regress over time. In contrast, a Keloid (Option A) is a more aggressive fibrotic lesion that characteristically extends beyond the original boundaries of the wound, invading the surrounding normal skin, and rarely regresses spontaneously. Exuberant granulation (Option B), or "proud flesh," refers to red, friable tissue that grows above the skin level in a non-healing wound, rather than a mature scar. Granulation tissue (Option D) is the normal vascular tissue formed during the healing process. Because the description specifies the scar is exactly within the incision limits, Hypertrophic scar is the correct forensic and dermatological classification. This distinction is vital for planning treatment, as hypertrophic scars often respond well to pressure or silicone sheets
questions.learning: A thickened, raised scar that remains confined within the boundaries of the original incision is definitively a Hypertrophic scar (Option C) . These typically develop within weeks of a surgical procedure or injury and may regress over time.

questions.text: During surgical intervention on the great saphenous vein situated 2.5 cm anterior to the medial malleolus, which structure should be protected from damage during the application of ligatures around the vein?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Saphenous nerve

During surgery on the great saphenous vein located 2.5 cm anterior to the medial malleolus, care must be taken to protect the nearby saphenous nerve from damage during ligature placement around the vein.

The Saphenous nerve accompanies the Great Saphenous Vein medially from the ankle to the level of the knee and supplies cutaneous sensation to the medial leg and ankle. Thus it is more prone to injury during stripping of GSV.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A man sustains trauma to the lateral aspect of his right knee. Two days later, he develops difficulty in walking due to dragging of the toes and reports numbness over the upper lateral part of the leg and the dorsum of the foot. Which nerve is most likely injured?
questions.explanation: Trauma to the lateral knee, particularly around the fibular neck, often damages the common peroneal nerve because it is superficial and highly vulnerable at that site. Damage here results in "foot drop"—where the toes drag during walking—due to paralysis of the dorsiflexors. It also causes sensory loss over the lateral leg and the dorsum of the foot. The tibial nerve (Option A) controls plantarflexion and sensation on the sole; its injury would not cause foot drop or numbness on the foot's top. The deep peroneal nerve (Option C) is a branch that controls dorsiflexion, but injury to it alone would not explain the sensory loss over the lateral leg. The femoral nerve (Option D) innervates the anterior thigh and is unrelated to foot dorsiflexion. Therefore, the combined motor and sensory deficits specifically identify a common peroneal nerve injury
questions.learning: Trauma to the lateral knee, particularly around the fibular neck, often damages the common peroneal nerve because it is superficial and highly vulnerable at that site.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 2-week-old infant presents with elevated conjugated bilirubin levels, dark urine, and clay-colored stools. Upon examination, the infant appears jaundiced but is feeding normally. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Biliary atresia

The given clinical vignette suggests a probable diagnosis of biliary atresia.

Biliary atresia presents with progressive jaundice, persistent acholic stools, and hepatomegaly at a peak age of incidence between 2 - 6 weeks.

Biliary atresia is characterised by inflammatory fibrosis of the biliary tree, resulting in bile flow obstruction and conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. The clinical features include persistent jaundice, clay-coloured stools, and hepatomegaly. The meconium may be slightly bile-stained, but later, the stools will be pale, and the urine will be dark. Untreated newborns will show signs of liver cirrhosis and failure (ascites, portal hypertension, and failure to thrive). Associated anomalies include cardiac lesions, polysplenia, situs inversus, absent vena cava, and preduodenal portal vein.

Laboratory evaluation will show elevated direct and indirect bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase. An ultrasound of the abdomen will show a hypoplastic or absent gall bladder and a triangular cord sign.

Biliary atresia may also be termed as noncystic obliterative cholangiopathy. It is a disease of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts of unknown aetiology.

The HIDA test is used for screening, and liver biopsy is diagnostic for biliary atresia. A biopsy shows proliferation of the bile ductule, the presence of bile plugs, and portal or perilobular edema and fibrosis, with the basic hepatic lobular architecture intact.

The Japanese and Anglo-Saxon classification describes three main types (Kasai):

* Type I – Common bile duct

* Type II – Common hepatic duct

* Type IIa – only common hepatic duct

* Type IIb – Common bile duct, hepatic duct, cystic duct.

* Type III (most common type) – Common bile duct, right and left hepatic ducts, cystic duct; no anastomosable ducts at porta hepatis.

Clinical features include persistent jaundice, clay-coloured stools, and hepatomegaly. Untreated newborns will show signs of liver cirrhosis and failure (ascites, portal hypertension, and failure to thrive).

The definitive diagnosis is by intraoperative cholangiography. Preoperative percutaneous transhepatic cholecystocholangiography combined with liver biopsy in cholestatic infants has a sensitivity of 100% and a specificity of 93% for diagnosing biliary atresia.

According to Bailey's 28th edition:

* Fasting USG is the gold standard for diagnosis

* MRCP is highly sensitive and specific

* Cholangiography defines surgical anatomy.

Management of extrahepatic biliary atresia:

Type I

Atresia restricted to the common bile duct (CBD)
Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy

Type II

Atresia of the CBD + common hepatic duct (CHD)

Kasai procedure (Roux-en-Y hepatoportoenterostomy)

Type III
Atresia of the CBD + CHD + right and left hepatic duct
Kasai procedure (Roux-en-Y hepatoportoenterostomy)

The image given below shows the Kasai procedure.

Other options:

Option A: Accumulation of lipofuscin pigments in hepatocytes is seen in Gilbert's syndrome. Gilbert syndrome is a benign, familial disorder characterised by mild intermittent jaundice usually seen during stress, fatigue, or alcohol use. The condition is recognised to arise from a mutation in the UGT1A1 gene, which results in mildly decreased UDP-glucuronyltransferase production. This causes a reduction in the liver's ability to conjugate bilirubin, thus causing unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. The total bilirubin value is usually < 3 mg/dL.

Option B: Crigler-Najjar syndrome type I is due to the absence of the UDP-glucuronyl transferase enzyme. It is an autosomal recessive hyperbilirubinemia syndrome characterised by severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and usually presents with kernicterus. It is usually fatal in the neonatal period.

Option C: Physiological jaundice occurs due to increased bilirubin production due to the destruction of the foetal RBCs, along with a transient limitation in bilirubin conjugation in the immature neonatal liver. It first appears on the 2nd or 3rd day, usually peaks between the 2nd and 4th days, and decreases between the 5th and 7th days after birth.
questions.learning: Biliary atresia — The given clinical vignette suggests a probable diagnosis of biliary atresia. Biliary atresia presents with progressive jaundice, persistent acholic stools, and hepatomegaly at a peak age of incidence between 2 - 6 weeks.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
A female presents to you with 6 weeks of amenorrhea complaining of bleeding per vagina and slight abdominal pain. The urine pregnancy test is positive and hCG level is 2800 IU/L. A mass is seen on the left adnexa measuring 3 × 2.5 cm. She is hemodynamically stable. How will you manage this patient?

hCG- Human chorionic gonadotropin
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Single-dose methotrexate injection

The clinical scenario of a patient with 6 weeks of amenorrhea, abdominal pain, and vaginal bleeding with beta-hCG levels of 2800 mIU/mL and a gestational sac in the left adnexa measuring 3 × 2.5 cm points to the diagnosis of unruptured ectopic pregnancy. The most appropriate management for this patient is a single dose of methotrexate injection.

Symptoms and signs of ectopic pregnancy are often subtle or absent in unruptured ectopic pregnancy. The classic triad includes amenorrhea, which is followed by pain and vaginal bleeding. Lower abdominal and pelvic pain is usually seen with tubal rupture. The pain is severe and frequently described as sharp, stabbing, or tearing.

Management of ectopic pregnancy:

1. Medical management is preferred in the following cases:

• Low initial serum beta-hCG level (Less than 5,000 IU/L)
• Small ectopic pregnancy size (Less than 3.5 cm)
• Absent fetal cardiac activity
• Hemodynamically stable

The most popular method of treating ectopic pregnancies is intramuscular methotrexate injection, which can be done in single-dose or multidose protocols. The dose for single-dose therapy is 50 mg/m2 body surface area (BSA).

Single-dose therapy is preferred over the multidose protocol as the former offers simplicity, lower costs, and less involved post-therapy monitoring.

2. Expectant management: A low initial serum hCG concentration, a considerable reduction in levels over 48 hours, and a sonographic inhomogeneous mass instead of a tubal halo or other gestational features are predictive variables for success.

3. Surgical management with salpingectomy or salpingostomy is done when:

• Criteria for expectant and medical management are not met
• Gestational sac >3.5 cm
• Fetal cardiac activity present
• Beta-hCG >5000 mIU/mL
• Significant pain and hemoperitoneum
• Failure of expectant or medical management
• Clinical status of the patient warrants urgent intervention
• Doubtful compliance with medical management

Other options:

Option A: Oral methotrexate is not the preferred route for treating ectopic pregnancy, as it may lead to variable absorption and unreliable dosing. Intramuscular injection is the preferred route of administration for methotrexate in the management of ectopic pregnancy.

Option C: Serial methotrexate with leucovorin rescue is a multidose protocol that can be used to treat ectopic pregnancy. However, the single-dose methotrexate injection is preferred in this case due to its simplicity, lower costs, and less involved post-therapy monitoring.

Option D: Salpingectomy, the surgical removal of the affected fallopian tube, is reserved for patients who do not meet the criteria for medical management or expectant management, have significant pain and hemoperitoneum, or have failed medical management. This patient does not fulfill the criteria for surgical management.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the gold standard method for intraocular pressure measurement?
questions.explanation: The Goldmann applanation tonometer (GAT) is universally recognized as the gold standard method for measuring intraocular pressure (IOP). It works on the Imbert-Fick principle, measuring the force required to flatten a constant area (3.06 mm) of the cornea. It is highly accurate and is the standard against which all other tonometers are compared. Hertel's exophthalmometer (Option A) measures the degree of eyeball protrusion (proptosis) from the orbit, not pressure. A Gonioscope (Option B) is used to visualize the drainage angle of the eye. The Tonopen (Option D) is a portable handheld device that is useful for patients who cannot sit at a slit lamp, but it is less accurate than GAT. Accurate IOP measurement is fundamental for the diagnosis and management of glaucoma. GAT readings can be influenced by central corneal thickness, which must be accounted for using pachymetry. Regular GAT assessment is the cornerstone of monitoring glaucoma patients to ensure they remain at their target pressure to prevent optic nerve damage
questions.learning: The Goldmann applanation tonometer (GAT) is universally recognized as the gold standard method for measuring intraocular pressure (IOP). It works on the Imbert-Fick principle, measuring the force required to flatten a constant area (3.06 mm) of the cornea.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: During isometric (static) exercise, which of the following hemodynamic changes is most characteristic?
options: Increase in both systolic and diastolic blood pressure
Increase in stroke volume with fall in heart rate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increase in both systolic and diastolic blood pressure

During isometric (static) exercise (e.g., handgrip, weight holding), sustained muscle contraction compresses blood vessels within the muscle, increasing total peripheral resistance (TPR). Hemodynamic effects:

• Sympathetic activation
• Increased heart rate and cardiac output
• Increased total peripheral resistance

As a result, both systolic and diastolic blood pressure rise.

Contrast with dynamic exercise:

• Dynamic exercise (running, cycling): ↓ TPR due to vasodilation → SBP ↑ but DBP normal or ↓.
• Isometric exercise: ↑ TPR → both SBP and DBP increase.
questions.learning: Increase in both systolic and diastolic blood pressure During isometric (static) exercise (e.g., handgrip, weight holding), sustained muscle contraction compresses blood vessels within the muscle, increasing total peripheral resistance (TPR).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 50-year-old female patient, who is a known case of ovarian cancer, presents with difficulty in activities like climbing stairs, getting up from the chair, combing hair, etc. The following characteristic sign was found on examination. The most probable diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dermatomyositis

The most probable diagnosis is dermatomyositis.

The given image shows upper eyelid lilac erythema or heliotrope rash which is pathognomonic of dermatomyositis. The clinical presentation of proximal myopathy with a rash in an elderly female, with a history of internal malignancy, is also suggestive of dermatomyositis.

Other classic cutaneous signs in dermatomyositis:

* Heliotrope rash/ eyelid erythema- Violaceous erythema of the upper eyelids

* V sign- Confluent macular erythema over the lower anterior neck and upper anterior chest

* Shawl sign- Confluent macular erythema over the upper back and lateral aspect of arms

* Gottron’s papules- Erythematous papules and plaques over extensor surface of the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 55-year-old male undergoes esophagectomy for carcinoma of the middle third of the esophagus. Postoperatively, he develops milky white fluid in the chest drain with high triglyceride content. Imaging confirms injury to a lymphatic structure in the posterior mediastinum. Which of the following best describes the anatomical course of the injured structure?
options: Ascends on the right side and drains into right venous angle
Ascends on the left side throughout and drains into left subclavian vein
Ascends on the right, crosses to the left at T5 level, and drains into left venous angle
Ascends on the left, crosses to the right at T8 level, and drains into right venous angle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ascends on the right, crosses to the left at T5 level, and drains into left venous angle

This question tests understanding of thoracic duct anatomy and its clinical relevance in chyle leak (chylothorax) after thoracic surgery.

• Thoracic duct injury → chylothorax

• Milky pleural fluid
• High triglyceride content

• Anatomical course of thoracic duct:

• Originates from cisterna chyli (L2)
• Ascends in posterior mediastinum on the right side
• Crosses to the left at T5 level
• Drains into left venous angle (junction of left internal jugular + subclavian vein)

• Clinical relevance:

• Vulnerable during esophageal and thoracic surgeries
• Injury → chyle leak → nutritional and immunological compromise

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A diabetic patient comes to you for advice regarding his diet. You advise him to include foods with a low glycemic index in the diet. Which of the following would you advise him for the same?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Papaya

The patient should be advised to take papaya since it has a low glycemic index.

The Glycemic index (GI) is the area under the two-hour blood glucose response curve (AUC) following ingestion of a fixed portion of test carbohydrate as a proportion of the AUC of the standard (glucose or white bread).

The classification of foods according to Glycemic index (GI) is as follows,

* Low GI foods (GI = 55 or less): Most fruits and vegetables (except potatoes, watermelon, and sweet corn), whole grains, pasta foods, beans, and lentils.

* Moderate GI foods (GI = 56 to 69): Sucrose, basmati rice, and brown rice.

* High GI foods (GI = 70 or more): Corn flakes, baked potatoes, white bread, candies, and syrupy foods.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is most likely to show the following finding on USG?
options: Metastasis to the breast from another primary site
questions.explanation: The ultrasound image displays a classic Fibroadenoma. Its key benign sonographic features include a well-circumscribed margin, an oval shape, and a characteristic "wider than tall" orientation (horizontal diameter is greater than the vertical height). A breast cyst (Option B) would be completely "anechoic" (black) with posterior acoustic enhancement. Breast carcinoma (Option C) characteristically appears as an irregular, ill-defined mass that is often "taller than wide" with posterior acoustic shadowing. Metastasis (Option D) usually presents as multiple, discrete solid masses but is much rarer than a primary fibroadenoma. The "wider than tall" sign is a very reliable indicator of a benign lesion in breast imaging. In a young woman, such a finding on USG often precludes the need for biopsy unless the lesion is growing or atypical. Standard management for a classic fibroadenoma is clinical observation and reassurance

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Who conducts inquest in Police custodial death?
questions.explanation: An inquest is a preliminary investigation to determine the cause and circumstances of an unnatural death. Under the laws of India (specifically Section 176 of the CrPC), a Judicial Magistrate is legally required to conduct an inquest in any case of death that occurs while a person is in police custody. This is a critical safeguard designed to ensure transparency, impartiality, and to prevent potential human rights abuses or cover-ups by the police force themselves. A higher police official (Option A) may conduct an internal departmental inquiry, but the official legal inquest must be independent. Medical examiners (Option C) and Coroners (Option D) are systems used in other countries like the US or UK, but in India, the role is filled by Magistrates or the Police. This mandatory judicial oversight is fundamental to the rule of law and the protection of the constitutional rights of individuals, even those who have been lawfully detained

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following dosage regimens for the adult leprosy treatment kit is incorrect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rifampicin 450 mg weekly

According to the WHO-recommended Multi-Drug Therapy (MDT) for leprosy, the incorrect dosage for adults is Rifampicin 450 mg weekly, as the correct dose is 600 mg once a month.

Leprosy, caused by Mycobacterium leprae, is treated using Multi-Drug Therapy (MDT), recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO). The treatment regimen depends on the classification of the disease.

Paucibacillary (PB) leprosy, which involves fewer skin lesions and a lower bacterial load, is treated with rifampicin (600 mg once a month) and dapsone (100 mg daily) for six months.

Multibacillary (MB) leprosy, which has widespread lesions and a higher bacterial load, is treated with rifampicin (600 mg once a month), clofazimine, 300 mg once a month (Option D)+ 50 mg daily(Option B), and dapsone (100 mg daily) for 12 months. These drugs help kill the bacteria, prevent resistance, and reduce transmission.

Early diagnosis and treatment adherence are crucial to preventing complications, disability, and further transmission of the disease. MDT is provided free of cost through national leprosy programs worldwide, ensuring patient accessibility. Along with antibiotics, supportive care such as wound care, physiotherapy, and management of nerve damage are essential in preventing deformities and disability. Corticosteroids may be used in cases of lepra reactions to manage inflammation and nerve damage. With proper treatment and early intervention, leprosy is completely curable, reducing the risk of long-term complications.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Substances and the type of transport across a membrane are given below, choose the correct combination:

1. Oxygen: Simple diffusion
2. Glucose: Facilitated diffusion
3. Sodium: Voltage-gated channel
4. Sodium: Secondary active transport
5. Calcium: Active transport
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 are correct

All the given combinations 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 are correct.

1) Oxygen is a non-polar molecule and hence can diffuse across the lipid membrane of the cells.

2) Facilitated diffusion - Transporting the molecule from one side of the cell membrane to the other is done with the help of transport proteins called carriers. Molecules move from areas of high concentration to areas of low concentration. No energy input is required when carrier proteins move substances in the direction of their gradients. Glucose transport by the glucose transporter is an example, which moves glucose down its concentration gradient from the ECF to the cytoplasm of the cell.

3) Voltage-gated channels are simple ion channels acting as transport proteins, gated by membrane potential alterations. Sodium transported via voltage-gated channels is an example.

4) Transporting more than one substance together using a single transport protein against the gradient is known as secondary active transport. An example is SGLT 1, the cotransporter of sodium and glucose from the intestinal lumen into mucosal cells.

5)Active transport - Transporting of substances against the gradients, and requires energy. Ca2+ ATPase that pumps out calcium out of the cells is an example.
questions.learning: 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 are correct All the given combinations 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 are correct. 1) Oxygen is a non-polar molecule and hence can diffuse across the lipid membrane of the cells.

questions.text: Which of the following occur during the beginning cough reflex?
options: Forced expiration against a closed glottis
Forced expiration against an open glottis
Forced inspiration against a closed glottis
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Forced expiration against a closed glottis

| Phase | Event

| ----- | -----

| Inspiratory phase | Deep inspiration

| Compression phase | Forced expiration against closed glottis

| Expulsive phase | Sudden opening of glottis → explosive airflow

The cough reflex begins with deep inspiration followed by closure of the glottis.

This is followed by forced expiration against a closed glottis, generating high intrathoracic pressure.

Sudden opening of the glottis then expels air explosively to clear irritants.

Hence, forced expiration against a closed glottis marks the beginning of the cough reflex.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The diagram below shows the pressure-volume curves for 3 different lungs. Which of the following is the best representation of compliance between the three lungs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. B>A>C

• The pressure-volume relationship is the fundamental relation between the work of breathing and lung mechanics.
• The diagram depicts the change in volume with respect to the change in intrapleural pressure, which is compliance. Here, the change is more (steep curve) with B and least (flat curve) with C.
• The “stiffer” lung displays a more horizontal curve (C), meaning that it takes a greater pressure to achieve the same inflation volume compared with a normal lung (A). These lungs are called less compliant.
• Curve (B) is more compliant as it takes lesser pressure to achieve the same inflation volume compared to normal (A).

Applied aspect:

Compliance is increased in emphysema. The mechanism is shown in the flow chart below.

Compliance is decreased in case of pulmonary edema or fibrosis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: At what stage does secondary postpartum hemorrhage occur?
options: Shortly after the delivery of placenta
questions.explanation: Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is classified based on the timing of the bleeding after childbirth. Primary PPH refers to excessive bleeding that occurs within the first 24 hours of delivery (Options A, B, and D). In contrast, secondary postpartum hemorrhage is defined as excessive vaginal bleeding that occurs between 24 hours and 12 weeks after delivery (Option C). The most common causes of secondary PPH include retained products of conception, subinvolution of the placental site, and infection (endometritis). Recognizing this distinction is vital because primary PPH is often managed with aggressive uterotonics like oxytocin for atony, while secondary PPH frequently requires investigations like ultrasound to rule out retained tissue and may necessitate antibiotics or evacuation. Therefore, the 24-hour mark is the critical clinical threshold for the definition of "secondary" hemorrhage
questions.learning: Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is classified based on the timing of the bleeding after childbirth. Primary PPH refers to excessive bleeding that occurs within the first 24 hours of delivery (Options A, B, and D).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient presents to the casualty with a chronic dry cough with no fever or other associated symptoms. He had recently been started on an antihypertensive for hypertension. Which among the following is most likely responsible to cause these symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bradykinin and substance P

Chronic dry cough is a common adverse effect of Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme inhibitor that occurs due to the accumulation of bradykinin, substance P, or prostaglandins in the lungs.

ACE has structural similarities to another enzyme called kininase. Kininase normally metabolizes bradykinin, substance P, and prostaglandins. ACE inhibitors when administered also block kininase enzymes which results in an increase in the concentration of these substrates. An increase in the level of bradykinin/ substance P levels results in persistent brassy cough and angioedema in the patients.

Adverse effects of ACE inhibitors:

* Hypotension: care should be undertaken in patients who are on multiple antihypertensive drugs or have congestive heart failure.

* Cough: dry cough due to the accumulation of bradykinin, substance P, or prostaglandins, once they are stopped symptoms disappear after around 4 days.

* Hyperkalemia: in renal insufficiency, diabetes, or patients taking K+ sparing diuretics.

* Acute renal failure: In patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis, heart failure, diuretics use.

* Angioedema: rapid swelling in the nose, throat, mouth, glottis, larynx, lips, or tongue. It is an emergency and treatment is by protecting the airway and administering epinephrine, glucocorticoids, and antihistamines.

* Fetal abnormalities mostly in the 3rd trimester of pregnancy, cause renal developmental defects.

* Others: Skin rashes, dysgeusia, neutropenia, glycosuria, anemia, hepatotoxicity,

questions.text: Which of the following is not a contraindication for the induction of labor? (NEET PG 2019)
options: History of lower transverse cesarean section in last two pregnancies
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Heart disease

Induction of labor is contraindicated when vaginal delivery would pose significant maternal or fetal risk.

Contraindications include:

• Pelvic tumors obstructing the birth canal
• Active genital herpes infection
• Multiple previous cesarean sections with risk of uterine rupture
• Placenta previa
• Transverse fetal lie

Heart disease is not an absolute contraindication to induction of labor. In many cardiac conditions:

• Vaginal delivery is preferred over cesarean section
• Carefully monitored induction may be performed to reduce maternal stress and hemodynamic instability

A prior low transverse cesarean scar may allow trial of labor in selected cases, but repeated scars increase rupture risk.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old HIV-positive man presents with fever for 3 weeks, dry cough, and significant weight loss. He complains of retrosternal chest pain that is worse on inspiration. His chest X-ray is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia

The most likely diagnosis in a case of pneumonia in a HIV positive patient, along with the presence of fever, and non-productive cough with radiographic findings of diffuse interstitial infiltrates and symmetric perihilar involvement is Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP). A characteristic feature of PCP is retrosternal chest pain, which worsens on inspiration and is described as sharp or burning.

It is important to note that even though the incidence of PCP is the highest at CD4+ counts of <200/μL (80%), it can be seen in patients with higher counts.

Other options:

Option D: Tuberculosis (TB) should be considered as a possibility in cases of pneumonia in people living with HIV. However, the absence of hilar lymph node involvement, non-productive cough, and no extrapulmonary (pleural, pericardial, lymphatic) features are not consistent with tuberculosis.

TB can occur at any stage of HIV infection. In the early stages, pulmonary TB appears typically with upper-lobe infiltrates and cavitation. In advanced HIV infection, with CD4+ T-cell count below 200/μL, TB presents with diffuse interstitial infiltrates, minimal cavitation, pleural effusion, and lymphadenopathy. Extrapulmonary TB is fairly common in HIV, with it being documented in 40-60% of cases.

Option A: Staphylococcal pneumonia most commonly presents with a productive cough, and radiologically presents with pneumatoceles (cavitations)

Option B: Patients with pneumococcal pneumonia also present with fever, dyspnea, and productive cough. Imaging usually shows lobar involvement.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: In a fasting state, glucagon promotes the production of glucose by which of the following pathways?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis

The source of blood glucose in a fasting state is Gluconeogenesis and Glycogenolysis. It is promoted by glucagon.

The first stage of fasting: The fasting state begins two to four hours after the absorptive/well-fed state. In early fasting i.e; 4-18 hours after the well-fed state, the blood glucose level is maintained by hepatic glycogenolysis. The glycogen stores are sufficient for around 18 hours after a meal following which they start to deplete. So the source of blood glucose in a person fasting for 11 hours will be liver glycogenolysis.

Second stage of fasting: Gluconeogenesis begins 4–6 hours after the last meal but becomes fully active only after stores of liver glycogen are depleted (after 18 hours). They can serve as a source of glucose for up to 2 days.

Substrates for gluconeogenesis are:

* Glucogenic amino acids ( mainly alanine) from the muscle and

* Glycerol from adipose tissue

During fasting, the glucogenic amino acids are transported to the liver, transaminated into pyruvate, and converted to glucose.

Third stage of fasting:

* Lipolysis occurs in the adipose tissue due to the activity of hormone-sensitive lipase, stimulated by increased glucagon: insulin ratio.

* Free fatty acids are the source of energy in this stage and not glucose. Triacylglycerols will be hydrolyzed to fatty acids and glycerol.

* Beta oxidation of fatty acids takes place which provides acetyl CoA.

* In prolonged starvation (>3 days), acetyl CoA is converted to ketone bodies in the liver which will act as the main fuel source for skeletal and heart muscle and can meet up to 20% of the brain’s energy needs.

Final stage of fasting: After several weeks of starvation, ketone body synthesis will not take place due to depleted triacylglycerol stores. Proteins remain the only source of fuel. Protein degradation increases, and death results from a loss of heart, liver, or kidney function.

Role of insulin and glucagon:

When blood glucose falls during fasting, there is increased secretion of glucagon and decreased release of insulin. Hence glucagon: insulin ratio is increased.

Effects of increased glucagon: insulin ratio on enzymes of glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis:

* It activates glycogen phosphorylase, the key enzyme of glycogenolysis, and deactivates glycogen synthase. This causes a rapid mobilization of liver glycogen stores to be utilized as fuel.

* It favors the synthesis of glucose-6-phosphatase which converts glucose-6-phosphate to glucose. The resulting glucose is used by red blood cells (lack mitochondria) and the brain as they are largely dependent on glucose in the fasting state.

* Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase and fructose-1, 6-bisphosphatase are induced, leading to increased gluconeogenesis.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 14-year-old boy is reported by his neighbour to the police for repeated aggressive activities including beating up children in neighbourhood. The boy’s neighbour also noticed that he snorts heroin sometimes. He will be categorized legally as suffering from:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Juvenile delinquency

To differentiate psychiatric diagnoses of childhood behavioral disorders from legal terminology. Antisocial or criminal behavior committed by a minor is categorized as juvenile delinquency, irrespective of whether the child may also meet criteria for a psychiatric disorder or substance-use disorder.

The question specifically asks how the 14-year-old is categorized legally, not psychiatrically.

• A. Oppositional defiant disorder: A psychiatric diagnosis characterized by persistent defiant, hostile, and disobedient behavior toward authority figures.
• B. Conduct disorder: A psychiatric disorder involving repetitive violation of the rights of others and societal norms.
• C. Juvenile delinquency: Correct. Repeated antisocial or criminal behavior committed by a person below the legally defined age of adulthood is termed juvenile delinquency.
• D. Drug addiction: Describes substance dependence/use disorder and does not represent the legal categorization asked here.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which part of the placenta is shown in this picture?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fetal side

Fetal side of the placenta is depicted in the picture.

Placenta has two components - basal plate (the one on the maternal side) and chorionic plate (the one towards the fetal side which gives rise to the chorionic villi).

Usually, in a normal placenta, both basal and chorionic plates end simultaneously at the margin of the placenta.

The fetal surface, known as the chorionic plate, creates the roof of the intervillous space and is covered by the amnion, a thin avascular membrane. This plate contains chorionic vessels that branch from the umbilical vessels and is composed of distinct layers including the amniotic epithelium, connective tissue layer, primary stem villi containing fetal vessels, and both cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast layers. This complex arrangement facilitates the crucial transfer of nutrients and gases between mother and fetus.

The placental structure, from the maternal aspect, begins with the basal plate which forms the maternal floor of the intervillous space (Option B). This critical interface contains multiple components arranged in layers, including the decidual layer (composed of decidual cells from the endometrium) (Option A), the fibrinoid or Nitabuch's layer (containing fibrin deposits marking the boundary between maternal and fetal tissues), and the cytotrophoblastic shell. The basal plate is characterized by grooves that create cotyledons and houses the spiral arteries and veins from maternal circulation, making it essential for maternal-fetal exchange  (Option D).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which occupational exposure is most strongly linked to the development of mesothelioma?
questions.explanation: Malignant mesothelioma is a rare cancer of the pleura, peritoneum, or pericardium that is almost exclusively associated with asbestos exposure. Inhaled asbestos fibers lodge in the pleura, causing chronic inflammation and eventual malignant transformation over a long latency period of 20–40 years. Silica dust (Option B) causes silicosis and increases the risk of tuberculosis and lung cancer but is not a primary driver of mesothelioma. Cotton dust (Option C) is linked to byssinosis, an obstructive lung disease known as "Monday fever". Coal dust (Option D) results in coal workers' pneumoconiosis or "black lung". While asbestos is also the most common cause of general lung carcinoma, mesothelioma is its most "specific" neoplastic complication. High-risk occupations include shipbuilding, insulation manufacturing, and mining

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: At which volume or capacity, pressure measured at the upper airway becomes zero?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Functional residual capacity

Pressure measured at the upper airway becomes zero at functional residual capacity.

The curve of airway pressure obtained is plotted against the volume, which is the pressure-volume curve of the total respiratory system. This curve is used in understanding the fundamental relationship between the compliance of the lungs and the chest wall. It is measured by a spirometer.

The functional residual capacity is the volume of the air that remains in the lungs after normal expiration. The normal value is about 2.5 liters. At the lung volume of functional residual capacity (FRC), which is the relaxed state of the lungs, the pressure inside the lungs is effectively zero.

Other options:

Option A: Residual volume is the air left in the lungs after a maximal expiratory effort.

Option C: Total lung capacity is the sum of tidal volume, inspiratory reserve volume, expiratory reserve volume, and residual volume.

Option D: Inspiratory capacity is the maximum amount of air inspired from the end-expiratory level. It is the sum of tidal volume and inspiratory reserve volume.
questions.learning: Functional residual capacity Pressure measured at the upper airway becomes zero at functional residual capacity. The curve of airway pressure obtained is plotted against the volume, which is the pressure-volume curve of the total respiratory system.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text:
Which of the following can be considered as effective CPR?

1. Respiratory rate: 20 - 24 breaths per minute.

2. Chest compressions: 100-120/min.

3. Allow complete chest recoil.

4. 5-6 cm depression.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 2, 3, and 4

The ideal rescue breath rate for adults is 10 breaths/min, while in infants and children up to puberty it is 20-30 breaths/min. As the person's age group is not specified in the question, assuming an adult, statement 1 is incorrect, while 2, 3, and 4 are correct.

Effective chest compression in adults:

• Provide 100-120 compressions per minute (30 compressions for every 15-18 sec).
• Place your arms, one over the other in the midline, on the lower 1/3rd of the patient's sternum, and lock your arms.
• Use both arms to press the chest to a depth of 5-6 cm (2 - 2.4 inches) or more.
• Press hard and fast
• Allow for full chest recoil after every compression.

Effective chest compressions in a child older than 1 year and up to puberty:

• The compression rate is 100 - 120/min  (30 compressions for every 15-18 sec).
• One or both palms are placed in the midline.
• The depth of compression is 2 inches.
• Press hard and fast
• Allow for full chest recoil after every compression.

Effective chest compressions in infants (<1 year):

• 100 to 120 compressions per minute (30 compressions for every 15-18 sec).
• One provider: Place two fingers, one between the nipple line and the other 1 cm below.
• Two providers: Encircle the infant's torso with both hands with both thumbs pointing cephalic positioned 1cm below the nipples over the sternum.
• Depth of compressions should be at least 1.5 inches or 1/3 the depth of the infant’s chest.
• Press hard and fast
• Allow for full chest recoil after every compression.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Under which name (brand) does the National AIDS Control Organisation provide the STI/RTI services?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Suraksha Clinic

The National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO) provides Sexually Transmitted Infection (STI) and Reproductive Tract Infection (RTI) services through designated Suraksha Clinics. These clinics offer confidential, accessible, and standardized diagnosis, treatment, counselling, partner management, and referral services to reduce STI transmission and prevent HIV infection.

• Brand name for NACO STI/RTI services: Suraksha Clinic
• Services provided:

• Syndromic diagnosis and treatment of STIs/RTIs
• HIV counselling and testing referral
• Condom promotion
• Partner notification and treatment
• Health education and counselling

• Syndromic management is the cornerstone of STI management under NACO, especially at peripheral health facilities.
• Colour-coded STI/RTI drug kits (Kit 1–7) are used for standardized syndromic treatment.
questions.learning: Suraksha Clinic — The National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO) provides Sexually Transmitted Infection (STI) and Reproductive Tract Infection (RTI) services through designated Suraksha Clinics.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In which of the following conditions is the following clinical finding seen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anterior cranial fossa fracture

The image shows bilateral periorbital ecchymoses, which is called the panda sign, and it is seen in anterior cranial fossa fractures. It is also known as panda eyes/raccoon eyes.

Anterior cranial fossa fracture occurs due to direct impact. It is a contrecoup injury that occurs when there is a direct blow to the chin (in boxing). The impact is transmitted to the maxilla and base of the skull and results in a contrecoup fracture of the cribriform plate of the ethmoid. It presents with CSF rhinorrhea and periorbital hematoma or raccoon eyes and the image is shown below.

The pooling of blood surrounding the eyes is most commonly associated with fractures of the anterior cranial fossa. This finding is typically not present during the initial evaluation.  It is delayed by 1 to 3 days. If bilateral, this finding is highly predictive of a basilar skull fracture.
questions.learning: Anterior cranial fossa fracture — The image shows bilateral periorbital ecchymoses, which is called the panda sign, and it is seen in anterior cranial fossa fractures.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is the best screening investigation for metabolic disorders?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tandem mass spectrometry

Tandem mass spectrometry (MS) is the technique of choice for screening neonates for inherited metabolic diseases.

Tandem MS employs the equivalent of two mass spectrometers linked in series (MS-MS or MS2). It can be used to screen blood samples from newborns for the presence and concentrations of amino acids, fatty acids, and other metabolites.

Abnormalities in metabolite levels indicate inherited metabolic diseases, such as phenylketonuria, ethylmalonic encephalopathy, and glutaric acidemia type 1.
questions.learning: Tandem mass spectrometry Tandem mass spectrometry (MS) is the technique of choice for screening neonates for inherited metabolic diseases. Tandem MS employs the equivalent of two mass spectrometers linked in series (MS-MS or MS2).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presents with a neck swelling that moves with deglutition and undergoes surgical excision. Postoperatively, she is unable to raise the pitch of her voice. Which nerve is most likely injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. External laryngeal nerve

The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (external laryngeal nerve) is closely related to the superior thyroid artery and is therefore at risk during thyroid surgery. It supplies the cricothyroid muscle, the only tensor of the vocal cords. Injury to this nerve results in inability to tense and elongate the vocal cords, causing difficulty producing high-pitched sounds, voice fatigue, and reduced vocal projection, while normal speech may remain relatively preserved.

Why not the other options?

• A. Internal laryngeal nerve: Provides sensory innervation above the vocal cords. Injury causes loss of supraglottic sensation and an increased risk of aspiration but does not affect pitch.
• C. Recurrent laryngeal nerve: Supplies all intrinsic muscles of the larynx except the cricothyroid. Injury causes hoarseness, weak/breathy voice, and vocal cord paralysis; bilateral injury may lead to airway obstruction and stridor.
• D. Glossopharyngeal nerve: Supplies the stylopharyngeus muscle, sensation to the posterior one-third of the tongue, and afferent limb of the gag reflex; it is not responsible for pitch control.
questions.learning: External laryngeal nerve — The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (external laryngeal nerve) is closely related to the superior thyroid artery and is therefore at risk during thyroid surgery.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A young female presented with complaints of lower abdominal pain, vaginal discharge, history of IUCD use for last 3–4 years. On examination, the patient had fever, adnexal/cervical motion tenderness and increased ESR and C-reactive protein. What is the probable clinical diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Acute PID

Acute Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) is an ascending polymicrobial infection of the upper female genital tract, involving the uterus, fallopian tubes, ovaries, and pelvic peritoneum. The patient has the classical features:

• Lower abdominal pain
• Vaginal discharge
• Long-term IUCD use (risk factor)
• Fever
• Cervical motion tenderness and adnexal tenderness
• Raised ESR and CRP indicating inflammation

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Ectopic pregnancy: Usually presents with amenorrhea, abdominal pain, and vaginal bleeding. Pregnancy should always be excluded with a β-hCG test, but vaginal discharge and cervical motion tenderness with inflammatory markers favor PID.
• B. Acute appendicitis: Typically causes right iliac fossa pain, anorexia, nausea, and localized peritoneal signs without vaginal discharge or cervical motion tenderness.
• C. Diverticulitis: Usually occurs in older patients, presenting with left lower quadrant pain, fever, and bowel symptoms rather than gynecological findings.
questions.learning: Acute PID Acute Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) is an ascending polymicrobial infection of the upper female genital tract, involving the uterus, fallopian tubes, ovaries, and pelvic peritoneum.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following amino acids, which is categorized as a nonessential amino acid?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Proline

Amino acids are classified as essential and nonessential based on whether they can be synthesized by the human body.

• Essential amino acids must be obtained from the diet.
• Nonessential amino acids can be synthesized in sufficient amounts by the body.

Proline is a nonessential amino acid because it is synthesized from glutamate in the body. It is important for collagen synthesis and wound healing.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Leucine: Essential, branched-chain amino acid (BCAA).
• B. Threonine: Essential amino acid.
• C. Tryptophan: Essential amino acid; precursor of serotonin, melatonin, and niacin (vitamin B3).
questions.learning: Proline Amino acids are classified as essential and nonessential based on whether they can be synthesized by the human body. • Essential amino acids must be obtained from the diet. • Nonessential amino acids can be synthesized in sufficient amounts by the…

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following should not be prescribed with theophylline?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Erythromycin

Erythromycin should not be prescribed with theophylline.

Theophylline is mainly metabolized by CYP1A2 in the liver. Erythromycin inhibits CYP1A2 and thereby decreases the clearance of theophylline.

Factors decreasing the clearance of theophylline are:

• Drugs - erythromycin, cimetidine, ciprofloxacin, allopurinol, fluvoxamine, zileuton, zafirlukast
• Congestive heart failure
• Liver disease
• Pneumonia
• Viral infection and vaccination
• High-carbohydrate diet
• Old age
questions.learning: Erythromycin Erythromycin should not be prescribed with theophylline. Theophylline is mainly metabolized by CYP1A2 in the liver.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Antimicrobial combinations are used in all except
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gonorrhea

Gonorrhea is not managed by antimicrobial combinations. According to the latest CDC guidelines, single-agent therapy with ceftriaxone is the preferred treatment for gonococcal infections.

Single-dose of 500mg intramuscular(IM) ceftriaxone is given for gonorrhea. It is important to note that the previous guidelines that recommended dual therapy with ceftriaxone and azithromycin are no longer preferred.

Monotherapy with ceftriaxone is given when concurrent chlamydia infection is ruled out by molecular testing. If this is not done then presumptive treatment for chlamydia should be given along with the treatment of gonorrhea. According to CDC guidelines, 100mg doxycycline twice daily for 7 days is given as presumptive treatment of chlamydia in nonpregnant individuals.

Other options:

Tuberculosis: Multidrug therapy is given in tuberculosis for proper cure and to prevent the selection of drug-resistant mutants. ATT regimen is given in detail in the pearl attached.

Intraabdominal infections: It is usually polymicrobial and can result in an intraabdominal abscess or secondary peritonitis. These are managed with either single-agent or combination therapy. Broad-spectrum agents with gram-negative cover such as meropenem or piperacillin-tazobactam can be used alone. Combination therapy with metronidazole and other agents like ciprofloxacin, cefepime, etc are used as empirical agents in intraabdominal infections.

Malaria: It is also treated with antimicrobial combinations. In plasmodium vivax and ovale malaria, schizontocides like chloroquine are combined with agents that attack the hypnozoites like primaquine for radical cure. Primaquine is also given in combination with Artemisinin combined therapy(ACT) for plasmodium falciparum infections as a gametocidal agent. Treatment regimens are given in the pearl attached.
questions.learning: Gonorrhea Gonorrhea is not managed by antimicrobial combinations. According to the latest CDC guidelines, single-agent therapy with ceftriaxone is the preferred treatment for gonococcal infections.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the ideal time for umbilical cord clamping after birth?
questions.explanation: Current global and Indian clinical guidelines recommend delayed cord clamping (DCC), performed between 1 and 3 minutes after the birth of the baby. DCC allows for the transfer of approximately of placental blood to the newborn, which significantly increases neonatal iron stores and hemoglobin levels, reducing the risk of anemia later in infancy. Immediate clamping (Option A) or clamping within 30 seconds (Option B) is now reserved for specific emergencies where immediate maternal or neonatal resuscitation is required. Clamping more than 3 minutes after birth (Option D) does not provide significant additional benefit and may complicate the timing of active management of the third stage of labor. In preterm infants, DCC is particularly beneficial as it reduces the need for blood transfusions and decreases the incidence of intraventricular hemorrhage. Therefore, the "ideal" window for physiological benefit is the 1–3 minute mark
questions.learning: Current global and Indian clinical guidelines recommend delayed cord clamping (DCC), performed between 1 and 3 minutes after the birth of the baby. DCC allows for the transfer of approximately of placental blood to the newborn, which significantly…

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 1½-year-old child presents to the emergency department with breathlessness, cough, cold, and a temperature below 37 °C. On examination, the respiratory rate is 46 breaths per minute, and there are no signs of chest indrawing or other danger signs. What is the most appropriate management for this child?
options: Administer IV antibiotics and refer to a higher center
Administer oral antibiotics, warn of danger signs, and send home
questions.explanation: According to the IMCI (Integrated Management of Childhood Illness) guidelines, the classification of pneumonia depends on the respiratory rate and presence of "danger signs". For a child aged 12–59 months, fast breathing is defined as a respiratory rate 40 breaths per minute. Since this 18-month-old child has a rate of 46 but NO chest indrawing or other danger signs, they are classified as having "Pneumonia" (not "Severe Pneumonia"). The appropriate management for non-severe pneumonia is treatment with oral antibiotics (typically amoxicillin) for 5 days. The child can be managed at home (Option C) after the mother is taught about danger signs that require immediate return. IV antibiotics (Options A and B) are reserved for "Severe Pneumonia" where there is chest indrawing or inability to drink. Home remedies alone (Option D) are insufficient for bacterial pneumonia
questions.learning: According to the IMCI (Integrated Management of Childhood Illness) guidelines, the classification of pneumonia depends on the respiratory rate and presence of "danger signs".

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: The first step in the management of a hemodynamically stable patient with the following rhythm is_____________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Intravenous Amiodarone

Intravenous Amiodarone is the first step in the management of a hemodynamically stable patient with a rhythm strip showing ventricular tachycardia. The above EKG shows rapid heart rate (>100 bpm), regular rhythm, wide complex QRS (>120 ms), all QRS complexes are similar (monomorphic). This EKG diagnostic of a sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT).

Intravenous amiodarone is recommended by the AHA/ACC 2015 guidelines for the treatment of hemodynamically stable ventricular tachycardia.

Chest compressions are the first step in unresponsive patients without a pulse.

Synchronized cardioversion is the treatment of choice for hemodynamically unstable patients (hypotension, respiratory distress, altered sensorium) with ventricular tachycardia.

Carotid massage is contraindicated in ventricular tachycardia.

Note: IV Lidocaine / IV Procainamide can also be used if amiodarone is unavailable in the above scenario depicted in the question.
questions.learning: Intravenous Amiodarone Intravenous Amiodarone is the first step in the management of a hemodynamically stable patient with a rhythm strip showing ventricular tachycardia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient presents with swelling in MCP joints and his serum uric acid levels were increased.The doctor prescribed a medicine which is considered as the first line agent in the management of this condition. What is the mechanism of this drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Xanthine oxidase inhibitor

Allopurinol is recommended as the first-line urate-lowering agent in all patients with gout. It is a purine antimetabolite and an inhibitor of xanthine oxidase enzyme.

It prevents the conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid reducing plasma uric acid levels. Allopurinol is also a substrate for xanthine oxidase. The metabolite of allopurinol called oxypurinol is a non-competitive inhibitor of xanthine oxidase.

Febuxostat is a uric acid synthesis inhibitor that acts by inhibiting the enzyme xanthine oxidase and it is indicated in gout management.

Both Febuxostat and Allopurinol are Xanthine Oxidase inhibitors, of which Allopurinol is a hypoxanthine analog.
questions.learning: Xanthine oxidase inhibitor Allopurinol is recommended as the first-line urate-lowering agent in all patients with gout. It is a purine antimetabolite and an inhibitor of xanthine oxidase enzyme.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 32-year-old male chronic smoker presents with pain in the fingers for a few months. On examination, gangrenous ulcers were present in the fingers as shown below. Investigations showed blood glucose and lipid profile within normal limits. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Buerger's disease

The above clinical vignette along with the image is suggestive of Buerger's disease or thromboangitis obliterans (TAO).

A young male smoker, presenting with chronic pain, with no history of diabetes and hyperlipidemia and gangrenous ulcers as shown in the image are points in favor of Buerger's disease.

Buerger's disease is a nonatherosclerotic segmental inflammatory occlusive vascular disorder involving small and medium-sized arteries of the upper and lower limb.

It is predominantly seen in young male smokers. Patients mainly present with claudication pain of extremities and later with ischemic rest pain and ulcers. Atherogenic conditions like diabetes and dyslipidemia should be excluded.

The following criteria must be met for the diagnosis of TAO:

* Age younger than 45 years

* History of tobacco use

* Distal extremity ischemia like claudication pain or ulcer

* Autoimmune diseases, hypercoagulable state, dyslipidemia, diabetes mellitus must be excluded

* Consistent arteriographic findings in the limbs

* A proximal source of atheroemboli must be excluded

Angiography shows segmental occlusions as skip lesions of the small and medium-sized vessels with the formation of extensive collaterals around the occlusions. These are called corkscrew collaterals. These represent dilated vaso vasorm of the occluded vessels.

They may also present with pain, paraesthesia, and color changes of the digits of the hand and feet in response to cold and anxiety. The is called as Raynaud phenomenon.

The image below shows the Raynaud phenomenon in the digits of the hand.
