questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 42-year-old woman who works as a laborer presents with a visible, soft, and fluctuant swelling located anterior to the knee over the patella, accompanied by discomfort and difficulty in knee movements. MRI findings are provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: "Housemaid's knee" is the clinical term for prepatellar bursitis, which is the inflammation of the fluid-filled bursa located directly in front of the patella. It is caused by repetitive trauma or prolonged pressure from kneeling, making it common in laborers. The characteristic presentation is a soft, fluctuating swelling over the kneecap that causes discomfort during movement. A subdermal abscess (Option B) would be tender, red, and warm with pus accumulation rather than just fluid. Gout (Option C) typically causes intense inflammation within the joint itself, presenting with severe pain and redness. Rheumatoid arthritis (Option D) is a systemic autoimmune disease affecting joints symmetrically with stiffness and deformity. MRI findings in bursitis show a clear fluid-filled space anterior to the bone. This condition is distinct from "clergyman's knee," which involves the infrapatellar bursa
questions.learning: "Housemaid's knee" is the clinical term for prepatellar bursitis, which is the inflammation of the fluid-filled bursa located directly in front of the patella.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Saturnine gout is seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lead poisoning

Saturnine gout is seen in chronic lead intoxication or poisoning.

The features of saturnine gout are the same as primary gout but it affects the knee more than the first metatarsophalangeal joint and tophi rarely develop. Lead exposure should be suspected if a patient presents with the triad of:

• Saturnine gout
• Hypertension
• Renal insufficiency (renal failure and interstitial fibrosis)
questions.learning: Lead poisoning Saturnine gout is seen in chronic lead intoxication or poisoning. The features of saturnine gout are the same as primary gout but it affects the knee more than the first metatarsophalangeal joint and tophi rarely develop.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: During a medical ethics discussion, students learn about the unethical practice in which doctors and radiologists exchange payments for patient referrals for CT scans. What is this practice called?
questions.explanation: In medical ethics and forensics, the practice of a doctor receiving a kickback or "fee-splitting" payment from a consultant or facility for a patient referral is termed Dichotomy (Option A). This is considered a highly unethical practice as it compromises the physician's objectivity and may lead to unnecessary testing for financial gain. Medical maloccurrence (Option B) refers to an unexpected, adverse clinical outcome that occurs despite proper care. Criminal negligence (Option C) involves a gross disregard for human life or safety during medical treatment. Commission (Option D) is a general financial term but "Dichotomy" is the specific ethical term used in medical jurisprudence to describe this illegal splitting of fees. This practice is prohibited under the Indian Medical Council (Professional Conduct, Etiquette and Ethics) Regulations. Therefore, dichotomy is the definitive term for this referral-based kickback scheme
questions.learning: In medical ethics and forensics, the practice of a doctor receiving a kickback or "fee-splitting" payment from a consultant or facility for a patient referral is termed Dichotomy (Option A).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) reduce gastric acid secretion by acting on which specific target?
questions.explanation: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) such as omeprazole and pantoprazole suppress gastric acid secretion by irreversibly inhibiting the H⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump, also known as the gastric proton pump. This pump is located on the apical membrane of parietal cells and represents the final common pathway for hydrochloric acid secretion in the stomach. The H⁺/K⁺ ATPase exchanges intracellular hydrogen ions (H⁺) for extracellular potassium ions (K⁺). By blocking this exchange, PPIs effectively shut down acid production regardless of the stimulus (histamine, acetylcholine, or gastrin). Why the other options are incorrect: 1. H⁺/Cl⁻ ATPase: No such pump exists. 2. Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase: Maintains membrane potential in all cells; not involved in acid secretion. 3. Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ cotransporter: Found in the loop of Henle; target of loop diuretics. Thus, H⁺/K⁺ ATPase is the specific molecular target of PPIs
questions.learning: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) such as omeprazole and pantoprazole suppress gastric acid secretion by irreversibly inhibiting the H⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump, also known as the gastric proton pump.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following antimalarial drugs are commonly used for the clinical cure of malaria? a. Artemisinin b. Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine c. Chloroquine d. Primaquine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. a, b, c

Clinical cure of malaria refers to clearance of asexual erythrocytic forms responsible for symptoms.

Drugs used for clinical cure:

• Artemisinin (and ACTs) → rapidly clears parasitemia
• Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine → inhibits folate synthesis in parasites
• Chloroquine → effective against sensitive strains

Not used for clinical cure:

• Primaquine → acts on hepatic hypnozoites and gametocytes (used for radical cure and transmission blocking, not for treating acute blood-stage infection)
questions.learning: a, b, c Clinical cure of malaria refers to clearance of asexual erythrocytic forms responsible for symptoms. Drugs used for clinical cure: • Artemisinin (and ACTs) → rapidly clears parasitemia • Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine → inhibits folate synthesis in…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: When the fetal scalp becomes visible at the vulva, the maneuver performed to control delivery of the head and prevent perineal tears is the Ritgen’s maneuver.
questions.explanation: The image depicts the Ritgen maneuver, a clinical technique used during the second stage of labor when the fetal scalp is visible at the vulva (crowning). The clinician applies pressure through the perineum onto the fetal chin with one hand while the other hand controls the crowning vertex. The primary objective is to facilitate the slow, controlled delivery of the fetal head in a state of extension, thereby minimizing the risk of severe perineal tears. By ensuring the head emerges during the interval between contractions, the maneuver protects the maternal pelvic floor. Loveset’s maneuver (Option B) is used for delivering the arms in a breech presentation. Pinard maneuver (Option C) is utilized to bring down a leg in a frank breech. The Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit maneuver (Option D) is employed for the delivery of the after-coming head in breech. Therefore, given the visual of head crowning and the specific protective hand placement shown, Ritgen maneuver is the correct identification for this obstetric procedure
questions.learning: The image depicts the Ritgen maneuver, a clinical technique used during the second stage of labor when the fetal scalp is visible at the vulva (crowning).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: If an individual has visual acuity worse than 3/60 but better than 1/60 in the better eye, along with a visual field restricted to less than 10° around the central fixation, how should this level of visual impairment be classified?
questions.explanation: Visual impairment is classified based on visual acuity in the better eye with best possible correction and visual field. According to standard public health definitions used in India and by the WHO, social blindness refers to a level of vision where a person has visual acuity worse than 6/60 but equal to or better than 1/60, or a visual field restricted to less than 10° around central fixation. In the given case, the individual has: 1. Visual acuity worse than 3/60 but better than 1/60, and 2. Visual field < 10° These findings clearly fall within the category of social blindness, as both the acuity and field criteria match this classification. Other options are incorrect: (B) Economic blindness is not a standard WHO classification. (C) Curable blindness refers to cause, not severity. (D) Manifest blindness is not a recognized classification term
questions.learning: Visual impairment is classified based on visual acuity in the better eye with best possible correction and visual field. According to standard public health definitions used in India and by the WHO, social blindness refers to a level of vision where a…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient with carcinoma endometrium is treated with pelvic external beam irradiation to the whole pelvis. Which of the following organs is most radiosensitive in the pelvic region?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ovary

Among the options most radiosensitive organ is ovary> rectum> bladder> vagina.

The radiation tolerance dose for the ovary is 2-3 Gy whereas the vagina 90 Gy.

The radiation dose necessary to induce ovarian failure is age-dependent. A single dose of 3-4 Gray can induce amenorrhea in almost all women >40 yrs of age. In young women, oogenesis is much less sensitive to radiation as compared to the elderly.

* Most radioresistant organ: Vagina

* Radiation most commonly affects the stratum basalis layer of the skin.
questions.learning: Ovary Among the options most radiosensitive organ is ovary> rectum> bladder> vagina. The radiation tolerance dose for the ovary is 2-3 Gy whereas the vagina 90 Gy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Shoulder dystocia is diagnosed when delivery of the anterior shoulder is delayed beyond how much time after the delivery of the fetal head?
questions.explanation: Shoulder dystocia is defined as a delivery that requires maneuvers beyond gentle traction to deliver the shoulders. A specific clinical criterion used is a head-to-body delivery time exceeding 60 seconds. It occurs when the anterior fetal shoulder impacts the maternal symphysis pubis. A key clinical indicator is the "turtle sign," where the fetal head retracts against the perineum. Options A, B, and C represent timeframes shorter than the standard diagnostic threshold. Management involves a sequential series of maneuvers, starting with the McRoberts maneuver, which involves hyperflexing the maternal thighs to increase the pelvic outlet. Suprapubic pressure is also applied to rotate the shoulder. If these fail, more invasive rotational maneuvers like Wood’s corkscrew or delivery of the posterior arm are attempted. This condition is an obstetric emergency due to the high risk of neonatal brachial plexus injury and maternal soft tissue lacerations
questions.learning: Shoulder dystocia is defined as a delivery that requires maneuvers beyond gentle traction to deliver the shoulders. A specific clinical criterion used is a head-to-body delivery time exceeding 60 seconds.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text:
Match the following:

1. Facial nerve
A. Shrugging of shoulder

2. Spinal accessory nerve
B. Taste from anterior two third of the tongue

3. Glossopharyngeal nerve
C. Taste from posterior one-third of the tongue

4. Mandibular nerve
D. Chewing
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1-B, 2-A, 3-C, 4-D

The correct match is as follows:

1. Facial nerve
B. Taste from anterior two third of the tongue

2. Spinal accessory nerve
A. Shrugging of shoulder

3. Glossopharyngeal nerve
C. Taste from posterior one-third of the tongue

4. Mandibular nerve
D. Chewing

Chorda tympani nerve which is a branch of facial nerve carries taste from anterior 2/3rd of the tongue.

The trapezius is innervated by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI). It causes retraction of scapula, shrugging of the shoulder and overhead abduction (along with serratus anterior). Paralysis of trapezius causes drooping of the shoulder and slight winging of the scapula (the superior angle of scapula becomes more prominent).

The glossopharyngeal nerve carries taste sensation from the posterior 1/3rd of the tongue.

The mandibular nerve (V3) is responsible for chewing movements as it gives motor supply to muscles of mastication. It contains both sensory and motor fibers.

• Sensory from

• Skin of cheek, over mandible and side of head
• Teeth of lower jaw and temporomandibular joint
• Mucous membrane of mouth and anterior part of tongue

• Motor to

• Muscles of mastication (pterygoids, masster and temporalis)
• Tensor tympani
• Anterior belly of digastric
• Mylohyoid

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 19-year-old unconscious female patient requires urgent neurosurgical treatment for hydrocephalus, but no relatives or attendants are available to provide identification or consent. In this situation, what should the doctor do?
options: Take consent by calling the relatives
questions.explanation: In medical ethics and law, the "Doctrine of Necessity" allows a physician to provide life-saving treatment to a patient who is unable to give consent due to an emergency condition (such as being unconscious). In this scenario, immediate neurosurgical intervention is necessary to prevent death or permanent disability from hydrocephalus. Therefore, the surgeon can and should "operate without consent". Waiting for relatives (Option B) or delaying for formal identification (Option A) would be a breach of the duty of care and could lead to medical negligence. Calling relatives (Option D) is ideal but should not delay the emergency procedure if they cannot be reached immediately. The doctor should document the situation clearly and seek a second opinion from another senior colleague if possible, but the priority is always to preserve life in an emergency where "implied consent" is assumed
questions.learning: In medical ethics and law, the "Doctrine of Necessity" allows a physician to provide life-saving treatment to a patient who is unable to give consent due to an emergency condition (such as being unconscious).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the pathology in the child.
questions.explanation: The image shows a soft swelling protruding directly through the navel, which is characteristic of an umbilical hernia. This condition occurs in children due to the incomplete closure of the umbilical ring through which abdominal contents can bulge. The protrusion typically becomes more apparent when the child cries or strains. Spigelian hernia (Option B) occurs laterally along the semilunar line and is very rare in children. Inguinal hernia (Option C) presents as a swelling in the groin or scrotum due to a patent processus vaginalis. Femoral hernia (Option D) appears below the inguinal ligament and is mostly seen in adult females. Most pediatric umbilical hernias close spontaneously by age 2 to 3 years and require only observation unless they persist or become symptomatic. Therefore, based on the anatomical site, umbilical hernia is the correct identification
questions.learning: The image shows a soft swelling protruding directly through the navel, which is characteristic of an umbilical hernia. This condition occurs in children due to the incomplete closure of the umbilical ring through which abdominal contents can bulge.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: An alcoholic patient presented with itchy lesions as shown in the image, He also has a red-colored beefy tongue. Which of the following histories would you like to additionally ask/ elicit in this patient?
options: Ask for diarrhea and history of memory loss
Ask for diarrhea, thiamine deficiency features, and detailed dietary history
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ask for diarrhea and history of memory loss

An alcoholic patient with a red-colored beefy tongue, itching and the characteristic Casal's necklace, shown in the image, is suggestive of pellagra. It is caused by niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency. Hence, one should ask for a history of diarrhea and memory loss in this case.

Pellagra presents with 4 Ds: Diarrhea, Dermatitis, Dementia, and if untreated, Death. Early symptoms of pellagra are loss of appetite, generalized weakness and irritability, abdominal pain, and vomiting. Photosensitive dermatitis is seen over sun-exposed areas. Diarrhea occurs due to proctitis or malabsorption. Bright red glossitis (beefy tongue) and Casal’s necklace (a pigmented, scaly skin rash that forms a ring around the neck) follow. Depressive psychosis and dementia also commonly occur.

Corn/ maize/ jowar based diets are the main causes of niacin deficiency. Corn/maize lacks niacin and tryptophan. The excess leucine in jowar and maize disrupts the conversion of tryptophan to niacin. Niacin deficiency is also seen in alcoholism. Hence, additional histories of diarrhea and memory loss will aid in supporting the diagnosis of pellagra (along with dietary history).

Treatment includes oral supplementation with 100–200 mg of nicotinamide or nicotinic acid three times daily for 5 days.

Option B: Thiamine deficiency (vitamin B1) features include CVS manifestations like heart failure and edema (wet beriberi), peripheral neuritis (dry beriberi), and Wernicke encephalopathy (in alcoholics).

Option C: Dermatitis seen in pellagra is due to dietary deficiency of niacin and so allergy history is not relevant.

Option D: Conjunctivitis is not a feature of niacin deficiency.
questions.learning: Ask for diarrhea and history of memory loss — An alcoholic patient with a red-colored beefy tongue, itching and the characteristic Casal's necklace, shown in the image, is suggestive of pellagra.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which ligament connects medial cuneiform to the base of the 2nd metatarsal?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Lisfranc

The Lisfranc ligament connects the medial cuneiform to the base of the 2nd metatarsal.

Lisfranc ligament is a cuneometatarsal interosseous ligament. It is the strongest ligament among the three cuneometatarsal interosseous ligaments. It passes from the lateral surface of the medial cuneiform to the adjacent angle of the second metatarsal bone.

Deformity of this ligament can lead to instability and deformity of the tarsometatarsal joint.

Other options:
Option A: Chopart's ligament is related to both calcaneocuboid and calcaneonavicular joints. It is a strong Y-shaped band, having a proximal stem and 2 distal limbs.

• The proximal limb is attached by a stem to the anterior part of the upper calcaneal surface.
• The distal limb divides into calcaneocuboid and calcaneonavicular parts.

Option B: Spring ligament also known as the plantar calcaneonavicular ligament connects the sustentaculum tali to the navicular. It ties the calcaneus to the navicular and maintains the medial longitudinal arch of the foot. It is made up of the superomedial calcaneonavicular portion and the inferior calcaneonavicular portion.

Option D: Deltoid ligament also called the medial collateral ligament is attached to the apex, anterior and posterior borders of the medial malleolus. It has 2 layers, superficial and deep:

• The superficial layer consists of tibionavicular fibres anteriorly, tibiocalcaneal fibres in the middle, and superficial posterior tibiotalar fibres posteriorly.
• Deep layer consists of anterior tibiotalar fibres, tibiocalcaneal in the middle and deep posterior tibiotalar posteriorly.
questions.learning: Lisfranc — The Lisfranc ligament connects the medial cuneiform to the base of the 2nd metatarsal. Lisfranc ligament is a cuneometatarsal interosseous ligament.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An 11-year-old presented with the following growth in the eye as shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Limbal dermoid

The image shows the presence of a limbal dermoid.

Limbal Dermoid is a choristoma (a mass of histologically normal tissue in an abnormal location). It consists of collagenous tissue containing dermal elements and covered by stratified squamous epithelium. Limbal dermoid present in early childhood as a subconjunctival mass in the infratemporal limbus. Treatment is indicated for chronic irritation, amblyopia, vision impairment and corneal dellen formation. Small dermoids can be excised, larger lesions may need lamellar keratosclerectomy.
questions.learning: Limbal dermoid — The image shows the presence of a limbal dermoid. Limbal Dermoid is a choristoma (a mass of histologically normal tissue in an abnormal location).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: True statement about intermittent claudication:
options: Most commonly felt in the calf muscles
Day to day distance is variable
Relived after getting out of bed
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Most commonly felt in the calf muscles

Intermittent claudication is most commonly felt in the calf muscles because of the involvement of the superficial femoral artery in chronic vascular occlusive disease.

Intermittent claudication:

• Intermittent claudication is the debilitating cramp-like pain felt in the leg muscles due to reduced blood flow and anaerobic metabolism brought on by peripheral arterial disease.
• It usually signifies mild to moderate chronic vascular occlusive disease
• The pain is brought on by walking (option D)
• Not present on taking the first step
• Relieved by rest in both the standing and sitting positions, usually within 5 minutes (option A).
• The distance that a patient is able to walk without stopping is known as claudication distance. It varies only slightly from day to day (option C).
• The superficial femoral artery (70%) is the most commonly affected artery by claudication and manifests as pain in the calf muscles.
• Aorto-iliac occlusion may cause thigh or buttock claudication. Leriche's syndrome occurs due to aortoiliac occlusion and presents with a triad of claudication, impotence, and absent femoral pulses.

Boyd's classification of claudication:

• Grade I: Patient complains of pain after walking. If the patient continues to walk, due to increased blood flow in muscle and opening of collaterals metabolites causing pain are washed away and the pain subsides.
• Grade II: Pain still persists on continuing to walk; but can walk with effort.
• Grade III: The patient has to take rest to relieve the pain.
questions.learning: Most commonly felt in the calf muscles Intermittent claudication is most commonly felt in the calf muscles because of the involvement of the superficial femoral artery in chronic vascular occlusive disease.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with a head injury opens their eyes in response to a loud voice, localizes pain, and is confused with disorientation. Based on these findings, what is the patient’s Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score?
questions.explanation: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) assesses three components: Eye-opening (E), Motor response (M), and Verbal response (V). "Eye-opening in response to a loud voice" corresponds to an E3 score (normal spontaneous opening is E4). "Pain localization" (moving the hand to the site of a noxious stimulus) corresponds to an M5 score (obeying commands is M6). "Confusion with disorientation" corresponds to a V4 score (fully oriented is V5). Therefore, the total GCS is . Option B, C, and D are incorrect based on these specific clinical findings. A GCS of 12 is classified as a "moderate" head injury. Patients with a GCS of 8 or less are considered "comatose" and typically require airway protection via endotracheal intubation. Consistent monitoring of the GCS is vital to detect early neurological deterioration in trauma patients
questions.learning: The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) assesses three components: Eye-opening (E), Motor response (M), and Verbal response (V). "Eye-opening in response to a loud voice" corresponds to an E3 score (normal spontaneous opening is E4).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Minimum number of antenatal visits according to WHO is ______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 8

According to WHO, the minimum number of antenatal visits should be 8.

Ideal number of antenatal visits is 12-14.

The ideal number of antenatal visits should be:

* Monthly visits upto 28 weeks

* Two weekly visits between 28-36 weeks

* Weekly visits from 36 weeks onwards

This means a total of 12-15 visits.

In the Indian scenario, according to MCH the suggested schedule is as follows and requires minimum of 4 visits:

* 1st visit: within 12 weeks preferably as soon as pregnancy is suspected, for the registration of pregnancy and 1st antenatal check-up.

* 2nd visit: between 14-26 weeks

* 3rd visit: between 28-34 weeks

* 4th visit: between 36 weeks and term

A booked case is one that has at least 3 antenatal visits, with two visits in the third trimester.
questions.learning: 8 According to WHO, the minimum number of antenatal visits should be 8. Ideal number of antenatal visits is 12-14.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: What is the mechanism of action of local anesthetics?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Block sodium channels

Local anesthetics primarily act by blocking the sodium channels bound to the membrane.

Sodium channels have one larger α subunit and one or two smaller β subunits. These voltage-gated sodium channels exist in 3 states :

* Resting (non conducting)

* Open (conducting) and

* Inactivated (non conducting)

The local anesthetics bind to the α subunit of sodium channels, thereby preventing their activation and inhibiting the influx of sodium.

Local anesthetics have a higher affinity for the sodium channels in open and inactivated state than in the resting state.

Local anesthetic inhibition is both voltage and frequency-dependent and is higher when nerve fibers are firing rapidly than with slow, infrequent depolarizations.

Note:

Local anesthetics may also bind and inhibit calcium, potassium, transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) and many other channels and receptors. But blocking of sodium channels is the best answer, of all the given options.

Amino ester
Amino amide

Relatively unstable in solution
Relatively more stable due to the presence of di-ortho methyl (methoxy) group

Metabolized by plasma cholinesterase

Exception: Cocaine is metabolized predominantly by hepatic carboxylesterase

Metabolized in the liver by amidase

Exception: Articaine is inactivated by plasma carboxylesterase.

Shorter-acting

Exception: Tetracaine is a long-acting amino ester.

Longer-acting

Exception: Articaine is a short-acting amino amide

High incidence of allergic reaction due to the metabolite PABA
The incidence of allergic reaction is rare

Eg:

• Procaine
• Chlorprocaine
• Cocaine
• Benzocaine
• Tetracaine

Eg:

• Lidocaine
• Mepivacaine
• Prilocaine
• Bupivacaine
• Ropivacaine

• Dibucaine

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child was brought with pedal edema and cheilosis. Further investigations revealed cardiomegaly. What is the vitamin deficiency associated with this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thiamine

Thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency leads to beriberi, which can present with both cardiac and peripheral manifestations. Types relevant here:

• Wet beriberi:

o    Cardiomegaly, high-output cardiac failure

o    Edema (pedal edema)

• Dry beriberi:

o    Peripheral neuropathy

Thiamine is a cofactor for key enzymes in energy metabolism:

• Pyruvate dehydrogenase
• α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
• Transketolase

Cheilosis: Though classically seen in riboflavin deficiency, it can coexist in malnutrition, but the cardiomegaly + edema strongly points to thiamine deficiency.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Riboflavin: Causes cheilosis and glossitis but not cardiomegaly
• Pyridoxine: Causes neuropathy and sideroblastic anemia
• Niacin: Causes pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia)

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of single-unit (visceral) smooth muscle?
options: Innervated by a single nerve ending per fiber
Fibers are connected via many gap junctions and contract as a syncytium
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fibers are connected via many gap junctions and contract as a syncytium

Single-unit (visceral) smooth muscle functions as a functional syncytium because the individual muscle fibers are electrically coupled by numerous gap junctions.

• Many gap junctions connect adjacent cells.
• Electrical activity spreads from cell to cell, so the muscle contracts as a coordinated unit (syncytium).
• Usually innervated by a few nerve fibers, not one nerve per cell.
• Often shows spontaneous rhythmic activity.

Examples:
• Gastrointestinal tract
• Uterus
• Urinary bladder
• Small blood vessels

Contrast with multiunit smooth muscle:
• Fibers act independently
• Few or no gap junctions
• Each fiber has individual innervation (e.g., iris, ciliary muscle).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old woman presents with persistent dry mouth and gritty sensation in the eyes, along with dental caries and enlarged cervical lymph nodes on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of xerostomia (dry mouth) and xerophthalmia (dry eyes, often described as "grittiness") is the hallmark clinical presentation of Sjogren syndrome. This chronic autoimmune disorder involves lymphocytic infiltration of the exocrine glands, particularly the salivary and lacrimal glands. Persistent dry mouth leads to complications like severe dental caries. Enlarged cervical lymph nodes (or parotid enlargement) are common features. MCTD (Option A) involves features of multiple autoimmune diseases but lacks the primary focus on exocrine sicca symptoms. Sarcoidosis (Option B) can cause sicca symptoms but is primarily characterized by non-caseating granulomas in the lungs. Wegener's granulomatosis (Option D) is a vasculitis affecting the respiratory tract and kidneys. Diagnosis of Sjogren is confirmed by anti-SSA (Ro) and anti-SSB (La) antibodies or a minor salivary gland biopsy. Treatment is primarily symptomatic, using artificial tears and lubricants, although immunosuppressants may be needed for systemic involvement. These patients have a significantly increased risk of developing B-cell lymphomas
questions.learning: The combination of xerostomia (dry mouth) and xerophthalmia (dry eyes, often described as "grittiness") is the hallmark clinical presentation of Sjogren syndrome.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 40-year-old patient presents with a history of mood disturbance, as illustrated in the accompanying image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The image shows a mood chart depicting 4 or more distinct mood episodes within 12 months, oscillating between mania and severe depression — the defining feature of Rapid Cycling Disorder. Key Diagnostic Features visible in chart: 1. 4+ episodes within 12 months 2. Swings between full mania and severe depression 3. Episodes separated by periods of normal mood 4. Meets DSM-5 criteria for rapid cycling specifier in Bipolar disorder Why other options are wrong: (A) Bipolar disorder is incorrect because while rapid cycling is a specifier of bipolar disorder, the chart specifically shows 4+ episodes in 12 months making rapid cycling the more precise and specific diagnosis here. (B) Dysthymia is incorrect because dysthymia presents as chronic, persistent mild depression lasting at least 2 years — no manic or hypomanic episodes occur, completely inconsistent with the mood chart shown. (D) Cyclothymia is incorrect because cyclothymia shows hypomanic and mild depressive episodes — never reaching full mania or severe depression thresholds. The chart clearly shows full manic and severe depressive episodes ruling out cyclothymia
questions.learning: The image shows a mood chart depicting 4 or more distinct mood episodes within 12 months, oscillating between mania and severe depression — the defining feature of Rapid Cycling Disorder.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: To establish the cause of death, a post-mortem examination was performed on an 82-year-old man. Histopathological evaluation of a cardiac tissue section revealed the presence of pigment deposition. What is the pigment shown in the image provided?
questions.explanation: Lipofuscin is a yellowish-brown, granular, autofluorescent pigment that accumulates in cells as a result of "wear and tear" or aging. It is composed of polymers of lipids and phospholipids complexed with protein, derived from the peroxidized lipids of subcellular membranes. In an 82-year-old man, its presence in cardiac myocytes is a normal finding of aging, often called "brown atrophy" of the heart. Melanin (Option A) is a black-brown pigment found in the skin or brain (substantia nigra) and is not typical for aging cardiac tissue. Hemosiderin (Option C) and Iron (Option D) would appear as golden-yellow but would stain bright blue with a Perl’s Prussian blue stain; they indicate iron overload (hemosiderosis), not simple aging. Lipofuscin is typically located in a perinuclear distribution, as seen in the slide. Therefore, given the patient's advanced age and the classic appearance of the pigment in the heart, Lipofuscin is the correct identification

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A boy presents with recurrent episodes of spontaneous nasal bleeding. Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the head is taken, which is shown below. Which of the following is not true regarding this patient's condition?
options: Biopsy is the investigation of choice
Blood supply is mostly from the external carotid artery.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Biopsy is the investigation of choice

The given clinical picture along with a CT scan showing the Holman-Miller sign is suggestive of nasopharyngeal angiofibroma commonly arising from the sphenopalatine foramen. The statement "Biopsy is the investigation of choice" is incorrect because in this condition, biopsy is avoided due to the risk of bleeding.

It is a benign tumor, which commonly arises from the sphenopalatine foramen. From here, the tumor grows into the:

* Nasal cavity

* Nasopharynx

* Pterygopalatine fossa

* Pterygomaxillary fossa

* Infratemporal fossa

Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a benign but locally invasive tumor predominant in adolescent males in the age group of 10-20 years. It arises from the posterior part of the nasal cavity that is close to the superior margin of the sphenopalatine foramen. These patients have a hamartomatous nidus of vascular tissue in the nasopharynx that forms angiofibroma when testosterone appears. Therefore, it is thought to be testosterone-dependent.

Angiofibroma can extend into the nasal cavity causing obstruction, epistaxis, paranasal sinuses, pterygomaxillary fossa, infratemporal fossa, cheek, orbits causing proptosis, frog-face deformity, and cranial cavity. The clinical features include:

* Profuse, recurrent, spontaneous epistaxis- most common

* Progressive nasal obstruction and denasal speech- due to mass in the postnasal space

* Conductive hearing loss and otitis media with effusion- due to obstruction of the eustachian tube

* Sessile, lobulated, or smooth mass in the nasopharynx

* Other clinical features include the broadening of the nasal bridge, proptosis, cheek swelling, involvement of IInd, IIIrd, IVth, and VIth cranial nerves

Diagnosis is based on the clinical picture. Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the head is the investigation of choice that reveals anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus (antral sign/Holman-Miller sign) which is pathognomonic of angiofibroma as shown below.

MRI can also be done that reveals soft tissue extensions. Carotid angiography is also done which shows the extent of the tumor with its vascularity. The feeding vessels mostly come from the external carotid artery. In large tumors with intracranial extension, vessels come from the internal carotid system also.

Given below is a CT image showing the anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus - antral sign or Holman-Miller sign.

Staging of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma

Stage
Spread

IA
Limited to the nose and/or nasopharynx

IB
Extension into ≥ one paranasal sinus

IIA
Minimal extension into the sphenopalatine foramen with minimal part of pterygopalatine fossa

IIB
Full occupation of pterygopalatine fossa with Holman-Miller sign, may with an erosion of orbital bones

IIC
Extension into the cheek, temporal fossa, or posterior to pterygoids through the pterygomaxillary fossa

IIIA
Erosion of skull base with minimal intracranial

IIIB
Erosion of skull base with extensive intracranial with or without cavernous sinus

Treatment: Surgical approach is the treatment of choice. Embolization of the vessels can be done prior to surgery to reduce the risk of bleeding during the surgery. Radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and hormonal therapy can also be considered.
questions.learning: Biopsy is the investigation of choice — The given clinical picture along with a CT scan showing the Holman-Miller sign is suggestive of nasopharyngeal angiofibroma commonly arising from the sphenopalatine foramen.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Revised A nurse got an accidental prick from a needle used for an HIV+ patient. Which single test would lead to a confirmatory diagnosis in her?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Western blot assay

The single test that would lead to a confirmatory diagnosis in this patient is Western blot assay.

The Western blot assay detects specific antibodies against various HIV proteins in the patient's blood sample. It is considered highly specific and is used to confirm the presence of HIV antibodies after a positive screening test, such as an ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay). The Western blot assay helps differentiate between true HIV infection and false-positive results that may occur with screening tests.

ELISA even though is done as a 2-test protocol, one single test is not considered a positive case. The two-test protocol for the diagnosis of HIV needs two ELISA tests to be positive. (i.e. If the initial ELISA is positive, a second ELISA is carried out. If the second ELISA is also positive, only then, the case is reported to be positive).

Investigations involved in HIV testing strategies:

* ELISA/ rapid tests

* Confirmatory tests with high specificity like Western Blot and line immunoassays are used in indeterminate/ discordant cases of rapid tests.

In India, NACO provides Western Blot Confirmatory testing only to resolve indeterminate results on previous serological testing and not for routine confirmation after a positive result on screening tests. The drawbacks of Western Blot include low rates of detection during acute HIV infection and misclassification of HIV-2 infection.

Other options:

p24 antigen:

* The p24 antigen is a viral protein that is detectable in the blood during the early stages of HIV infection.

* It can be detected within a few days to a few weeks after infection before antibodies are produced.

* While a positive p24 antigen test suggests HIV infection, it is not considered a confirmatory test on its own and is often used in combination with other tests.

PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction):

* PCR is a sensitive molecular test that can detect the genetic material (RNA or DNA) of the HIV virus in a person's blood.

* It can detect HIV at an early stage, even before antibodies are produced.

* PCR is commonly used for early diagnosis in infants born to HIV-positive mothers or in cases where early detection is crucial, such as occupational exposures.

HIV ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay):

* The ELISA is a screening test that detects antibodies produced by the immune system in response to HIV infection.

* It is highly sensitive and widely used as an initial test for HIV.

* However, a positive ELISA result needs to be confirmed by additional tests, such as the Western blot assay, to differentiate between true infection and false-positive results.
questions.learning: Western blot assay — The single test that would lead to a confirmatory diagnosis in this patient is Western blot assay. The Western blot assay detects specific antibodies against various HIV proteins in the patient's blood sample.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Maximum absorption of water takes place in:
questions.explanation: This question reinforces the fundamental concept from Question 15. The Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT) is responsible for the maximum reabsorption of water in the kidney, handling approximately 65-70% of the total glomerular filtrate. This reabsorption is iso-osmotic and is driven by the active transport of solutes like sodium and glucose. The Distal Convoluted Tubule (Option B) and Collecting Duct (Option C) perform regulated reabsorption of smaller volumes of water under the influence of hormones like Aldosterone and ADH. The Loop of Henle (Option D) is primarily responsible for establishing the osmotic gradient in the renal medulla, which allows the collecting duct to concentrate urine, but its absolute volume of water reabsorption is much lower than that of the PCT. Understanding this "bulk flow" in the PCT is essential for pharmacology, as diuretics like acetazolamide work in this segment to block sodium and water recovery, leading to increased urine output
questions.learning: This question reinforces the fundamental concept from Question 15. The Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT) is responsible for the maximum reabsorption of water in the kidney, handling approximately 65-70% of the total glomerular filtrate.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which among the following is the most common presentation of postpartum nerve injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Foot drop

The most common postpartum nerve injury is an injury to the peroneal nerve causing foot drop.

The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is the most commonly injured nerve after vaginal delivery followed by femoral neuropathies.

Obstetrical neuropathies are due to the pressure on branches of the lumbosacral nerve plexus during labor. They can manifest as complaints of intense neuralgia or cramp-like pains extending down one or both legs as soon as the head descends into the pelvis. Footdrop can be secondary to injury at the level of the lumbosacral plexus, sciatic nerve, or common fibular (peroneal) nerve. Injury of the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves may occur with cesarean delivery, which may manifest as an inguinal hernia and loss of sensation at the pubic region respectively.

Note: Since there are no options relating to intense neuralgia in the lower limb, foot drop becomes the best possible answer.
questions.learning: Foot drop — The most common postpartum nerve injury is an injury to the peroneal nerve causing foot drop. The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is the most commonly injured nerve after vaginal delivery followed by femoral neuropathies.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy has a history of spontaneous excessive bruising and hemarthrosis, with laboratory findings of a normal platelet count, prolonged partial thromboplastin time (PTT), and a normal prothrombin time (PT). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of spontaneous bruising, hemarthrosis (bleeding into joints), and an isolated prolonged PTT in a young boy is highly characteristic of Hemophilia A. Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by a deficiency of Factor VIII. Factors in the intrinsic pathway, such as Factor VIII, are measured by the PTT. Because the extrinsic and common pathways (measured by PT) and platelet function are normal, those tests remain within normal limits. Von Willebrand disease (Option A) could show a prolonged PTT but typically presents with mucosal bleeding (nosebleeds, gum bleeding) rather than deep joint bleeds. Bernard-Soulier (Option C) and Glanzmann thrombasthenia (Option D) are qualitative platelet disorders that would present with an increased bleeding time and abnormal platelet function tests, which are not described here . Therefore, the specific joint bleeding pattern and clotting profile definitively identify Hemophilia A
questions.learning: The clinical triad of spontaneous bruising, hemarthrosis (bleeding into joints), and an isolated prolonged PTT in a young boy is highly characteristic of Hemophilia A.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is a tributary of the inferior vena cava?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Left inferior phrenic vein

The inferior vena cava (IVC) directly receives the inferior phrenic veins, including the left one.

In contrast, the left suprarenal and left gonadal veins drain into the left renal vein, not directly into the IVC.

The ascending lumbar veins contribute to the azygos system, not the IVC.
questions.learning: Left inferior phrenic vein — The inferior vena cava (IVC) directly receives the inferior phrenic veins, including the left one. In contrast, the left suprarenal and left gonadal veins drain into the left renal vein, not directly into the IVC.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is the correct arrangement about the levels of health care?
options: 1- Medical colleges and hospitals are primary level, 2- CHC is secondary level, 3- Sub Centre and PHC are tertiary
1- Sub Centre and PHC are primary level, 2- CHC is secondary level, 3- Medical colleges and hospitals are tertiary
1- CHC is primary level, 2- Sub Centre and PHC are secondary level, 3- Medical colleges and hospitals are tertiary
1- PHC is primary level, 2- Sub Centre is secondary level, 3- Medical colleges and hospitals are tertiary
questions.explanation: The Indian healthcare system is structured into three tiers: 1. Primary Level: Sub Centres and Primary Health Centres (PHCs) act as the first point of contact for basic curative and preventive services. 2. Secondary Level: Community Health Centres (CHCs) and District Hospitals provide specialized care and serve as referral centers for PHCs. 3. Tertiary Level: Medical colleges, regional hospitals, and super-specialty institutions handle complex cases requiring advanced expertise. Option A is incorrect as it swaps primary and tertiary levels. Option C wrongly classifies CHCs as primary. Option D incorrectly places Sub Centres at the secondary level. This tiered structure ensures an efficient referral chain, allowing basic ailments to be managed locally while reserving advanced resources for critical cases
questions.learning: The Indian healthcare system is structured into three tiers: 1. Primary Level: Sub Centres and Primary Health Centres (PHCs) act as the first point of contact for basic curative and preventive services.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Identify the virus given in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. HIV

The image shows an HIV virus.

The human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) virus is a spherical, enveloped RNA virus. The nucleocapsid has an icosahedral shell and a cone-shaped core, enclosing the ribonucleoproteins. The genome comprises two identical single-stranded, RNA copies, with the reverse transcriptase enzyme, which is a characteristic feature of retroviruses.

The viral core is surrounded by a matrix protein called p17, which lies underneath the virion envelope. It contains

* Major capsid protein p24

* Nucleocapsid protein p7/p9

* Two copies of viral genomic RNA

* Three viral enzymes (protease, reverse transcriptase, and integrase).

The viral envelope is studded by two viral glycoproteins, gp120 and gp41, which are critical for HIV infection of cells.

Other options:

The structure of CMV is shown below

The structure of EBV is shown below

The structure of coronavirus is shown below
questions.learning: The human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) virus is a spherical, enveloped RNA virus. The nucleocapsid has an icosahedral shell and a cone-shaped core, enclosing the ribonucleoproteins.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not a component of qSOFA?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Bilateral pupillary reflex

qSOFA score (quickSOFA) is a bedside prompt that may identify patients with suspected infection who are at greater risk for a poor outcome outside the intensive care unit (ICU).

It uses three criteria, assigning one point each for

• Low blood pressure (SBP≤100 mmHg),
• High respiratory rate (≥22 breaths per min)
• Altered mentation (Glasgow coma scale, <15).

The score ranges from 0 to 3 points. The presence of 2 or more qSOFA points is a simple prompt to identify infected patients outside the ICU who are likely to develop sepsis.
questions.learning: Bilateral pupillary reflex qSOFA score (quickSOFA) is a bedside prompt that may identify patients with suspected infection who are at greater risk for a poor outcome outside the intensive care unit (ICU).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A young boy with fatigue is found to have a haemoglobin of 9 g/dl. Peripheral smear showed sickle-shaped RBCs. What is the next best step in managing this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Blood transfusion

The given clinical scenario and image are diagnostic of sickle cell anemia. The next best step is blood transfusion.

Sickle cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder that occurs due to the T-to-A point mutation in the sixth codon of the β-globin gene. This results in the replacement of glutamate residue with valine. This causes the production of sickle-shaped red blood cells due to the polymerization of deoxygenated hemoglobin (HbS).

The clinical features of sickle cell disease are due to the tendency of HbS molecules to stack into polymers when deoxygenated. The features are:

* Moderately severe hemolytic anemia with jaundice.

* Painful bone crisis- hand-foot syndrome or dactylitis of the bones of hands and feet.

* Acute chest syndrome typically presents with fever, cough, chest pain, and pulmonary infiltrates.

* Hyposthenuria- inability to concentrate urine.

* Aplastic crisis stems from the infection of red cell progenitors by parvovirus B19, which causes a transient cessation of erythropoiesis and a sudden worsening of the anemia.

* Spleen

* In children- splenic sequestration crises occur which results in splenomegaly due to red pulp congestion.

* Adolescence or early adulthood- autosplenectomy occurs due to splenic infarction, fibrosis, and progressive shrinkage.

* Increased susceptibility to infection with encapsulated organisms like pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Haemophilus influenza septicemia, but can be reduced by vaccination and prophylactic antibiotics.

* Other clinical features- priapism, leg ulcers, stroke, retinopathy, pigment gallstones, and growth retardation.

The diagnosis is suggested by the clinical findings, the presence of irreversibly sickled RBCs on peripheral smear, and hemoglobin electrophoresis showing increased HbA2, HbF, and S spike.

Disease-modifying drugs such as hydroxyurea can be given to patients with sickle cell anemia since it reduces the incidence of adverse vaso-occlusive vents. Blood transfusions are used to treat and prevent complications of sickle cell disease, including preparation for surgery, symptomatic anemia, acute stroke, multi-organ failure and acute chest syndrome
questions.learning: Blood transfusion — The given clinical scenario and image are diagnostic of sickle cell anemia. The next best step is blood transfusion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: New A patient with leprosy presented with the deformity as shown below. Which nerve injury causes the given condition ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ulnar nerve

The given image shows extension at the metacarpophalangeal joint and flexion at interphalangeal joints of the ring and little finger, caused by ulnar nerve injury. It produces a claw hand (main en griffe). Leprosy can affect peripheral nerves and lead to their associated conditions.

In ulnar nerve palsy, only the medial two fingers develop clawing, while in a combined median and ulnar nerve palsy, all four fingers develop clawing.

The ulnar nerve supplies the medial two lumbricals in the hand. The lumbricals have a combined action on metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint flexion and interphalangeal (IP) joint extension (glass holding posture). In ulnar nerve injury, since the medial lumbricals are not functional, the forearm muscles are unopposed. Hence, there is hyperextension at MCP joints and flexion at IP joints. This causes claw hand deformity. There is also numbness of the ulnar one and a half fingers.

Elbow fractures or dislocations lead to high lesions of the ulnar nerve. Here, the hand is not markedly deformed because the ulnar half of the flexor digitorum profundus is paralyzed and the fingers, therefore, appear less clawed. This is called the high ulnar paradox.

The following tests are done to test the integrity of the ulnar nerve:

* Egawa's test - In a positive test, due to the weakness of the dorsal interossei, side-to-side movements of the middle finger is weak.

* Book test or Froment's sign - The patient is asked to hold a book forcefully while the doctor tries to pull it. In a positive test, due to weakness of adductor pollicis muscle, adduction of thumb is lost. The patient tries to hold the book by using flexor pollicis longus muscle. This produces flexion at the inter-phalangeal joint while holding the book.

* Card test - In the case of weak palmar interossei, it is easy for the examiner to pull out the card when held between the fingers. This is due to the loss of adduction by palmar interossei muscles.

Other options

Option B - In radial nerve palsy, the patient presents with 'wrist drop' in case of paralyzed wrist extensors, and 'finger drop' when extensor digitorum is paralyzed. When there is compression in the axilla, radial nerve palsy is called Saturday night palsy. There is paralysis of the triceps, and weakness of the wrist and hand. In high lesions, there is sensory loss on the dorsum of the hand over the anatomical stuff box.

Option C - In median nerve injury, paralysis of opponens pollicis muscle leads to 'ape thumb' deformity. In forearm or elbow injuries, there is paralysis of long flexors of the thumb, index, and middle fingers, radial wrist flexors, and forearm pronators. This leads to the characteristic 'pointing index finger'. There is sensory loss over three and a half digits on the radial side.

Option D -Posterior interosseous nerve injury, is seen in posterior interosseous syndrome. The wrist is in radial deviation and there is loss of metacarpophalangeal joint extension. However, wrist extension is preserved.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is not used for uncomplicated falciparum malaria?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Chloroquine

Chloroquine is not used in uncomplicated falciparum malaria due to widespread resistance of Plasmodium falciparum.

Current Treatment (as per NVBDCP guidelines)

• First-line therapy: → Artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) for 3 days
• Additional drug: → Single dose of primaquine (0.75 mg/kg) on Day 2

(used for gametocyte clearance → reduces transmission)
• North-East India: → Artemether + lumefantrine (3 days)
• Rest of India:→ Artesunate (3 days) + single dose sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (Day 1)

Key Point

• Chloroquine is ineffective in falciparum malaria → hence not used
• Other options (primaquine, artemether, SP) are part of recommended regimens

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What particular benefit does a patient receive when treated at an ESI hospital under the Employees’ State Insurance (ESI) Act?
questions.explanation: The Employees' State Insurance (ESI) Act provides several types of benefits to insured workers. However, the question specifically asks for the benefit provided when a patient receives "treatment at an ESI hospital." This direct provision of healthcare services—including outpatient, inpatient, and specialist care—is classified as a Medical Benefit. Sickness benefit (Option A) refers to a cash payment made during periods of certified illness when the worker is unable to attend work. Maternity benefit (Option C) involves cash payments for pregnant female employees. Dependent's benefit (Option D) is a monthly pension paid to the family of an insured person who dies due to an employment-related injury. While all these are components of the ESI scheme, the "medical benefit" is the only one that refers to the actual delivery of clinical services and treatments within the ESI facility infrastructure. This benefit is unique because it is available to both the insured person and their family members from the first day of employment

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A child presents to the outpatient department with clinical features as shown in the given image. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The image depicts a child with generalized edema (anasarca), particularly noticeable in the face and limbs. This clinical presentation is characteristic of "Kwashiorkor," a form of severe protein-energy malnutrition. The edema results from severe hypoalbuminemia, which reduces plasma oncotic pressure. Other classic signs include a "moon face," "flaky paint" dermatosis, and sparse, reddish hair. "Marasmus" (Option B) is characterized by severe muscle wasting and a "skin and bones" appearance without edema. While Nephrotic syndrome (Option C) also presents with generalized edema and hypoalbuminemia, Kwashiorkor is far more common in pediatric populations in specific social contexts and is usually accompanied by growth failure and dietary history. Nephritic syndrome (Option D) presents with hematuria, hypertension, and more localized (periorbital) edema. Management of Kwashiorkor requires careful nutritional rehabilitation to avoid refeeding syndrome
questions.learning: The image depicts a child with generalized edema (anasarca), particularly noticeable in the face and limbs. This clinical presentation is characteristic of "Kwashiorkor," a form of severe protein-energy malnutrition.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Program for improvement of quality of labor room comes under:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. LaQshya

The Laqshya initiative launched recently by the government of India refers to initiative for labor room quality improvement.

There is enough evidence to show that improving the quality of care in labor rooms, especially on the day of birth, is central to maternal and neonatal survival.

• Laqshya is expected to improve the quality of care that is being provided to the pregnant mother in the labor room and maternity operation theatres, thereby preventing the undesirable adverse outcomes associated with childbirth.
• This initiative will be implemented in government medical colleges (MCs) besides district hospitals (DHs), and high delivery load sub-district hospitals (SDHs) and community health centers (CHCs).
• The initiative plans to conduct quality certification of labor rooms and also incentivize facilities achieving the targets outlined.
• The goal of this initiative is to reduce preventable maternal and new-born mortality, morbidity, and stillbirths associated with the care around delivery in the labor room and maternity OT and ensure respectful maternity care.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which among the following culture media is used in the identification of Salmonella?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Wilson and Blair medium

Wilson and Blair bismuth sulphite medium is used for the identification of Salmonella. It is a type of selective and indicator media.

Salmonella typhi reduces sulphite to sulphide in the presence of glucose and produces jet black colonies with a metallic sheen due to the production of H2S on Wilson and Blair bismuth sulphite medium. It is an example of indicator media. It is also a selective media because inhibiting substances are added to inhibit the growth of unwanted bacteria.

On the Wilson-Blair medium, S. paratyphi A produces green colonies due to the absence of H2S production.

On Deoxycholate citrate media and XLD (xylose lysine deoxycholate), colonies show blackheads due to H2S production.

Other options:

Option 1) PLET medium is used to isolate B. anthracis. It is a selective medium consisting of polymyxin, lysozyme, ethylene diamine tetraacetic acid (EDTA), and thallous acetate added to heart infusion agar.

Option 2) BCYE medium (Buffered charcoal yeast extract agar) is used to culture Legionella.

Option 4) Stuart Transport Medium is recommended for the preservation and transportation of Neisseria species and other fastidious organisms from the clinic to the laboratory.

The image below shows black colonies of Salmonella.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: All of the following are features of tetralogy of Fallot except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Atrial septal defect

An atrial septal defect is not seen in a patient with tetralogy of Fallot.

The primary defect gives rise to the 4 anatomical components of TOF which are:

* Ventricular septal defect (VSD)

* Obstruction to right ventricular outflow - Pulmonic stenosis (PS)

* Right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH)

* Overriding (or dextroposition) of the aorta

Tetrology of Fallot(TOF):

* TOF is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease

* The primary defect is an anterior deviation of the infundibular septum (the muscular septum that separates the aortic and pulmonary outflows).

* Obstruction to pulmonary arterial blood flow is usually at both the right ventricular infundibulum (subpulmonic area) and the pulmonary valve.

* The degree of pulmonary outflow obstruction determines the degree of the patient’s cyanosis and the age of first presentation.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the condition shown in the given image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Miliary tuberculosis

The above radiograph depicts the miliary pattern seen in tuberculosis.

Miliary tuberculosis is a form of disseminated pulmonary tuberculosis that occurs when organisms draining through the lymphatics enter the venous blood and circulate back to the lung. It can result from progressive primary disease, reactivation of latent foci, and iatrogenic exposure (lithotripsy, urethral catheterization, cardiac valve homograft placement, and solid organ transplantation).

The risk factors for the development of miliary TB include extremes of age, alcohol use, malignancy, HIV, corticosteroid use, connective tissue disease, renal failure, diabetes, and pregnancy.

The clinicopathological patterns of this condition include acute miliary TB (which may present as multi-organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) and ARDS, as in this patient), late generalized TB, and anergic TB (defined histologically by the absence of granulomata). Individual lesions either microscopic or small <2 mm foci of yellow-white consolidation scattered throughout the lung parenchyma. The lesions may coalesce resulting in large areas of consolidation. Serous pleural effusions, tuberculous emyema or obliterative fibrous pleuritis may occur

Laboratory tests may show pancytopenia due to bone marrow infiltration. Other findings could include anemia, thrombocytopenia/cytosis, hyponatremia, and sterile pyuria.

Chest radiography shows a faint reticulonodular pattern distributed fairly uniformly throughout the lungs.

Histopathology shows granulomas of tuberculosis characteristically contain epithelioid macrophages, Langhans giant cells, and lymphocytes with central caseation necrosis.

Other options:

Option B: Chest x-ray appearance of acute respiratory distress syndrome varies depending on the severity and typically appears as bilateral diffuse alveolar opacities with dependent atelectasis in some cases. The opacities may have a patchy ground-glass appearance.

Option C: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is a hypersensitivity reaction involving the major airways. Radiographic findings in ABPA include lobar collapse, non-segmental areas of opacities commonly involving the upper lobe, and branching thick tubular opacities due to distended bronchi filled with fungus and mucus - Finger-in-glove appearance

Option D: Pulmonary metastasis typically appears as peripheral, rounded nodules of variable size, scattered throughout both lungs (cannon-ball lesions).
The most common primaries to result in pulmonary metastases in adults include:

* Breast carcinoma

* Colorectal carcinoma

* Renal cell carcinoma

* Uterine leiomyosarcoma

* Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma

The chest radiograph given below shows cannon-ball lesions of metastatic lung cancer.

* Healed varicella

* Long-standing MS – can lead to pulmonary hemosiderosis

* Alveolar microlithiasis

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: On thyroid function test analysis, TSH value was much higher than normal with a low free T4. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Primary hypothyroidism

An elevated TSH value with low free T4 is suggestive of primary hypothyroidism (Option D).

Option A: In subclinical hypothyroidism, free T4 levels remain normal despite elevated TSH.

Option B: TSH is low in hyperthyroidism.

Option C: The diagnosis of secondary hypothyroidism is made along with a deficiency of other pituitary hormones. TSH levels may be low, normal, or slightly increased. The elevation in TSH levels can be attributed to the secretion of immunoreactive but biologically inactive forms of TSH. To confirm the diagnosis, it is essential to detect a low level of unbound T4.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A woman is brought to the hospital after an argument with her husband and complains that she is unable to speak. On examination, there are no neurological or physical abnormalities, and she appears unconcerned about her condition. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with mutism following an emotional conflict, yet her examinations are normal and she lacks distress regarding her symptoms. This specific lack of concern about a serious neurological deficit is known as "La belle indifférence," a hallmark of conversion disorder. It reflects an apparent indifference to symptoms like paralysis or mutism that have no underlying medical cause. Malingering (Option A) involves the intentional faking of symptoms for clear external gain, such as financial rewards, which is not evident here. Adaptation (Option C) refers to a normal psychological adjustment to stress, not the development of functional neurological deficits. Somatic symptom disorder (Option D) typically involves excessive anxiety and distress regarding physical symptoms, contrasting sharply with the indifference seen in this case. **************

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following options correctly describes the enzyme used in this test (RT-PCR)?
questions.explanation: The Reverse Transcriptase Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR) is the gold standard for detecting RNA viruses, such as Poliovirus, which causes acute flaccid paralysis. The critical first step of this test involves the enzyme Reverse Transcriptase, which is an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (Option B). This enzyme transcribes the viral RNA template into a complementary DNA (cDNA) strand. Only after this conversion can the cDNA be amplified by a standard DNA-dependent DNA polymerase (Option C). DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (Option A) is used in natural transcription to create RNA from DNA. RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (Option D) is an enzyme used by certain RNA viruses to replicate their genome but is not the tool used for RT-PCR assays. Understanding this enzymatic pathway is essential for interpreting molecular diagnostics. Thus, the specific capability to synthesize DNA from an RNA template defines the "Reverse Transcriptase" used in RT-PCR
questions.learning: The Reverse Transcriptase Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR) is the gold standard for detecting RNA viruses, such as Poliovirus, which causes acute flaccid paralysis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 16-year-old girl presents to the outpatient department with primary amenorrhea and recurrent cyclical pain. On perineal examination, a bulging mass is seen protruding at the vaginal opening. What is the most likely underlying cause of this condition?
options: Transverse septum in the proximal vagina
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of primary amenorrhea (absence of periods), cyclical pelvic pain, and a visible vaginal protrusion is pathognomonic for an imperforate hymen . The protrusion is a bulging, often bluish membrane caused by hematocolpos (the accumulation of menstrual blood trapped behind the hymen). A transverse vaginal septum (Option A) would also cause obstructive amenorrhea and cyclical pain, but the obstruction is typically higher up and would not present as a protrusion at the introitus. Complete vaginal atresia (Option B) involves a lack of the vaginal canal, meaning no protrusion would be visible. Cervical agenesis (Option D) would present with amenorrhea and pain due to hematometra, but without the vaginal bulge. The classic visual sign of a tense, bulging membrane between the labia in an adolescent girl confirms the diagnosis. Treatment involves a cruciate incision to drain the accumulated blood and create a permanent opening
questions.learning: The clinical triad of primary amenorrhea (absence of periods), cyclical pelvic pain, and a visible vaginal protrusion is pathognomonic for an imperforate hymen .

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Painless lesions over the vulval area as below is suggestive of ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Condylomata acuminata

The probable diagnosis is Condylomata acuminata.
It is also called as venereal warts. It is a sexually transmitted disease caused by Human Papilloma Virus 6 or 11.
Verrucous, exophytic cauliflower like growths can be seen over the skin of vulval region, perineum, perianal region which are usually non tender.

Treatment -
local application of Podophyllin 25% in alcohol or Podophyllin 20% in tincture benzoin for 6 hour daily,
Podofilox 0.5% solution
Trichloroacetic acid and bichloroacetic acid applied serially
Intralesional injection of Interferon

Vaccination - Cervarix at 0, 1 and 6 months; Gardasil at 0, 2 and 6 months.

Genital herpes - presents with painful blisters/ genital ulcer. It is caused by Herpes simplex virus 2.
Gonococcal vulvovaginitis - caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. The patient usually presents with swollen, painful external genitalia and erythema around external urinary meatus along with foul smelling vaginal discharge.
Condyloma lata - these are infectious plaques which are broad, pink or gray-white present in warm, moist body areas. It is hallmark of secondary syphilis.
questions.learning: Condylomata acuminata — The probable diagnosis is Condylomata acuminata. It is also called as venereal warts.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What type of shock is most likely in a patient with profuse bleeding, cold extremities, and a reduced central venous pressure (CVP)?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of "excessive bleeding" (hemorrhage) is the primary cause of acute volume loss, leading to Hypovolemic Shock (Option B). The physiological response to low circulating volume includes intense peripheral vasoconstriction to divert blood to vital organs, resulting in the "cool extremities" observed. Central Venous Pressure (CVP) is a direct measure of the preload and volume status; a "decreased CVP" confirms that the heart is not receiving enough blood to maintain cardiac output. Cardiogenic shock (Option A) would show an increased CVP due to the heart's failure to pump available blood. Obstructive shock (Option C), such as cardiac tamponade, would also present with an elevated CVP. Hypoadrenal shock (Option D) is a distributive type of shock and would not be the primary diagnosis in a patient with active bleeding. Therefore, the combination of blood loss and low filling pressures is diagnostic of hypovolemia. Management requires immediate hemorrhage control and volume replacement

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 22-year-old man presented with diarrhea and intolerance to dairy products. On investigation, he was found to have a lactase deficiency. Which of the following agents is least likely to cause symptoms of lactose intolerance?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Yogurt

Yogurt is the least likely to cause symptoms of lactose intolerance. It contains lactobacillus that produces lactase and is generally well tolerated.

Lactase is a brush border enzyme that hydrolyzes lactose into glucose and galactose. In lactase deficiency, patients have great variability in clinical symptoms, depending on both the severity of lactase deficiency and the amount of lactose ingested.

The goal of treatment in patients with isolated lactase deficiency is achieving patient comfort through the elimination of dietary lactose.

Foods that are high in lactose include milk (12 g/cup), ice cream (9 g/cup), and cottage cheese (8 g/cup). Aged cheese has lower lactose content. Most people can tolerate up to 12g of lactose a day without significant symptoms.
questions.learning: Yogurt Yogurt is the least likely to cause symptoms of lactose intolerance. It contains lactobacillus that produces lactase and is generally well tolerated.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency department two hours after a road traffic accident with altered consciousness and a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 10. A CT scan of the brain is shown below. Based on the clinical presentation and imaging findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The CT scan demonstrates a "biconvex" (lenticular), sharply demarcated, hyperdense mass in the peripheral space, which is the pathognomonic radiological appearance of an Extradural Hematoma (EDH). EDH occurs between the skull and the dura mater and is most commonly caused by an arterial bleed from the middle meningeal artery following a temporal bone fracture. A Subdural Hematoma (SDH, Option A) appears as a "crescent-shaped" mass that crosses suture lines. Intracerebral hemorrhage (Option B) and hemorrhagic contusions (Option D) occur within the brain parenchyma itself rather than the extra-axial spaces. Clinically, EDH patients may exhibit a "lucid interval" followed by rapid neurological deterioration as the hematoma expands and causes midline shift or herniation. This is a neurosurgical emergency requiring prompt evacuation of the clot. The hyperdense (white) appearance indicates acute bleeding, consistent with the history of an accident occurring only two hours prior
questions.learning: The CT scan demonstrates a "biconvex" (lenticular), sharply demarcated, hyperdense mass in the peripheral space, which is the pathognomonic radiological appearance of an Extradural Hematoma (EDH).
