questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the CTG pattern?
questions.explanation: The CTG pattern shows early decelerations, which are characterized by a gradual decrease in fetal heart rate (FHR) where the nadir (lowest point) coincides exactly with the peak of the uterine contraction. The onset and recovery of the heart rate drop mirror the beginning and end of the contraction. This pattern is benign and typically results from fetal head compression during labor. Late decelerations (Option B) begin after the contraction starts and reach their nadir well after the contraction's peak, indicating uteroplacental insufficiency. Variable decelerations (Option C) are abrupt drops in heart rate with an irregular shape (often V or W) that vary in their relationship to contractions, usually signaling umbilical cord compression. A "normal" CTG (Option D) would show accelerations and good variability without these specific drops. Early decelerations require only monitoring as they are not indicative of fetal distress
questions.learning: The CTG pattern shows early decelerations, which are characterized by a gradual decrease in fetal heart rate (FHR) where the nadir (lowest point) coincides exactly with the peak of the uterine contraction.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient comes to the casualty with organophosphate poisoning. He was started on atropine infusion and pralidoxime. After 2 hours, the patient had a sudden rise in temperature. What is the likely cause of fever?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Atropine toxicity

The most likely cause of fever in this patient is atropine toxicity.

The clinical scenario is suggestive of organophosphate consumption and atropine is used for its management. Atropine is a muscarinic receptor antagonist, and it competitively blocks the acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors.

Organophosphates are powerful acetylcholinesterase inhibitors. It is absorbed by inhalation or through the skin. Mucous membranes and the gastrointestinal tract are also the sites for absorption.

The predominant initial signs are of muscarinic excess which includes: (DUMBBELSS)

• Diarrhoea
• Urination
• Miosis
• Bronchospasm
• Bradycardia
• Emesis
• Lacrimation
• Salivation
• Sweating

Nicotinic manifestations include twitching of eyelids, tongue, and facial muscles which then leads to paralysis. CNS stimulation results in headache, tremors, ataxia, coma, and death.

Atropine in larger doses can lead to atropine toxicity. The features are depicted in the following image:
questions.learning: Atropine toxicity — The most likely cause of fever in this patient is atropine toxicity. The clinical scenario is suggestive of organophosphate consumption and atropine is used for its management.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A newborn infant presented with features of intestinal obstruction, X-ray showed the following image and an annular pancreas was seen in CT abdomen. The probable diagnosis is _______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Duodenal Atresia

The above plain abdominal radiograph shows a typical double-bubble sign suggestive of duodenal Atresia which is seen in associaton with annular pancreas.

* Most common cause of neonatal intestinal obstruction is duodenal Atresia.

* 1 in 6000 to 10,000 live births.

* Duodenal atresia is thought to occur as a result of failure of vacuolization of the duodenum from its solid cord stage.

* It is associated with several conditions, including Prematurity, Down syndrome, Maternal polyhydramnios, Malrotation, Annular pancreas, and Biliary atresia.

* The duodenal obstruction is distal to the ampulla of Vater in most cases therefore the infant infants present with Bilious vomiting.

* Treatment is by Duodenoduodenostomy.

Annular pancreas:

* Annular pancreas is due to result of the failure of the complete rotation of the ventral pancreatic bud during development so that a ring of pancreatic tissue surrounds the second or third part of the duodenum.

* Annular pancreas is most often seen in association with congenital duodenal stenosis or atresia and is, therefore, more prevalent in children with Down’s syndrome.

* Duodenal obstruction typically causes vomiting in neonates.

* The treatment for annular pancreas is bypass (duodenoduodenostomy).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 29-year-old G2P1 comes to the physician at 32 weeks of gestation. She underwent OGTT(75 g of glucose) and her values were fasting 110 mg/dl and 2 hours of glucose at 180 mg/dl. Which among the following is the next step regarding the management of this patient?
options: Induce labour due to risk of fetal macrosomia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Admit and start insulin

Since her values are more than the normal limits with a 75 g OGTT she is having gestational diabetes and the next step in the management is to admit her and start insulin.

The glucose tolerance test is considered the diagnostic test for gestational diabetes mellitus and insulin is the drug of choice for the treatment of gestational diabetes mellitus. It does not cross the placenta and tight glycemic control can typically be achieved.

Diagnosis of GDM with 75 g OGTT according to IADPSG is made if any one of the following are met:

* Fasting: ≥92 mg/dl

* 1 hour: ≥180 mg/dl

* 2 hours: ≥153 mg/dl

The initial management of GDM is maternal nutrition therapy with diet and exercise. Insulin therapy is started if :

* Fasting plasma glucose levels persistently ≥95 mg/dl or the 2-hour postprandial plasma glucose ≥120 mg/dL in women with gestational diabetes treated with maternal nutrition therapy.

* Glucose levels on OGTT are in the range for overt diabetes.

Since this question does not have the option of Maternal nutrition therapy, the best step would be to start her on insulin.

The starting dose is typically 0.7 to 1 unit/kg/d and is given in divided doses. A combination of intermediate-acting and short-acting insulin may be used.

50% of women with gestational diabetes develop overt diabetes within 20 years. Hence, they are recommended to undergo screening & revaluation between 4-12 weeks postpartum.

Earlier, a two-step approach was used to diagnose GDM. In this, the first step (screening) is a 50-gram one-hour glucose challenge test (GCT). The patients having a positive result for this test were then subject to the second step, a 100-gram, three-hour oral glucose tolerance test (GTT), which is the diagnostic test for gestational diabetes mellitus. This has now been replaced by the one-step approach that omits the screening test and simplifies diagnostic testing by performing only a 75-gram, two-hour oral GTT.
questions.learning: Admit and start insulin Since her values are more than the normal limits with a 75 g OGTT she is having gestational diabetes and the next step in the management is to admit her and start insulin.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The most likely condition is traumatic cataract, which can develop months after blunt ocular trauma and commonly presents with progressive blurring of vision.
questions.explanation: Iridodialysis is the traumatic detachment of the iris from its root at the ciliary body, which typically occurs after non-penetrating blunt force trauma. The resulting structural change often creates a "D-shaped" pupil and a visible biconvex gap at the periphery, leading to symptoms like blurring of vision, photophobia, or monocular diplopia. Ankyloblepharon (Option B) refers to the abnormal fusion of the eyelid margins and is not an internal iris injury. Vossius Ring (Option C) is a pigment ring on the anterior lens capsule shaped exactly like the pupil, also caused by blunt trauma, but it does not cause a displaced pupil. Cycloiriditis (Option D) is an inflammation of the iris and ciliary body; while trauma can be a trigger, it presents with acute pain and redness rather than a structural peripheral gap. Diagnosis is made by clinical examination and slit-lamp biomicroscopy, and treatment depends on the severity of the visual symptoms
questions.learning: Iridodialysis is the traumatic detachment of the iris from its root at the ciliary body, which typically occurs after non-penetrating blunt force trauma.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What will be the line of management for the condition shown in the image given below?
questions.explanation: The image shows a well-defined, smooth, rounded swelling at the medial aspect of the upper eyelid — classic appearance of a dermoid cyst, which is a benign choristomatous lesion commonly occurring at the superomedial or superolateral orbital rim in young patients. Key Clinical Features visible: 1. Well-circumscribed, smooth swelling 2. Located near medial canthus/orbital rim 3. Non-inflammatory appearance 4. No overlying skin changes Treatment: Complete surgical excision is the definitive treatment. The cyst must be removed intact to prevent recurrence and inflammatory reaction from cyst contents spillage. Why other options are wrong: (B) Radiotherapy is incorrect because dermoid cysts are benign lesions — radiotherapy is reserved for malignant tumors. It has absolutely no role in managing benign orbital cysts. (C) Antibiotics is incorrect because dermoid cysts are non-infectious developmental anomalies, not bacterial infections. Antibiotics have no therapeutic effect on cystic lesions of this nature. (D) International steroids is incorrect because steroid injections are used for chalazion or inflammatory lesions. Dermoid cysts have a true epithelial lining requiring complete surgical removal — steroids cannot resolve them

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 7-year-old child presented with complaints of headache and blurring of vision. On examination, there was a difference in visual acuity. In the right eye, it was (+5D) and in the left, it was (+1D). After the best possible correction for vision, visual acuity in the right eye is 6/18 and in the left is 6/24. On fundoscopy, no pathology could be appreciated. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Anisometric Amblyopia

The presence of unequal refractive errors (+5D vs +1D), poor visual acuity even after correction, and a normal fundus examination strongly point towards Anisometropic Amblyopia.

A young child with a difference of vision in both eyes that is not improved after correction for refractive error supports the diagnosis. Due to the difference in refractive power, vision in one eye gets suppressed which is not apparent on examination.

Amblyopia is an uncorrectable decrease in vision in one or both eyes with no apparent structural abnormality seen to explain it. It is a diagnosis of exclusion. Generally, a difference of two lines or more on Snellen's visual acuity chart between the two eyes would be defined as unilateral amblyopia.

It may be of the following types:

* Strabismic - monocular suppression of the deviating eye in case of abnormal binocular interaction may develop in children with an accommodative squint. It is the most common type.

* Refractory- Anisometropic, Isoametropic, Meridional - due to a difference in refractive error between the two eyes

* Stimulus deprivation - in the case of vision deprivation

* Organic

* Reverse

* Idiopathic

Clinical features:

* Decreased contrast sensitivity

* Diminution of vision

* Sunglass effect- brightness is less compared to the normal eye

* Crowding phenomenon- slipping of images

Treatment of choice:

* Occlusion of the normal eye (4 to 6 hours/day) using patches.

* Penalization: Blurring of vision using atropine.

Other options:

Option A: Refractive error will be corrected after using visual corrections.

Option B: Astigmatism is a type of refractive error due to rotational asymmetry in the eye's refractive power. There is a difference in refractive power in the visual axis of the same eye.

Option C: It cannot be a case of malingering as the differences in vision and refractory error have been documented.
questions.learning: Anisometric Amblyopia — The presence of unequal refractive errors (+5D vs +1D), poor visual acuity even after correction, and a normal fundus examination strongly point towards Anisometropic Amblyopia.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is a cause of bilateral sudden painless loss of vision?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diabetic retinopathy

Diabetic retinopathy is a cause of bilateral sudden painless loss of vision due to vascular complications.

Bilateral sudden painless loss of vision is a hallmark of advanced diabetic retinopathy, particularly when associated with complications such as:

• Vitreous haemorrhage: Leakage of blood into the vitreous cavity due to rupture of fragile neovascular vessels.

• Tractional retinal detachment: Occurs when fibrovascular tissue pulls the retina away from its underlying structures.

• Macular oedema: Severe swelling in the macula can lead to central vision loss.

These conditions can cause sudden and significant visual impairment, often affecting both eyes in patients with long-standing, poorly controlled diabetes.

Other options

Option A: Acute congestive glaucoma: Typically causes sudden vision loss, but it is painful and unilateral in most cases.

Option C: Keratoconus is a progressive condition that leads to gradual vision loss due to corneal thinning and irregular astigmatism, not sudden or bilateral loss.

Option D: Iridocyclitis is associated with pain, redness, and photophobia, and it is usually unilateral.
questions.learning: Diabetic retinopathy Diabetic retinopathy is a cause of bilateral sudden painless loss of vision due to vascular complications. Bilateral sudden painless loss of vision is a hallmark of advanced diabetic retinopathy, particularly when associated with…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What does the point labeled C denote?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Onset of symptoms

The given diagram shows the natural history of disease in an individual over time, in which the point labeled C denotes the onset of symptoms. The natural history of disease refers to the progression of a disease in an individual over time, in the absence of treatment.

Exposure (point A): the disease process begins with appropriate exposure to or accumulation of factors sufficient for the disease process to begin in a susceptible host. For example in infectious disease, the exposure is a microorganism. For lung cancer, it is any factor that initiates the process, such as asbestos fibers or components in tobacco smoke.

Pathological changes (point B): after the disease process has been triggered, pathological changes occur without the individual being aware of it. This stage of subclinical disease, extending from the time of exposure to onset of symptoms, is usually called the incubation period for infectious diseases, and the latency period for chronic diseases. During this stage, the disease remains asymptomatic.

The onset of clinical symptoms (point C): it is the beginning of the clinical stage of the disease.

The usual time of diagnosis (point D): the onset of symptoms is followed by a short interval (varies from disease to disease) after which the patient presents to a healthcare setup where a diagnosis of the disease is made. Based on treatment and prognosis, the patient can progress to either recovery, disability, or death.
questions.learning: Onset of symptoms — The given diagram shows the natural history of disease in an individual over time, in which the point labeled C denotes the onset of symptoms.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A male child presented with arthralgia and abdominal pain. On examination, there was palpable purpura over the lower limbs. There is past history of upper respiratory tract infection prior to the onset of presenting symptoms. Which of the following is the treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glucocorticoids

The clinical scenario is suggestive of Henoch Schonlein's purpura (HSP). Glucocorticoids are used to treat HSP.

Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP), also known as IgA vasculitis, is a common small vessel vasculitis in childhood. It is a type III hypersensitivity reaction characterized by the deposition of IgA in the small vessels of the skin, joints, gastrointestinal tract, and kidney, resulting in vasculitis.

The exact etiology of HSP remains unknown. But, it usually occurs following an upper respiratory tract infection caused by group A Streptococcus, Staphylococcus aureus, Mycoplasma, and Adenovirus.

Children usually present with the following features:

• Palpable purpura is symmetric and occurs in the lower extremities, extensor aspect of the upper limbs, and buttocks.
• Arthralgia and arthritis- commonly affecting hip, knee, or ankle joints.
• Gastrointestinal manifestations like abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, and intussusception.
• About 30% of the patients with HSP develop renal manifestations, presenting as microscopic hematuria, hypertension, and progressive glomerulonephritis.

Glucocorticoids such as prednisolone are used for the treatment of gastrointestinal manifestations in HSP. Nephritis due to IgA vasculitis should be treated with immunosuppressants like prednisolone and azathioprine.

The image given below shows palpable purpura in the lower limbs seen in HSP.

The criteria for diagnosis of childhood HSP are:

Palpable purpura with at least one of the following-

• Diffuse abdominal pain
• Any biopsy showing predominant IgA deposition
• Arthritis or arthralgia
• Renal involvement (proteinuria >3 g/24 hr), hematuria, or red cell casts

Lab findings seen in HSP are nonspecific and include leukocytosis, mild anemia, and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP). The platelet count is normal in HSP. A skin biopsy specimen can be useful in confirming leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA and C3 deposition by immunofluorescence.

The image given below shows IgA and C3 deposition in vessels seen on immunofluorescence of skin biopsy in HSP.

Other options:

Immunosuppressants like azathioprine, methotrexate and cyclosporine are used in a variety of rheumatologic disorders like vasculitis, arthritis, inflammatory bowel diseases like Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, autoimmune hepatitis, and lupus nephritis.
questions.learning: Glucocorticoids — The clinical scenario is suggestive of Henoch Schonlein's purpura (HSP). Glucocorticoids are used to treat HSP.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 26-year-old woman presents with a palpable thyroid nodule and intermittent neck discomfort. Ultrasonography shows a hypoechoic nodule with microcalcifications, and fine-needle aspiration reveals characteristic nuclear features. What is the most common type of thyroid cancer suggested by these findings?
questions.explanation: In a young female with a palpable thyroid nodule and ultrasound features such as microcalcifications (psammoma bodies), Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common and most likely diagnosis. It represents approximately 80% of all thyroid malignancies. The "characteristic nuclear changes" mentioned typically include enlarged, pale nuclei with "Orphan Annie eye" appearance, nuclear grooves, and intranuclear inclusions. Follicular carcinoma (Option B) is the second most common but usually lacks microcalcifications and presents in slightly older age groups. Medullary carcinoma (Option C) arises from C-cells and is less common. Anaplastic carcinoma (Option D) is an extremely aggressive tumor typically seen in elderly patients, which does not fit the 26-year-old profile. Papillary cancer has a very favorable prognosis despite its tendency for early lymph node spread. Management involves surgical resection followed by radioiodine ablation and TSH suppression therapy. The combination of patient age, ultrasound findings, and specific nuclear histology is diagnostic
questions.learning: In a young female with a palpable thyroid nodule and ultrasound features such as microcalcifications (psammoma bodies), Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the most common and most likely diagnosis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 70-year-old man presents with unilateral hearing loss. On examination, a small perforation is noted on his left tympanic membrane. What will be the left-sided Rinne's test finding in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Negative

This patient with unilateral hearing loss and a small perforation of his tympanic membrane is likely to have conductive hearing loss in the left ear, which will show a negative Rinne's test in the affected ear.

Tuning fork tests are performed commonly with tuning forks of frequencies such as 128, 256, 512, 1024, etc. The tuning fork of 512 Hz is considered ideal as forks of lower frequencies produce a sense of bone vibration while those of higher frequencies have a shorter decay time. Some examples of commonly done tuning fork tests are as follows:

Rinne’s test is done by placing a vibrating tuning fork on the patient’s mastoid and when he stops hearing, it is brought beside the external auditory meatus (EAC). If he still hears the sound, air conduction (AC) is better than bone conduction (BC). The inferences are as follows:

• Rinne's test is considered positive (normal) when the air conduction AC>BC is seen in normal people and people with sensorineural deafness.
• It is considered negative when the BC>AC, and is seen in patients with conductive deafness. It suggests a minimum hearing loss of 15-20 dB.

Weber test is done by placing a vibrating tuning in the middle of the forehead or the vertex and the patient is asked in which ear the sound is heard. The inferences are as follows:

• A normal result is achieved when the sound heard equally in both ears
• In conductive deafness, it is lateralized to the worse ear
• In sensorineural deafness, it is lateralized to the better ear

Other options:

Option A: Rinne's test is positive in normal subjects.

Option B: Rinne's test is falsely negative in patients with sudden severe unilateral sensorineural hearing loss.

Option B: There is no such interpretation as intermediate in Rinne's test.
questions.learning: Negative — This patient with unilateral hearing loss and a small perforation of his tympanic membrane is likely to have conductive hearing loss in the left ear, which will show a negative Rinne's test in the affected ear.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
Which of the following statements are true?

1. Due to increasing mammography, there occurs over-diagnosis of breast carcinoma
2. Colon cancer screening is done by digital rectal examination
3. Oral cancer screening is done by visual inspection
4. Cervix cancer screening is done by a pap smear
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 3, 4

Statements 1, 3 and 4 are true.

Screening with noninvasive tests for common cancers aims to achieve early diagnosis, enable less invasive surgical treatments with reduced complications, and potentially improve surgical cure and overall survival rates.

Statement 1: Mammography as a routine screening tool has been found to lower breast cancer mortality at an acceptable cost. In the United Kingdom, an expert panel reported a 20% reduction in breast cancer mortality due to screening, despite the occurrence of overdiagnosis. The panel recommended continuing breast screening due to its significant benefits.

Statement 3: Visual inspection of the oral cavity is widely used for screening oral cancer. The target population includes individuals aged 30 and above who use tobacco and/or alcohol. Visual inspection is advantageous due to its feasibility, safety, acceptability, accuracy in detecting precancerous and cancerous lesions, and cost-effectiveness in reducing oral cancer mortality.

Statement 4: Pap smear is a screening test for cervical cancer. Cervical cancer screening should start at age 21. Women aged 21-29 should have Pap smear every 3 years, while women aged 30-65 should have both HPV and Pap co-test every 5 years.

Other statements:

Statement 2: American Cancer Society guidelines recommend colon cancer screening for average-risk individuals starting at age 50. Screening options include:

• Yearly fecal occult blood testing (FOBT) / fecal immunohistochemical testing (FIT)
• Flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 years,
• FOBT/FIT and flexible sigmoidoscopy in combination every 5 years, or
• Colonoscopy every 10 years.
questions.learning: 1, 3, 4 Statements 1, 3 and 4 are true. Screening with noninvasive tests for common cancers aims to achieve early diagnosis, enable less invasive surgical treatments with reduced complications, and potentially improve surgical cure and overall survival rates.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A young child presented with mild intermittent upper abdominal pain. X-ray is given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Morgagni hernia

The clinical features and the chest X-ray showing an opacity in the right cardiophrenic angle are suggestive of Morgagni hernia.

Congenital diaphragmatic hernia(CDH) of anteromedial location is the Morgagni hernia. Here the defect is anterior and retrosternal. It is rarer than bochdalek hernia and accounts for only 2-5% of CDH. About 90% of the cases occur on the right side.

It is less symptomatic than bochdalek hernia and the diagnosis is usually delayed until childhood. The patient presents with respiratory or upper GI symptoms. Respiratory symptoms like distress, tachypnea, and recurrent pulmonary infections are common in children. Other symptoms are abdominal pain, dyspnea, flatulence, and indigestion.

Radiographic findings:

• Radiolucent paracardiac shadow may be seen retrosternally on lateral chest x-ray if there is bowel herniation.
• Rounded opacity in the right cardiophrenic angle may be seen if there is herniation of omentum or solid organs.
• A CT scan may be used to confirm the diagnosis.

Surgical repair is indicated in all cases either by a thoracic or abdominal approach.

Other options:

Bochdalek hernia: It is more common than Morgagni hernia. Here the defect is posterolateral in location. Respiratory distress is experienced by most infants. In the pediatric age group, symptoms are predominantly respiratory due to pulmonary hypoplasia. In adults, it is usually asymptomatic and is incidentally found. About 85% of the cases are left-sided.

Gastric volvulus: This is an uncommon condition and presents with the characteristic Borchardt triad which includes:

• Sudden-onset severe upper abdominal pain
• Recurrent retching with the production of little vomitus
• Inability to pass a nasogastric (NG) tube

It can be organoaxial or mesentroaxial. Chest X-ray may show intrathoracic upside-down stomach and retrosternal or mediastinal air-fluid level.

Image showing intrathoracic gastric volvulus with mediastinal gastric bubble-

Eventration of the diaphragm: It refers to the abnormal contour of the dome of the diaphragm without any disruption to the diaphragmatic continuity. It usually involves a segment of the hemidiaphragm. It can cause respiratory distress in newborns and is usually asymptomatic in adults.

Radiographic findings: The affected portion of the hemidiaphragm is elevated and is seen as a smooth hump, while the normal contour is seen in the remaining part. 'Double diaphragmatic contour' may be seen in frontal view and is confirmed with a lateral X-ray.

Image showing eventration of the right dome of the diaphragm-

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: CT scan of a patient with laryngeal carcinoma is shown below. What is the staging?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. T4N1M0

The given CT image depicts a mass invading the thyroid cartilage as pointed by the red arrows. This indicates a tumor (T) stage of T4. Among the given options, T4N1M0 is the only option with a T4 staging and hence the best answer.

Laryngeal cancer is more commonly seen in men. Alcohol, tobacco, and previous radiation to the neck region are some of the risk factors for the development of laryngeal cancer. The most common type is squamous cell carcinoma.

Larynx is divided into three regions - supraglottis, glottis, and subglottis. In the TNM system: T indicates the extent of the tumor, N indicates lymph node involvement, and M indicates distant metastasis.

TNM classification of laryngeal carcinoma:

Tumor (T)

• T1: Only one site/subsite is involved (one named structure) with both vocal cords mobile.

• T1a: Only one vocal cord involved
• T1b: Involvement of both vocal cords

• T2: Spread to adjacent sites/subsites

• T2a: Both vocal cords are mobile
• T2b: Slight impairment in the mobility of vocal cord

• T3

• Fixed vocal cord
• Involvement of pre-epiglottic space, para-glottic space, post-cricoid space, or inner cortex of thyroid

• T4a: Local invasion.

• Anteriorly: Thyroid cartilage, thyroid gland, strap muscles
• Superiorly: Tongue muscles
• Inferiorly: Trachea
• Posteriorly: Esophagus

• T4b: Unresectable

• Involvement of prevertebral space, carotid sheath, or mediastinum

Regional lymph nodes (N)

• Nx: Cannot be assessed
• No: No regional lymph node metastasis
• N1: Metastasis in a single ipsilateral lymph node, ≤3cm
• N2: Metastasis in a single ipsilateral lymph node, >3cm but <6cm or multiple ipsilateral lymph nodes or bilateral lymph nodes none more than 6cm
• N3: Metastasis in a lymph node more than 6cm

Distant metastasis (M)

• Mx: Metastasis cannot be assessed
• Mo: No distant metastasis
• M1: Distant metastasis
questions.learning: T4N1M0 — The given CT image depicts a mass invading the thyroid cartilage as pointed by the red arrows. This indicates a tumor (T) stage of T4.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is used for the treatment of Datura poisoning?
questions.explanation: Datura contains belladonna alkaloids (atropine, hyoscine, and hyoscyamine), which cause a severe anticholinergic syndrome. The specific antidote for Datura poisoning is Physostigmine. Physostigmine is a tertiary amine acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that, unlike neostigmine, crosses the blood-brain barrier. This allows it to reverse both the peripheral symptoms (tachycardia, dry skin) and, more importantly, the central nervous system symptoms (agitation, delirium, hallucinations) of Datura poisoning. Atropine (Option B) would worsen the poisoning since Datura already contains atropine. Sodium nitrite (Option C) is used in the treatment of cyanide poisoning. Neostigmine (Option D) is a quaternary amine that does not cross into the brain and therefore cannot address the critical central delirium seen in these patients. Because of the risk of causing seizures or bradycardia, physostigmine should be administered slowly and under close cardiac monitoring. It is a life-saving intervention for severe anticholinergic toxicity
questions.learning: Datura contains belladonna alkaloids (atropine, hyoscine, and hyoscyamine), which cause a severe anticholinergic syndrome. The specific antidote for Datura poisoning is Physostigmine.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Image of Rickettsial morula in a monocyte is shown below. Identify the organism.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ehrlichia chaffeensis

The organism given in the image is Ehrlichia chaffeensis. The peripheral blood smear shows a morula, an intracellular inclusion body in a monocyte.

Ehrlichia chaffeensis is a gram-negative, obligate intracellular bacteria that are transmitted by hard ticks such as the lone star tick.

Clinically, the symptom onset is typically within one-three weeks of exposure. Patients may present with fever, headache, myalgia, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, and weight loss. Rashes are generally absent. Severe human monocytic ehrlichiosis is characterized by meningoencephalitis, renal failure, respiratory failure, and shock.

Diagnosis is by demonstration of the characteristic morulae in the mononuclear cells such as monocytes. Serological studies such as indirect fluorescent antibody tests and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) detection can also be used.

The treatment of choice for human monocytic ehrlichiosis is doxycycline.

Other options:

Option A: Rickettsia rickettsii causes rocky mountain spotted fever. It is transmitted by ticks. Patients present with fever, headache and rash.

Option B: Rickettsia conorii causes Mediterranean spotted fever. The parasite is transmitted by ticks and the patients present with fever, headache, rash, and eschar (tache noire).

Option D: Anaplasma causes human granulocyte anaplasmosis. It is transmitted by ticks. Clinical features are fever, headache, and myalgia. Inclusions in granulocytes are seen.
questions.learning: Ehrlichia chaffeensis — The organism given in the image is Ehrlichia chaffeensis. The peripheral blood smear shows a morula, an intracellular inclusion body in a monocyte.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child with thalassemia is undergoing multiple blood transfusions. What is the best method to detect iron overload?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Liver iron concentration

The best method to assess iron overload is quantitative liver iron using T2 MRI. It eliminates the need for invasive procedures like liver biopsy.

Excessive iron stores resulting from transfusions are a major concern in the management of β-thalassemia major. Accurate assessment of iron overload is crucial for optimal treatment.

Quantitative measurement of cardiac iron by T2 MRI (option B) is initiated at the age of 10. However, there can be a discrepancy between liver iron and cardiac iron levels due to variations in tissue loading and unloading rates.

While serial serum ferritin levels (option C) can be used as a screening tool, they may not accurately reflect quantitative iron stores. Relying solely on serum ferritin levels can lead to undertreatment or overtreatment of iron overload.

Normally, iron in the plasma is bound to transferrin. But in iron-overload conditions, iron exceeds the iron binding capacity leading to the appearance of non-transferrin-bound iron (option D). It can act as an indicator of iron overload, but it is influenced by plasma factors like citrate, uric acid, and albumin. Hence, it cannot be used as a tool to measure quantitative iron overload that can help guide in planning chelation therapies.

Other tests that help calculate iron overload include echocardiography, bone mass densitometry, and testing for endocrinopathy. These tests are done at the time of diagnosis and done yearly to monitor iron overload. Serum ferritin tests can be done every 3 months.

Hypothyroidism, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, growth hormone deficiency, hypoparathyroidism, and diabetes mellitus are seen due to iron deposition in endocrine organs. Iron deposition in the heart can lead to heart failure, arrhythmias, and cardiac-related mortality.

Iron chelation therapy is recommended when serum ferritin levels exceed 1,000 ng/mL and/or liver iron concentration is above 5,000 µg/g dry weight. It is not approved for children under 2 years of age. Three iron chelators are available: deferoxamine, deferasirox, and deferiprone. Deferoxamine is administered subcutaneously or intravenously due to its poor oral bioavailability. Deferasirox is a once-daily oral iron chelator. Deferiprone is an oral iron chelator approved as a second-line agent.
questions.learning: Liver iron concentration — The best method to assess iron overload is quantitative liver iron using T2 MRI. It eliminates the need for invasive procedures like liver biopsy.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A young male who is a professional trumpet blower presented with a swelling on the left side of the neck. On examination, there is a gurgling sound when compressing the swelling. As the X-ray neck was inconclusive a CT neck was taken which is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Laryngocele

The given CT image along with the examination finding of Bryce sign is suggestive of laryngocoele.

Laryngocoele:

* Air-filled cavity within the larynx developing in the saccule.

* The patient presents with a neck swelling that is soft and compressible.

* Bryce sign: on compressing the swelling, there is a gurgling sound.

It is seen in trumpet players, glass-blowers, or weight lifters due to raised transglottic air pressure. It presents with hoarseness, cough, and if large, causes obstruction of the airway.

Types of laryngocoele are:

* Internal - confined within the larynx and presents as distension of false cord and aryepiglottic fold.

* External - the distended saccule herniates through the thyroid membrane and presents in the neck. It presents as a reducible swelling in the neck, increasing in size on coughing or performing Valsalva manoeuvres.

* Mixed - both external and internal compounds are seen

Diagnosis is done by indirect laryngoscopy, soft tissue AP and lateral views of the neck x-ray with Valsalva. CT scan helps to find out the extent of the lesion. External type is managed by surgical excision through an external neck incision. Internal type is managed by marsupialization and endoscopic carbon dioxide laser resection.

Other options:

Option A: Zenker diverticulum or pharyngeal pouch is a pulsion-pseudodiverticulum and results from herniation of mucosa and submucosa through the Killian triangle (or dehiscence of Killian). Killian’s triangle represents a weak space located between two parts of the inferior constrictor muscle.

Option C: A tracheoesophageal fistula is an abnormal fistula communication between the Esophagus and Trachea. Type C lesion is associated with proximal esophageal atresia and distal TEF, the proximal blind pouch ends approximately at the distance of one or two vertebral bodies from the distal TEF.

Option D: A tonsillar cyst is due to blockage of a tonsillar crypt and appears as a yellowish swelling over the tonsil. Very often it is symptomless. It can be easily drained.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following statements are false about collagen?
options: Prolysyl and lysyl hydroxylase are involved in post translational modification
Phenylalanine is the most abundant AA in its structure
Triple helix structure is important for its function
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Phenylalanine is the most abundant AA in its structure

Glycine is the most abundant amino acid(AA) in collagen and not phenylalanine.

Collagen is the most abundant protein in the animal world. It has a triple helical structure, forming a right-handed superhelix. A striking characteristic of collagen is the occurrence of glycine residues at every third position.

Proline and hydroxyproline confer rigidity on the collagen molecule. Hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine are formed by the post-translational hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues catalyzed by the enzyme prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase, whose cofactors are ascorbic acid (vitamin C) and α-ketoglutarate. Collagen is arranged in a quarter-staggered arrangement and further stabilized by covalent cross-links.
questions.learning: Phenylalanine is the most abundant AA in its structure Glycine is the most abundant amino acid(AA) in collagen and not phenylalanine. Collagen is the most abundant protein in the animal world.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old lady presents with complaints of fatigue, muscle weakness along with bilateral multiple renal calculi which were picked up on a routine ultrasound. Further workup revealed serum calcium levels of 11.4 mg%. What is the next best investigation required to arrive at a diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sestamibi scan

The patient has features suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism:

• Hypercalcemia (11.4 mg/dL)
• Recurrent/multiple renal calculi (“stones”)
• Muscle weakness and fatigue

The diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism is first established biochemically by demonstrating elevated or inappropriately normal serum PTH in the presence of hypercalcemia. Once the biochemical diagnosis is made, the best imaging modality for preoperative localization of a parathyroid adenoma is a Tc-99m Sestamibi scan.

Why not the other options?

• A. MRI neck: Not routinely used as the first imaging modality; reserved for difficult or recurrent cases.
• C. CECT head and neck: Not the standard initial investigation for parathyroid adenoma localization.
• D. NCCT head and neck: Does not adequately localize parathyroid lesions.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a hospital pharmacy, a total budget of ₹50,000 is allocated for purchasing three types of drugs: ₹35,000 for A drugs, ₹10,000 for B drugs, and the remaining amount for C drugs. Which type of analysis is being applied in this budgeting scenario?
questions.explanation: The scenario described is a classic application of ABC Analysis in inventory management. This method categorizes items based on their cumulative cost and consumption volume. Category A (Option B) items are the few high-value drugs that account for the majority of the budget (here, 35,000 Rs for type A). Category B items have moderate value (10,000 Rs), and Category C items are the numerous low-cost items that consume the smallest portion of the budget. VED Analysis (Option C) categorizes drugs based on their clinical criticality (Vital, Essential, Desirable) rather than cost. Network Analysis (Option A) and System Analysis (Option D) are broader management tools for planning and process evaluation. ABC analysis allows hospital administrators to prioritize strict control over high-investment (Type A) drugs while using more relaxed control for low-cost (Type C) items. Combining ABC and VED analyses is the gold standard for efficient hospital pharmacy management, ensuring that critical life-saving drugs are always available without wasting the budget on non-critical, expensive items
questions.learning: The scenario described is a classic application of ABC Analysis in inventory management. This method categorizes items based on their cumulative cost and consumption volume.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is the diluting segment of the kidney?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ascending thick loop of Henle

The ascending thick limb of the loop of Henle is called the diluting segment.

In the ascending limb, there is the movement of Na+ and Cl– out of the tubular lumen, and the tubular fluid becomes more dilute.

When the fluid reaches the top of the ascending limb, it becomes hypotonic to plasma.
questions.learning: Ascending thick loop of Henle — The ascending thick limb of the loop of Henle is called the diluting segment. In the ascending limb, there is the movement of Na+ and Cl– out of the tubular lumen, and the tubular fluid becomes more dilute.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is true about BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry)?
options: It can be used for screening of hearing loss.
It can be used for assessing sensorineural hearing loss.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It can be used for assessing sensorineural hearing loss.

BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry) or ABR (Auditory Brainstem Response) is an objective test that records electrical activity occurring in the auditory pathway and can be used for assessing sensorineural hearing loss.

* The recording is made from brain stem potentials

* Click stimulus is used

* Responses are not frequency specific

* Can be performed in awake and restless patients

* Responses begin after 1 -10 milliseconds after stimuli

* Suitable for even younger children

Uses:

* To objectively find hearing threshold- wave-V appears 10dB above the hearing level obtained through PTA

* Best audiometric test for:

* Confirming hearing loss in infants

* Diagnosing acoustic neuroma

*

* Differentiating cochlear and retro-cochlear hearing loss

* Diagnosing non-organic hearing loss.

Auditory brainstem response:

* Used to elicit brainstem responses to auditory stimulation by clicks or tone bursts.

* Non-invasive technique to find the integrity of central auditory pathways through the eighth nerve, pons and midbrain.

TYPE
SITE OF ORIGIN

Wave I
Distal part of CN VIII

Wave II
Proximal part of CN VIII near the brainstem.

Wave III
Cochlear nucleus

Wave IV
Superior olivary complex

Wave V
Lateral lemniscus

Wave VI and VII
Inferior colliculus

Pearl PF1553: BERA (Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry) or ABR (Auditory Brainstem Response)

It is an objective test that records electrical activity occurring in the auditory pathway.

Normally, 7 waves are produced in the first 10ms.

* Wave I – distal part of the cochlear nerve

* Wave II –proximal part of the cochlear nerve

* Wave III – cochlear nucleus

* Wave IV – superior olivary complex

* Wave V – lateral lemniscus

* Wave VI – inferior colliculus

* Wave VII - medial geniculate body

Findings:

* Conductive or cochlear pathology- delayed wave-I but inter-peak latency of I-V is normal

* Retrocochlear pathology- wave-I present, rest of the waves absent

* Acoustic neuroma or vestibular schwannoma- increased inter-peak latency of wave I-V and increased inter-aural latency of wave V > 0.2ms.

Uses:

* To objectively find hearing threshold- wave-V appears 10dB above the hearing level obtained through PTA

* Best audiometric test for:

* Confirming hearing loss in infants

* Diagnosing acoustic neuroma

*

* Differentiating cochlear and retro-cochlear hearing loss

* Diagnosing non-organic hearing loss.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Neurology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 34-year-old man comes to the emergency department due to severe headache. The patient describes unbearable, throbbing pain around his right eye that awakened him. Over the past week, he has had several similar episodes, which spontaneously resolved after 20-30 minutes. On physical examination, he appears restless and paces in the room. There is mild conjunctival injection and miosis of the right eye. Neurologic examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's current symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cluster headache

Cluster headache is a trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia characterized by severe unilateral periorbital pain with ipsilateral autonomic features like conjunctival injection, lacrimation, nasal congestion and horner syndrome.

• Severe, stabbing/throbbing periorbital unilateral pain
• Short attacks (15–180 min), occurring in clusters over weeks
• Often awakens patient from sleep
• Patient is restless/agitated (unlike migraine where patient prefers dark room)

Why not other options (short):

• A. Cavernous sinus thrombosis: Fever, toxic patient, ophthalmoplegia & CN palsies → not brief recurrent attacks.
• C. Migraine: Lasts hours–days, patient lies still in dark room → here patient is restless.
• D. Trigeminal neuralgia: Seconds-long electric shock pain, no autonomic signs.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which cellular component is exclusively present in gram-negative bacteria and not found in gram-positive organisms?
questions.explanation: Gram-negative bacteria possess a complex cell envelope that includes an outer membrane. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS), also known as endotoxin, is a major component located exclusively in the outer leaflet of this outer membrane. It is not found in gram-positive bacteria. Capsules (Option A) and Flagella (Option D) are found in both gram-positive and gram-negative species. Peptidoglycan (Option B) is a core component of the cell wall for both types, although gram-positive bacteria have a significantly thicker layer than gram-negative bacteria. LPS is clinically significant because its release into the bloodstream can trigger a massive immune response, leading to endotoxic shock and systemic inflammation. Therefore, lipopolysaccharide is the unique biochemical marker of the gram-negative cell wall
questions.learning: Gram-negative bacteria possess a complex cell envelope that includes an outer membrane. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS), also known as endotoxin, is a major component located exclusively in the outer leaflet of this outer membrane.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The formula for urea clearance is U*V/P, where U is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Urine urea in mg /100ml

‘U’ in the urea clearance stands for urine concentration of urea in mg /100ml.

The formula for renal clearance of a substance is,

Clearance (C) = U × V / P,

where

U = Urine concentration of the substance in mg / ml

V = Urine flow rate in ml/min

P = Plasma concentration of substance in mg /ml.

Renal clearance of a substance is the volume of plasma that is completely cleared of the substance by the kidneys per unit of time.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: During recovery from anaesthesia, which of the following drugs is used for the reversal of neuromuscular blockade?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Neostigmine

Neostigmine is a cholinesterase inhibitor commonly used during reversal of anaesthesia.

Reversal agents commonly used in clinical practice:

Cholinesterase inhibitors - Neostigmine (most common), edrophonium, and pyridostigmine.
Sugammadex, a cyclodextrin, is the first selective relaxant binding agent for rocuronium and vecuronium.
L-cysteine causes the inactivation of gantacurium.

Other options:

Option B, C:  Anticholinergic drugs like glycopyrrolate and atropine are not used for the reversal of neuromuscular blockade. They only attenuate the undesirable muscarinic effects of anticholinesterase reversal agents.

Option D: Propofol is a barbiturate group of drug which is used for induction of anaesthesia.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following conditions shown in the given CT is associated with the Holman-Miller sign?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Juvenile nasopharnygeal angiofibroma

The given CT showing the Holman-Miller sign is associated with nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.

Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a benign but locally invasive tumor predominant in adolescent males aged 10-20 years. It arises from the posterior part of the nasal cavity, close to the superior margin of the sphenopalatine foramen. These patients have a hamartomatous nidus of vascular tissue in the nasopharynx that grows to form angiofibroma under the influence of testosterone. Therefore, it is thought to be testosterone-dependent.

Angiofibroma can extend into the nasal cavity causing obstruction, epistaxis, paranasal sinuses, pterygomaxillary fossa, infratemporal fossa, cheek, orbits causing proptosis, frog-face deformity, and cranial cavity. The clinical features include:

* Profuse, recurrent, spontaneous epistaxis - most common; Internal maxillary artery is the most common source artery of nasal bleeding followed by ascending pharyngeal artery and external, internal, and common carotid arteries.

* Progressive nasal obstruction and denasal speech - due to mass in the postnasal space

* Conductive hearing loss and otitis media with effusion - due to obstruction of the eustachian tube

* Sessile, lobulated, or smooth mass in the nasopharynx

* Other clinical features include the broadening of the nasal bridge, proptosis, cheek swelling, involvement of IInd, IIIrd, IVth, and VIth cranial nerves

Diagnosis typically involves contrast-enhanced CT scans, which reveal the tumour's size and any bony destruction, along with characteristic signs such as anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary sinus known as the Antral sign or Holman-Miller sign (shown in the image below). Biopsy of the mass is generally avoided due to the risk of severe bleeding.

Surgical excision remains the mainstay of treatment, with various approaches depending on tumour extent. Common surgical techniques include:

* Transpalatine approach

* Lateral Rhinotomy

* Endoscopic Techniques: minimally invasive

* Maxillary Swing Approach: larger tumours.

* Intracranial-Extracranial Approach: significant intracranial extension

Other Options:

Option A: Haller cells are a type of ethmoidal cells that are situated on the roof of the maxillary sinus. Sometimes they may enlarge and block the opening of the maxillary sinus leading to maxillary sinusitis.

Option C: Antrochoanal polyp is a type of non-neoplastic nasal polypoidal masses of edematous nasal or sinus mucosa which arises from the mucosa of the maxillary antrum near its accessory ostium. The clinical features include unilateral nasal obstruction, mucoid nasal discharge, and a hyponasal voice.

Option D: Unilateral obstruction of the nasal cavity due to the presence of mass and nasal bleeding is suggestive of the diagnosis of rhinosporidiosis. Rhinosporidiosis is a chronic granulomatous disease caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi. It is most prevalent in rural districts, among persons bathing in public ponds or working in stagnant water, such as rice fields.
questions.learning: Juvenile nasopharnygeal angiofibroma — The given CT showing the Holman-Miller sign is associated with nasopharyngeal angiofibroma. Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a benign but locally invasive tumor predominant in adolescent males aged 10-20 years.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient is found on eye examination to have a deep anterior chamber and a jet-black pupil. He is prescribed +12 diopter spectacles. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical findings of a deep anterior chamber, jet-black pupil, and a strong +12D prescription are diagnostic of aphakia. Aphakia is the complete absence of the natural crystalline lens, typically following cataract surgery without intraocular lens (IOL) implantation. Without the lens, the eye's refractive power drops significantly (from ~60D to ~44D), necessitating a strong convex (plus) lens for correction. The jet-black appearance occurs because there are no lens reflections. Pseudophakia (Option A) refers to an eye with an artificial IOL; such patients usually require minimal correction. Myopia (Option C) requires concave (minus) lenses. Simple hypermetropia (Option D) usually requires much lower power convex lenses than +12D. Therefore, the total absence of the lens, confirmed by the extreme hypermetropia, defines the condition as aphakia

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In the homunculus, which of the following has maximum representation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Increased preciseness of movements

In a homunculus, the more the representation of an area, the more precise the movements are.

• The relative sizes of the cortical receiving areas of the sensory homunculus are proportionate to the use of the part.
• The sizes of these areas are directly proportional to the number of specialized sensory receptors in each respective peripheral area of the body.
• Some body parts are represented by large areas in the somatic cortex—the lips the greatest of all, followed by the face and thumb, whereas the trunk and lower part of the body are represented by relatively small areas.
