questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Punched-out ulcers in the esophagus are caused by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Herpes-simplex virus

Infection with Herpes simplex virus (HSV) typically results in punched-out ulcers in the esophagus.

HSV esophagitis commonly occurs in immunocompromised patients. For diagnosis, the biopsy sample should be taken from the edge of the ulcer. The following microscopic findings are noted:

• Ballooning degeneration
• Ground-glass changes in nuclei
• Cowdry type A intranuclear inclusion bodies

Note: CMV esophagitis causes shallow ulcerations. The biopsy is taken from the base of the ulcer and shows characteristic nuclear and cytoplasmic inclusions bodies.
questions.learning: Herpes-simplex virus Infection with Herpes simplex virus (HSV) typically results in punched-out ulcers in the esophagus. HSV esophagitis commonly occurs in immunocompromised patients.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: At a primary health center, a child received the BCG vaccine. On follow-up, the mother reports that no scar has developed at the vaccination site. Medical records confirm that the vaccine was administered. What should the medical officer advise the mother?
options: Reassure that nothing else is required
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Reassure that nothing else is required

Absence of a BCG scar does not indicate vaccine failure and does not correlate reliably with protection against tuberculosis.

As long as BCG vaccination is documented as given, revaccination is not recommended, regardless of scar formation.

Hence, the mother should be reassured, and no further intervention such as repeat BCG or Mantoux testing is required.
questions.learning: Reassure that nothing else is required Absence of a BCG scar does not indicate vaccine failure and does not correlate reliably with protection against tuberculosis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In which of the following is atropine contraindicated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acute congestive glaucoma

Atropine is contraindicated in acute congestive glaucoma.

Acute congestive or angle closure glaucoma is caused by the opposition of the peripheral iris against the trabecular meshwork. This obstructs the aqueous outflow by closing an already narrow-angle of the anterior chamber leading to an acute increase in intraocular pressure(IOP). It can be precipitated by dim light, mydriatics like atropine.

It presents as sudden onset of severe unilateral eye pain or a headache associated with blurred vision, rainbow-colored halos around bright lights, nausea, and vomiting. The physical exam will reveal a fixed midpoint pupil and a hazy or cloudy cornea with marked conjunctival injection.

Management of acute condition includes rapid lowering of IOP by mannitol or glycerol, acetazolamide, and topical antiglaucoma drugs. Definitive management is done by laser peripheral iridotomy or filtration surgery.

Atropine is indicated as cycloplegic to reduce pain and prevent synechiae in corneal ulcers and acute anterior uveitis. It is the initial management in malignant glaucoma.
questions.learning: Acute congestive glaucoma Atropine is contraindicated in acute congestive glaucoma. Acute congestive or angle closure glaucoma is caused by the opposition of the peripheral iris against the trabecular meshwork.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The long left recurrent laryngeal nerve is due to the persistence of which arch artery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 6th arch

The long left recurrent laryngeal nerve is due to the persistence of the left 6th arch artery.

During the development, the laryngeal nerves initially arise below the 6th arch artery and cross here to innervate the intrinsic muscles of the larynx. As the larynx moves cranially relative to the aortic arch arteries, the recurrent laryngeal nerves on the right and left sides are caught under the 6th arch arteries.

On the right side, the distal 6th arch artery disappears. Since there is no 5th arch artery, the right recurrent laryngeal nerve is caught under the 4th arch artery which becomes the future right subclavian artery.

On the left side, the 6th arch artery persists, which develops into ductus arteriosus, which later forms ligamentum arteriosum. Due to the persistence of the 6th arch artery, the left recurrent laryngeal nerve is caught under it and therefore, has a relatively long course.
questions.learning: 6th arch The long left recurrent laryngeal nerve is due to the persistence of the left 6th arch artery. During the development, the laryngeal nerves initially arise below the 6th arch artery and cross here to innervate the intrinsic muscles of the larynx.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 58-year-old man comes to the physician for evaluation of increasing swelling in his left cheek and recurrent oral ulcers for 1 year. He has smoked a pack of cigarettes daily for 25 years. Examination shows firm, nontender swelling above the angle of jaw. USG guided biopsy shows adenoid cystic carcinoma. A left sided total parotidectomy is performed. This patient is at greatest risk for which of the following complications?
options: Hyperesthesia of the left ear lobe
Impaired taste of the posterior 1/3 of the tongue
Flushing of the right cheek while eating
Inability to wrinkle the left side of the forehead
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Inability to wrinkle the left side of the forehead

The facial nerve runs through the parotid gland and divides into its branches inside it (classic “pes anserinus”). So when you remove the gland (especially total parotidectomy), you can injure:

• Temporal branch: loss of forehead wrinkling, eyebrow droop
• Zygomatic branch: inability to close eye
• Buccal branch: weak upper lip movement
• Marginal mandibular: asymmetric smile
• Cervical: platysma weakness

Other Options:

A) Hyperesthesia of the left ear lobe: Parotid surgery actually risks loss of sensation (hypoesthesia) of the ear lobe due to injury of the great auricular nerve(C2–C3). Hyperesthesia (increased sensation) isn’t the classic complication.

B) Impaired taste of posterior 1/3 of tongue: Posterior 1/3 taste = CN IX (glossopharyngeal).That’s not running through the parotid like CN VII does.

C) Flushing of the right cheek while eating: That’s Frey syndrome (gustatory sweating/flushing) — due to aberrant reinnervation of sweat glands by parasympathetic fibers after parotidectomy.

Two issues:

1. It would occur on the same side as surgery (left), not right.
2. Also, the question says “greatest risk” — facial nerve injury is the big one in total parotidectomy.

✅ D) Inability to wrinkle the left side of the forehead because wrinkling the forehead = frontal branch of the facial nerve.
questions.learning: Inability to wrinkle the left side of the forehead — The facial nerve runs through the parotid gland and divides into its branches inside it (classic “pes anserinus”).

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The image shows a histological section of the thyroid gland. Which substance is secreted by the cell labeled X in the image?
questions.explanation: The provided histological image shows thyroid follicles lined by follicular cells, with a distinct cluster of parafollicular cells (also known as C-cells) labeled as 'X'. These C-cells are responsible for the synthesis and secretion of calcitonin, a peptide hormone that plays a role in calcium homeostasis by inhibiting osteoclast activity and lowering blood calcium levels. Thyroxine (T4) (Option A) is produced by the follicular cells that surround the colloid. Parathormone (Option C) is produced by the parathyroid glands, which are distinct organs usually located posterior to the thyroid. Serotonin (Option D) is primarily produced by enterochromaffin cells in the gut or neurons in the brain. Because the cell labeled 'X' is clearly situated between the follicles (parafollicularly), its hormone product is definitively calcitonin. Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from these specific C-cells
questions.learning: The provided histological image shows thyroid follicles lined by follicular cells, with a distinct cluster of parafollicular cells (also known as C-cells) labeled as 'X'.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Revised A 70-year-old man presents with chronic low back pain, fatigue, and headaches for the last few weeks. On examination, he has pallor and bony tenderness. Lab investigations revealed an increased ESR and his skull radiograph revealed several punched-out lytic lesions. Which of the following is the best investigation for this patient in the options given below ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Serum electrophoresis showing IgG

The given clinical condition is highly suggestive of multiple myeloma and in the given options,  serum electrophoresis showing M band in the gamma globulin region is preferred for multiple myeloma.

Bone marrow biopsy is diagnostic for multiple myeloma, where the neoplastic plasma cells can be seen.

Plasma cell dyscrasias are B-cell proliferations that contain neoplastic plasma cells that secrete a monoclonal Ig or Ig fragment.

* Multiple myelomas: Malignant neoplasm of plasma cells characterized by:

* Presence of monoclonal immunoglobulin or light chains in the serum and urine

* Bone destruction (lytic lesions)

* The disease of older adults, with a peak age of incidence of 65 to 70 years

* Signs and symptoms

* Hypercalcemia

* Pathologic fractures/lytic bone lesions

* Renal failure

* Anemia

* Radiography: Punched-out lytic lesions on X-ray

* Electrophoresis: Monoclonal elevation of one immunoglobulin

* Urinalysis: Free kappa and lambda light chains (Bence Jones proteins)

* Bone marrow biopsy: 10 to 20%plasma cells (normal is < 5%)

* Peripheral smear: Rouleaux formation (High level of M proteins in myeloma causes red cells in the peripheral blood smears to stick to one another in linear arrays, a finding referred to as rouleaux formation.)

* Plasma cell tumors are positive for CD138

Pearl PF0580: WHO Classification of Plasma Cell Neoplasms

Plasma cell neoplasms and variants

Plasma cell myeloma

• Non secretory: No secretion of Ig, No M component.

• Smoldering: M protein in serum ≥ 30 g/L and/or ≥10% clonal plasma cells in bone marrow, and no related organ or tissue impairment.

• Plasma-cell leukemia: >20% plasma cells in the peripheral blood or Absolute plasma cell count of >2 X 109/L.

Plasmacytoma

• Solitary plasmacytoma: Localized tumour of monoclonal plasma cells with no clinical features of plasma cell myeloma.

• Extramedullary(extraosseous) plasmacytoma: Localized plasma cell neoplasms that arise in tissues other than bone.

Monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition diseases

• Primary amyloidosis: Tumor secreting light chains that are deposited as beta-pleated sheet structure (amyloid light chain).

• Systemic light and heavy chain diseases: Secrete abnormal light or heavy chain or both, which do not form beta pleated sheet, stain Congo Red or contain amyloid P component.

Plasma cell neoplasms with associated paraneoplastic syndrome

POEMS syndrome- Polyneuropathy, organomegaly, Endocrinopathy, Monoclonal gammopathy, Skin changes.

TEMPI syndrome
questions.learning: Serum electrophoresis showing IgG — The given clinical condition is highly suggestive of multiple myeloma and in the given options, serum electrophoresis showing M band in the gamma globulin region is preferred for multiple myeloma.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: While collecting a blood sample for serum calcium, which is easily alterable, which of the following should be prevented to measure it accurately?
options: If a tourniquet is needed, tie and release as soon as the sample is collected.
Making a fist is not recommended.
Not collecting samples from patients immobilized for long periods of time
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Collecting after exercise.

Blood collection after exercise should be prevented to measure serum calcium accurately.

Option A: A prolonged tourniquet is usually avoided while drawing blood for calcium measurements since hemoconcentration also leads to an increase in serum calcium levels. Hence, the tourniquet should be released as soon as the sample is collected.

Option C: Fist-clenching or forearm exercise can lead to falsely elevated ionized (free) calcium levels. Hence, making a fist while blood collection is not recommended.

Option D: Staying immobilised for long periods of time increases bone resorption and increases calcium levels. Hence, do not collect blood samples for serum calcium estimation in patients who are immobilised for long periods.
questions.learning: Blood collection after exercise should be prevented to measure serum calcium accurately. Option A: A prolonged tourniquet is usually avoided while drawing blood for calcium measurements since hemoconcentration also leads to an increase in serum calcium levels.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 77-year-old man presented with worsening hip and back pain. He also reports weight loss and loss of appetite. The X-ray revealed the given lesions. His PSA levels are elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Prostate cancer

Blastic lesions on X-Ray along with elevated PSA levels, loss of weight, and loss of appetite are suggestive of prostatic carcinoma with metastasis to bones.

Carcinoma of the prostate:

It is the most common malignant tumor in men over the age of 65 years  They may range from indolent lesions that cause no harm to aggressive metastatic tumors. Most cancers are clinically silent and are detected on routine rectal examination or PSA measurements.

Grossly, malignant tissue is gritty and firm in consistency (in contrast to the spongy appearance of benign tissue) and thus more readily palpable on digital rectal examination. They usually arise in the peripheral zone of the gland.

Prostate carcinoma is a type of adenocarcinoma. Therefore, histopathology shows the malignant cells arranged in the form of glands. In contrast to benign glands, malignant glands have tightly packed cells and characteristically lack branching and papillary infoldings. The outer basal cell layer typical of benign glands is absent. The cells may show increased nuclear-cytoplasmic ratio, nuclear atypia, etc. α-methyl acyl-coenzyme A-racemase (AMACR) is positive and is upregulated in prostate cancer.

Local extension most commonly involves the periprostatic tissue, seminal vesicles, and the base of the urinary bladder. Advanced disease may produce ureteral obstruction. Metastasis spreads via the lymphatics to the obturator nodes and the para-aortic nodes. Hematogenous spread occurs chiefly through the bones to the axial skeleton and rarely to the viscera. The bony metastasis is blastic in origin and involves the lumbar spine, proximal femur, pelvis, thoracic spine, and ribs in the decreasing order of frequency.

Management of Prostatic Carcinoma

Stage of cancer
Age>70 or Gleason score=6
Age<70 or Gleason score>6

Early prostate cancer: T1, T2A
Active surveillance
Radical prostatectomy

Locally advanced prostate cancer: T2B, T2C, T3, T4, N1
Brachytherapy + Androgen deprivation therapy
Brachytherapy + Radical prostatectomy

Metastatic prostate cancer

Androgen deprivation therapy

Chemotherapy and radiotherapy (hormone-resistant  tumor)

Radiopharmaceutical therapy (hormone-resistant bony metastasis)

Below image shows histopathology of Prostate carcinoma:

Pearl PF0895: Types of metastasis(osteoblastic or osteolytic) and their primary:

Predominantly osteoblastic:

* Prostate cancer

* Osteosarcoma

* Medullary carcinoma thyroid

Mixed osteoblastic and osteolytic:

* Breast cancer(preponderance toward osteolytic)

* Lymphoma

* Urothelial carcinoma

* Lung cancer

Predominantly osteolytic:

* Renal cell carcinoma

* Multiple myeloma

* Thyroid carcinoma(except medullary carcinoma thyroid)

* Gastrointestinal tract carcinoma

* Malignant melanoma
questions.learning: Prostate cancer Blastic lesions on X-Ray along with elevated PSA levels, loss of weight, and loss of appetite are suggestive of prostatic carcinoma with metastasis to bones.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Which neurotransmitter is involved in Alzheimer's disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acetylcholine

In Alzheimer’s disease there is decrease in Ach due to depletion of the cholinergic neurons. This is reason for the defect in the short term memory.

The cholinergic neurons are lost / decreased in the nucleus basalis of Meynert. There is deficiency of choline acetyltransferase.

Other neurotransmitters that are affected are- norepinephrine in locus ceruleus, somatostatin and corticotropin.

Pearl PF0318: Alzheimer’s disease

Alzheimer’s disease:

* Age of onset > 60 years

* MMSE < 24

* Diagnosis: Clinical

* 2 or more areas of cognitive deficits

* Progressive worsening of memory and other cognitive function

* No disturbance in consciousness

* Other systemic causes must be ruled out

Risk Factors:

* Most important risk factor: Old age

* Other risk factors – Family history, presenilin-1, presenilin-2, Apolipoprotein E4, Ubiquitin, Down syndrome and smoking.

Protective factors: NSAIDs and Apolipoprotein E2

Early findings:

* Anterograde memory loss (immediate recall affected, distant memories preserved)

* Visuospatial deficits (lost in own neighborhood)

* Language difficulties (difficulty finding words)

* Cognitive impairment with a progressive decline

Late findings:

* Psychotic symptoms: Hallucinations

* Dyspraxia: Difficulty to perform learned motor tasks

* Lack of insight regarding deficits

* Non-cognitive neurologic deficits: Pyramidal and extrapyramidal, myoclonus and seizures

* Urinary incontinence

Histopathology:

* Senile plaques (amyloid deposits), neurofibrillary tangles, neuronal loss, synaptic loss, and granulovacuolar degeneration of neurons.

CT/MRI:

* Later stages: Cortical and subcortical atrophy prominent in parietal and temporal lobes, particularly hippocampus.

Treatment:

* NMDA antagonist: Memantine

* Cholinesterase inhibitors: Donepezil, Galantamine, Rivastigmine.
questions.learning: Acetylcholine — In Alzheimer’s disease there is decrease in Ach due to depletion of the cholinergic neurons. This is reason for the defect in the short term memory.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 20-year-old man was brought to the emergency department after a RTA. On presentation, his pulse is 110/minute, RR is 18/minute and BP is 80/60 mmhg. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. eFAST

The given clinical scenario of a patient being hemodynamically unstable after a RTA indicates a probable ongoing hemorrhage and the next step in the management is to perform an eFAST.

Cardiogenic shock, hemorrhagic shock, or pneumothorax are the most likely causes of hypotension in a trauma patient. Ultrasound evaluation using eFAST to look for pericardium, pleural cavities, and abdomen in combination with plain radiographs of the chest and pelvis will usually identify the source of the bleed.

In patients with hypotension due to blunt trauma, the pelvis should be wrapped in a sheet for stabilization until radiography can be done.

eFAST stands for extended FAST and incorporates left and right thoracic views to assess for pneumothorax and haemothorax.

Limitations of eFAST are:

* Operator-dependent

* Bowel gas and subcutaneous air distort images.

* Can miss diaphragm, bowel, and pancreatic injuries

* Unreliable for assessment of the retroperitoneum

* Cannot reliably exclude injury in penetrating trauma

* May need repeating or supplementing with other investigations

FAST stands for Focussed Assessment with Sonography for Trauma. It is a rapid, non-invasive bedside test for detecting free fluid using sonography used to assess patients for potential thoracoabdominal injuries.

Technique:

* The patient is placed in a supine position and the following regions are scanned:

* Subxiphoid transverse view: assess for pericardial effusion and left lobe liver injuries

* Longitudinal view of the right upper quadrant: assess for right liver injuries, right kidney injury, and Morison pouch

* Longitudinal view of the left upper quadrant: assess for splenic injury and left kidney injury

* Transverse and longitudinal views of the suprapubic region: assess the bladder and pouch of Douglas
questions.learning: eFAST The given clinical scenario of a patient being hemodynamically unstable after a RTA indicates a probable ongoing hemorrhage and the next step in the management is to perform an eFAST.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A HIV patient presents with persistent diarrhea. Microscopic examination of the stool is given below. Identify the causative organism:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cryptosporidium

Diarrhea in an HIV patient is suggestive of a coccidean parasitic infestation. Kinyoun stain - positive oocysts as seen in the given image is suggestive of Cryptosporidium.

Points in favor:

• HIV patient with diarrhea
• Oocysts are round,  contains four sporozites which is uniformly acid fast on staining.

Comparison of coccidian parasites causing diarrhea in an immunocompromised host:

Property
Cryptosporidium
Cyclospora
Isospora

Sporulated oocyst
4-6 μm, round contains four sporozoites
8-12 μm, round contains 2 sporocyst each having two sporozoites
23-36 μm, oval contain two sporocyst, each having four sporozoites.

Acid-fast detection
Uniformly acid fast
Variable acid fast
Uniformly acid fast

Sporulation of the oocyst
Occurs inside host cell
Occurs in soil
Occurs in soil

Diagnostic form
Sporulated cyst
Unsporulated cyst
Unsporulated oocyst

Treatment is fluid replacement and cotrimoxazole.
questions.learning: Cryptosporidium Diarrhea in an HIV patient is suggestive of a coccidean parasitic infestation. Kinyoun stain - positive oocysts as seen in the given image is suggestive of Cryptosporidium.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 62-year-old presented with diminished vision 1 year after cataract surgery. The findings are shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. After cataract

Diminished vision 1 year after cataract surgery, supported with the image of vacoulated clusters seen behind IOL is suggestive of Elschnig’s pearls. It is a type of after cataract.

After cataract, or secondary cataract or posterior capsular opacification, is a late postoperative complication that follows extracapsular extraction of the lens. It is the most common late postoperative complication. It may be caused by residual opaque lens matter or proliferation of left out anterior epithelial cells. Different types of after cataract include:

• Elschnig’s pearls: The subcapsular epithelial cells proliferate and develop into vacuolated soap bubble like clusters along the posterior capsule.
• Soemmering’s ring: A peripheral dense ring is formed behind the iris and is enclosed between layers of the capsule.
• Dense membranous after-cataract: It is formed in the pupillary area impairing the vision.
• Thin membranous after-cataract: It is thickened posterior capsule.

Treatment of after cataract is by Nd-YAG laser capsulotomy of the posterior capsule, which works on the principle of photodisruption, or surgical posterior capsulotomy.

Option B: Irvine–Gass syndrome is cystoid macular edema (CME) that develops in post-cataract surgery patients. Though it is mostly clinically insignificant, some cases can present with blurring of vision, one to three months after surgery. In CME, on fundoscopy a honeycomb appearance and on fundus fluorescein angiography(FFA) flower petal pattern can be seen. The below image depicts the flower petal pattern seen on FFA.

Option C: Post operative endophthalmitis presents as ocular pain, diminished vision and hypopyon within months to years after the surgery. Fungal endophthalmitis can rarely occur with puff ball exudates in the vitreous cavity.

Option D: UGH syndrome is where uveitis, glaucoma and hyphema occurs simultaneously. It is seen commonly with rigid anterior chamber intraocular lens (IOL) implantation.
questions.learning: After cataract Diminished vision 1 year after cataract surgery, supported with the image of vacoulated clusters seen behind IOL is suggestive of Elschnig’s pearls.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A child presents with hepatitis and progressive neurological degeneration. A picture of his eye has been provided below. Among the following options, what would be the initial step regarding the investigations done for this child's diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Serum ceruloplasmin levels

The clinical features of hepatitis, progressive neurological degeneration, and the Kayser-Fleischer (KF) ring seen in the image are suggestive of Wilson's disease. The initial step regarding investigations done for the diagnosis is the measurement of serum ceruloplasmin levels.

Kayser-Fleischer (KF) ring is a golden to greenish-brown ring of deposition of copper in the Descemets membrane of the peripheral cornea. Patients with neurological manifestations manifest with KF ring in >95% of cases.

Lab investigations in Wilson's disease would show:

Lab markers
Change in Wilson's disease
Reason

Serum ceruloplasmin
↓↓↓
ATP7B deficiency results in reduced bound copper

24h urinary copper
↑↑  (>100 μg/24h)
Excess free copper excreted in urine

Total serum copper
↓
Due to marked reduction in ceruloplasmin

The gold standard technique for diagnosis of Wilson’s disease is percutaneous needle liver biopsy for measurement of hepatic copper levels >200 μg/g of dry weight.

Option B: The role of total serum copper in the diagnosis of Wilson's disease is limited. Measurement of serum ceruloplasmin and urinary copper is preferred.

Option C: ATP7B enzyme assays have shown promise in early studies as a neonatal screening test for Wilson's disease. However, it is not yet part of routine clinical practice.

Option D: Karyotyping is done for every asymptomatic 1st and 2nd degree relative of a patient with Wilson’s disease. This helps differentiate the carriers (heterozygous) from the patients (homozygous) and can lead to early initiation of treatment before the onset of symptoms.
questions.learning: Serum ceruloplasmin levels — The clinical features of hepatitis, progressive neurological degeneration, and the Kayser-Fleischer (KF) ring seen in the image are suggestive of Wilson's disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 46-year-old male with a history of depression has been treated with fluoxetine for the past six months. He presented to the emergency department with altered consciousness and an ECG showing QT prolongation, with a QTc of 447ms. Recently, he was prescribed an additional medication for chronic pain management. Which of the following drugs was most likely added to his regimen that could have contributed to his current condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Methadone

Methadone is well known to cause QT interval prolongation by blocking cardiac potassium channels. Methadone is an opioid analgesic used for:

• Chronic pain
• Opioid dependence therapy

However it can: Block delayed rectifier potassium channels (IKr)

Result:

• Delayed ventricular repolarization
• QT prolongation

Concomitant use with fluoxetine (CYP inhibitor) increases methadone levels, enhancing QT prolongation risk.

Dangerous Consequence: Torsades de Pointes-

Torsades de pointes is:

• Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia
• Associated with prolonged QT interval

Symptoms:

• Syncope
• Palpitations
• Sudden cardiac death

This predisposes to torsades de pointes and altered consciousness.

Morphine and tramadol have minimal QT effects, and piperidine is not implicated.

Common Drugs That Prolong QT

| Drug Class | Examples

| ---------- | --------

| Antiarrhythmics | Quinidine, Sotalol

| Antibiotics | Macrolides, Fluoroquinolones

| Antipsychotics | Haloperidol

| Antidepressants | SSRIs, TCAs

| Opioids | Methadone
questions.learning: Methadone Methadone is well known to cause QT interval prolongation by blocking cardiac potassium channels. Methadone is an opioid analgesic used for: • Chronic pain • Opioid dependence therapy However it can: Block delayed rectifier potassium channels…

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following layers is absent in esophagus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Serosa

The serosa is absent in the esophagus except in the intra-abdominal part.

The oesophagus consists of the following layers:

* Mucosa:Inner-most layer is the mucous membrane with the following sub-layers:

* Lining epithelium: non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium

* Lamina propria: connective tissue supporting the lining epithelium

* Muscularis mucosae: thin layer of smooth muscle

*  Submucosa: A special feature of the submucosa is the presence of compound tubuloalveolar mucous glands

*  Muscularis externa with the inner layer of circular muscle fibres and an outer layer of longitudinal muscle fibres

* Upper 1/3rd: Only skeletal muscle fibres are present

* Middle 1/3rd: Both skeletal and smooth muscle fibres are present

* Lower 1/3rd: Only smooth muscle fibres are present

The stomach has 3 layers in the muscularis externa, with an extra oblique layer.

In the colon, the outer longitudinal fibers join to form prominent bundles called the taenia coli.

* Adventitia: Most of the esophagus has a dense fibrous tissue covering called the adventitia. Only a short length of the esophagus in the lower part(Intra-abdominal) has a peritoneal covering (serosa).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Zellweger syndrome is due to a defect in the biogenesis of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Peroxisomes

Zellweger syndrome is due to a defect in the biogenesis of peroxisomes.

Zellweger syndrome is also known as cerebrohepatorenal syndrome. It is caused by mutations in the PEX family of genes. This results in defective beta-oxidation of very long-chain fatty acids.

The child presents with

• Dysmorphic facial features.
• Weakness, hypotonia.
• Neonatal seizures
• Eye abnormalities.

Biochemical findings will show :

• Accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acids, phytanic acid
• Abnormalities in the synthesis of bile acids
• Marked reduction of plasmalogens

There is no appropriate treatment for Zellweger syndrome. It is very severe and infants rarely survive beyond a few months.
questions.learning: Peroxisomes Zellweger syndrome is due to a defect in the biogenesis of peroxisomes. Zellweger syndrome is also known as cerebrohepatorenal syndrome.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents with hip pain and true shortening of the limb which was diagnosed as tuberculosis of the hip. Which stage of the disease is he currently in?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stage of advanced arthritis

In a patient with tuberculosis of the hip, true shortening of the limb is seen in the advanced arthritis.

Clinical features seen in the four stages of TB hip:

* Stage of synovitis presents with apparent lengthening of the limb due to abduction deformity.

* Stage of early arthritis presents with apparent shortening of the limb due to adduction deformity.

* Stage of advanced arthritis leads to true shortening of the limb because of the destruction of the articular cartilage of the femur and the acetabulum.

* Stage of arthritis with subluxation leads to true shortening of the limb. The destruction of acetabulum leads to dislocation of the femur head. This is also known as wandering acetabulum/ mortar and pestle hip because of the widened acetabulum and diminished size of femur head.

The TB of the hip finally results in fibrous ankylosis of the hip joint.

Note: The apparent length of the limb is measured from the umbilicus to the medial malleolus and the true length of the limb is measured from the anterior superior iliac spine to the medial malleolus. The apparent length is increased when there is abduction deformity of the limb and decreased when there is adduction deformity of the limb.
questions.learning: Stage of advanced arthritis — In a patient with tuberculosis of the hip, true shortening of the limb is seen in the advanced arthritis. Clinical features seen in the four stages of TB hip: * Stage of synovitis presents with apparent lengthening of the limb…

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: “Oncogene addiction” seen in tumors refers to:
options: Oncogenes are expressed only during embryonic development
Tumors use immune checkpoints to evade immune destruction
Tumors depend predominantly on a single oncogenic pathway for survival, allowing targeted therapy against that pathway
Dependence of cancer cells on multiple tumor suppressor genes for survival
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tumors depend predominantly on a single oncogenic pathway for survival, allowing targeted therapy against that pathway

Oncogene addiction refers to the phenomenon in which tumor cells become highly dependent on a single activated oncogenic pathway for their growth, survival, and proliferation, despite harboring multiple genetic abnormalities. This dependency forms the basis for targeted cancer therapy, as inhibition of the critical oncogenic driver can produce marked tumor regression.

Examples of oncogene addiction:

• BCR-ABL → Chronic myeloid leukemia (treated with imatinib)
• HER2 (ERBB2) → HER2-positive breast cancer (treated with trastuzumab)
• EGFR mutation → Non-small cell lung cancer (treated with EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors)
• BRAF V600E mutation → Melanoma (treated with BRAF inhibitors)

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are clinical features of Parkinson’s disease? I. Reduced eye blinking II. Drooling of saliva III. Soft voice IV. Macrographia
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II and III

Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, leading to dopamine deficiency in the nigrostriatal pathway. It is characterized by both motor and non-motor symptoms.

The classic motor features are:

• Bradykinesia (essential feature) ⭐
• Resting tremor
• Rigidity
• Postural instability

The following are characteristic clinical features of Parkinson’s disease:

• I. Reduced eye blinking: Due to facial bradykinesia, producing a masked facies (hypomimia).
• II. Drooling of saliva: Caused by reduced spontaneous swallowing, not excessive saliva production.
• III. Soft voice (Hypophonia): Speech becomes soft, monotonous, and low in volume.

Why is IV incorrect?

• IV. Macrographia: Parkinson’s disease causes micrographia (progressively smaller handwriting), which is a classic feature due to bradykinesia.
questions.learning: I, II and III Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, leading to dopamine deficiency in the nigrostriatal pathway.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The Doppler waveform of the venous blood flow in lower limb DVT is _____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Monophasic

The Doppler waveform of the venous blood flow in lower limb DVT is monophasic proximal to the level of obstruction.

The normal venous waveform shows a variation (phasicity) secondary to respiration referred to as respirophasic waveform. Loss of this phasic variation results in a monophasic waveform suggestive of venous obstruction proximal to the level of interrogation.

A normal artery has a triphasic signal. The waveform becomes biphasic in mild-moderate stenosis and monophasic in severe stenosis.

The image given below shows the normal triphasic signal from an artery.

Monophasic waveform:

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is decreased in acute inflammation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Albumin

Albumin, an acute-phase reactant, is decreased in acute inflammation.

Inflammation leads to changes in the levels of certain proteins known as acute phase reactants (APRs), which are regulated by cytokines such as interleukin-6 (IL-6). These changes support the body's defensive and adaptive functions.

APRs are classified as positive and negative based on whether their levels increase or decrease in inflammatory states, respectively.

Positive APRs
Negative APRs

•  C-reactive protein (CRP)
• Hepcidin
• Ferritin
• Serum amyloid A (SAA)
• Fibrinogen
• Haptoglobin

• Transthyretin
• Albumin
• Transferrin

APR levels are nonspecific and do not point to any particular disease. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is an indirect measure of APR levels, particularly influenced by the level of fibrinogen in the blood.

Coagulation factors, trapping invading microbes in blood clots.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Hemorrhagic cystitis is a serious side effect of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cyclophosphamide

Cyclophosphamide is an alkylating agent used in the treatment of malignancies and autoimmune diseases. A major dose-limiting adverse effect is hemorrhagic cystitis, caused by its toxic metabolite acrolein, which damages the bladder urothelium. This complication can be prevented by adequate hydration and Mesna (2-mercaptoethane sulfonate).

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Leflunomide: Common adverse effects include hepatotoxicity, diarrhea, hypertension, and teratogenicity, not hemorrhagic cystitis.
• B. Mycophenolate mofetil: Mainly causes gastrointestinal upset, leukopenia, and increased risk of infections.
• D. Methotrexate: Associated with myelosuppression, mucositis, hepatotoxicity, and pulmonary fibrosis, but not hemorrhagic cystitis.
questions.learning: Cyclophosphamide Cyclophosphamide is an alkylating agent used in the treatment of malignancies and autoimmune diseases. A major dose-limiting adverse effect is hemorrhagic cystitis, caused by its toxic metabolite acrolein, which damages the bladder urothelium.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 65-year-old male presents with urinary retention and pelvic discomfort. A digital rectal examination reveals an enlarged prostate gland. During surgery to relieve the obstruction, the urologist must take care to avoid damaging the structures that separate the prostate from the rectum. Which of the following structures separates the prostate gland from the rectum?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Denonvilliers’ fascia

The prostate gland lies anterior to the rectum, and the structure separating them is the Denonvilliers’ fascia (rectoprostatic fascia). Key features of Denonvilliers’ fascia:

• A fibrous fascial layer between the prostate/seminal vesicles anteriorly and the rectum posteriorly.
• Provides an important surgical plane during prostatectomy.
• Helps prevent direct spread of prostatic carcinoma to the rectum.

Other options:

• A. Waldeyer’s fascia: fascia related to the sacral region behind the rectum.
• B. Scarpa’s fascia: deep membranous layer of superficial fascia of the anterior abdominal wall.
• D. Camper’s fascia: fatty superficial layer of the anterior abdominal wall.
questions.learning: Denonvilliers’ fascia — The prostate gland lies anterior to the rectum, and the structure separating them is the Denonvilliers’ fascia (rectoprostatic fascia).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which one of the following statements regarding the composition of common crystalloid solutions is correct?
options: Normal saline contains 100 mEq/L of Na
Hartmann’s solution contains 111 mEq/L of Cl
Normal saline contains 130 mEq/L of Cl
Hartmann’s solution contains 111 mEq/L of Na
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hartmann’s solution contains 111 mEq/L of Cl

Hartmann’s solution (Lactated Ringer’s) is a balanced crystalloid whose electrolyte composition closely resembles plasma.

Why not the other options?

• A. Normal saline contains 100 mEq/L of Na+: Normal saline contains 154 mEq/L of Na⁺.
• C. Normal saline contains 130 mEq/L of Cl⁻: Normal saline contains 154 mEq/L of Cl⁻.
• D. Hartmann’s solution contains 111 mEq/L of Na⁺: Hartmann’s contains 131 mEq/L of Na⁺.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following antibodies is the most reliable marker for diagnosing an acute infection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. IgM

IgM is the first antibody produced during the initial immune response to an antigen.

Its early appearance in serum makes it the most reliable marker of acute or recent infection.

IgM levels rise rapidly and decline as class switching to IgG occurs.

IgG indicates past exposure or immunity, while IgA and IgE have specialized roles.

First exposure to antigen

↓

Naive B cell activation

↓

IgM production (early phase)

↓

Class switching (with T-cell help)

↓

IgG / IgA production (later phase)

↓

Memory cell formation

| Antibody | Appears When | Indicates | Key Feature

| -------- | ------------ | --------- | -----------

| IgM | Early | Acute infection | First responder

| IgG | Late | Past infection | Memory

| IgA | Mucosal | Local immunity | Secretions

| IgE | Variable | Allergy | Mast cell binding
questions.learning: IgM IgM is the first antibody produced during the initial immune response to an antigen. Its early appearance in serum makes it the most reliable marker of acute or recent infection.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which is the best confirmatory method to ensure the central line is in the jugular vein?
questions.explanation: Following the insertion of a central venous line, such as in the internal jugular or subclavian vein, a chest X-ray is the gold standard confirmatory method. It serves two vital purposes: verifying the correct anatomical position of the catheter tip (ideally at the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium) and ruling out immediate iatrogenic complications like a pneumothorax. While blood color (Option C) and blood pH (Option B) can provide clues about whether a vessel is arterial or venous, they are subjective and unreliable for definitive confirmation. ETCO2 (Option D) is used to confirm endotracheal tube placement, not central line position. Furthermore, if an insertion attempt fails on one side, an X-ray or ultrasound should be performed before attempting the opposite side to prevent bilateral complications. Thus, radiological verification remains the best confirmatory step
questions.learning: Following the insertion of a central venous line, such as in the internal jugular or subclavian vein, a chest X-ray is the gold standard confirmatory method.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which among the following serves as cofactor for Glycogen phosphorylase:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pyridoxal Phosphate

• Pyridoxal phosphate is a cofactor of glycogen phosphorylase, where the phosphate group is catalytically important.
• PLP also acts as the coenzyme for many enzymes involved in amino acid metabolism, especially transamination and decarboxylation.
• Glycogen phosphorylase is a debranching enzyme which cleaves alpha-1,4 bonds of the glycogen chain to produce glucose-1-phosphate in glycogenolysis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A male patient was brought to the emergency room with complaints of headache, vomiting, and blurring of vision after he consumed some locally produced spirit. Which of the following is used for the treatment of his condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Fomepizole

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of methanol toxicity. Ethanol and fomepizole is used for the treatment of this condition.

Methanol poisoning is caused due to ingestion of illicit liquor which contains ethanol adulterated with methanol. Methanol is metabolized to formaldehyde and formic acid by alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenases, respectively. The metabolites of methanol are responsible for the toxic effects.

Clinically, patients present with headache, vomiting, abdomen pain, uneasiness, confusion, delirium, and coma. Formic acid specifically damages the retina and optic nerve and results in blurring of vision and blindness.

Elevated levels of formic acid and other organic acids result in metabolic acidosis in arterial blood gas analysis(ABG).

Treatment of methanol poisoning includes gastric lavage with sodium bicarbonate if the patient is brought within 2 hours of ingesting methanol to combat acidosis. Ethanol infusion since ethanol is preferentially metabolized by alcohol dehydrogenase over methanol and helps by reducing the rate of generation of formaldehyde and formic acid.

Fomepizole is a competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase and the drug of choice for methanol poisoning. Folate therapy with calcium leucovorin reduces blood formate levels by enhancing its oxidation. Hemodialysis is used in severe cases of methanol toxicity.

Other options:

Option B: Flumazenil is the inverse agonist of benzodiazepine receptors and is used for the treatment of benzodiazepine overdose.

Option C: Diazepam can be used to manage delirium tremens, or seizures due to alcohol withdrawal.

Option D: Naloxone is a competitive opioid antagonist used for the treatment of opioid overdose.
questions.learning: Fomepizole — The above clinical scenario is suggestive of methanol toxicity. Ethanol and fomepizole is used for the treatment of this condition.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 12-year-old child presents with palpitations, tremors, dry mouth, tachycardia (heart rate 130/ min), and tachypnea (respiratory rate 34/min). Which substance is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.explanation: The combination of tachycardia (130 bpm), tremors, and dry mouth (an anticholinergic sign) is highly suggestive of a tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) overdose. TCAs exhibit potent anticholinergic and sympathomimetic effects, leading to the "anticholinergic toxidrome". Patients may also experience delirium, ECG changes, and life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias. Option A (Lithium) can cause tremors but lacks the profound tachycardia and dry mouth seen here. Option B (Opioids) causes the opposite effect: pinpoint pupils (miosis), respiratory depression, and bradycardia. Option C (Propranolol) is a beta-blocker that would significantly lower the heart rate rather than causing it to rise to 130 bpm. Treatment for TCA toxicity focuses on stabilization, including bicarbonate infusion for acidosis and benzodiazepines for seizures. Therefore, the described sympathetic and anticholinergic activation matches the TCA profile
questions.learning: The combination of tachycardia (130 bpm), tremors, and dry mouth (an anticholinergic sign) is highly suggestive of a tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) overdose.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In a middle-aged man, an X-ray reveals multiple lytic bone lesions, leading to further evaluation with urine analysis. The test detects the presence of Bence Jones proteins. Among the immunoglobulins, which type is most commonly associated with this finding?
questions.explanation: The clinical picture of a middle-aged patient with multiple "punched-out" lytic lesions on X-ray and Bence Jones proteins in the urine is classic for Multiple Myeloma. This is a plasma cell malignancy characterized by the production of monoclonal (M) proteins. In Multiple Myeloma, the most common immunoglobulin subtype secreted by the malignant plasma cells is IgG (found in approximately 50-60% of cases). IgA (Option A) is the second most common (about 20%). IgM (Option D) is associated with Waldenström macroglobulinemia, which typically presents with hyperviscosity rather than lytic bone lesions. IgD (Option B) is extremely rare. Therefore, while several types of monoclonal proteins can be present, IgG is the immunoglobulin most frequently linked to the classic skeletal and renal manifestations of Multiple Myeloma. Bence Jones proteins themselves represent the excessive monoclonal light chains excreted by the kidneys
questions.learning: The clinical picture of a middle-aged patient with multiple "punched-out" lytic lesions on X-ray and Bence Jones proteins in the urine is classic for Multiple Myeloma.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A newborn baby refuses breast milk since the 2nd day of birth but accepts glucose water. He develops vomiting and severe jaundice by the 5th day. Benedict's test was positive for urine and blood glucose was low. The most likely cause is due to the deficiency of
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase

The above clinical features on ingestion of breastmilk at birth suggest classical galactosemia, a disorder of galactose metabolism. Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase deficiency leads to classical galactosemia.

It is an autosomal recessive disorder. Clinical features include:

• Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the liver causes liver damage & leads to hepatomegaly, vomiting, convulsions.
• Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate depletes the liver of inorganic phosphate leading to diminished ATP synthesis which affects gluconeogenesis resulting in hypoglycemia.
• Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in the nerves causes intellectual disability.
• Accumulation of galactitol in the lens causes an oil-drop cataract.

Urinary reducing sugar (Benedict's test) and the Mucic acid test are positive.

Treatment is a galactose-free diet.

The flowchart given below depicts galactose metabolism.
questions.learning: Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase — The above clinical features on ingestion of breastmilk at birth suggest classical galactosemia, a disorder of galactose metabolism.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
Which of the following is not associated with G6PD deficiency?

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD)
options: Equal incidence in males and females
Predisposes the patient to oxidative stress
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Equal incidence in males and females

G6PD Deficiency does not have an equal incidence in males and females. It is an X-linked recessive (XLR) disorder, hence males are more affected than females.

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency causes congenital hemolytic anemia due to enzyme deficiency. G6PD is required to generate NADPH while oxidizing glucose-6-phosphate in the hexose monophosphate pathway (HMP). G6PD deficiency leads to reduced NADPH levels (option B) which then reduces the level of reduced glutathione. Reduced glutathione is required to protect the cells against oxidative stress to RBCs and hemolysis.

Clinically, most patients are asymptomatic. When exposed to triggers like fava beans, infections, drugs such as primaquine, chloroquine, sulfonamides/sulfones, dapsone, and nitrofurantoin patient develops:

• Episodic hemolysis, both intravascular and extravascular
• Hemolytic anaemia
• Hemoglobinemia
• Hemoglobinuria

Increased oxidative damage to RBCs leads to the formation of denatured precipitates known as Heinz bodies. These bodies can damage the RBC membrane leading to intravascular hemolysis. Additionally, when such RBCs pass through the splenic cords, macrophages pluck out these precipitates, giving them the characteristic appearance of bite cells.

The images below show the presence of Heinz bodies and bite cells.
questions.learning: Equal incidence in males and females G6PD Deficiency does not have an equal incidence in males and females. It is an X-linked recessive (XLR) disorder, hence males are more affected than females.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The vaginal pH in childbearing age normally ranges between:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 4–5.5

The normal vaginal pH in women of childbearing (reproductive) age is acidic, approximately 3.8–4.5 (many exam texts accept 4–5.5). This acidity is maintained by Lactobacilli (Döderlein bacilli), which convert glycogen into lactic acid under the influence of estrogen.

Why not the other options?

• A. 2.5–3.5: Too acidic.
• B. 1–2: Extremely acidic; not physiological.
• D. 7–8: Alkaline; seen in infections or postmenopausal women due to reduced estrogen.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant lady at 20 weeks of gestation comes with complaints of acute onset fever, and pain in the right lumbar region. It is associated with chills, nausea, and vomiting. Urinalysis reveals the presence of E.coli and a diagnosis of acute pyelonephritis is made. Which of the following is incorrect regarding the management of acute pyelonephritis in pregnancy?
options: Hospitalise, send urine and blood cultures and start on antibiotics.
Maintain urine output >50 ml/hr; Intravenous crystalloids can be given
Discharge if afebrile for 72 hrs; Continue antibiotics for 5 days
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Discharge if afebrile for 72 hrs; Continue antibiotics for 5 days

The incorrect statement regarding the management of acute pyelonephritis in pregnancy is option D. The patient can be discharged once afebrile for 24 hours, and antibiotics have to be continued for 7 to 10 days.

Acute Pyelonephritis is one of the frequent and serious medical complications occurring in 2nd-trimester of pregnancy. The most common causative organism is E.coli.

Clinical features include sudden onset fever, chills, and aching pain in the lumbar region (usually unilateral). It is associated with nausea, vomiting, and anorexia. Tenderness in the costovertebral angle can be elicited on examination.

Diagnosis is confirmed by the collection of urine (preferably from catheterization) and analysis to look for leukocytes and bacteria.

Management protocol for pyelonephritis during pregnancy is

• Hospitalization is recommended for all patients. Very rare cases of uncomplicated pyelonephritis can be managed on an outpatient basis
• Urine and blood (if temperature is > 39 degrees C) samples are collected for culture.
• Aggressive intravenous hydration to maintain adequate urine output is the mainstay of treatment. A urinary output ≥50 mL/hr is maintained with intravenous crystalloids.
• Vital signs such as blood pressure, pulse, temperature, and oxygen saturation along with urine output should be monitored for signs of worsening sepsis.
• Empirical intravenous antibiotic therapy is started with ampicillin plus gentamicin, cefazolin or ceftriaxone. It is switched to oral antibiotics once the patient is afebrile.
• In case of persistent infection or lack of clinical improvement by 48 to 72 hours, renal sonography is recommended to look for urinary tract abnormalities (like obstruction or calculi).
• The patient is discharged when afebrile for 24 hours and antimicrobial therapy is continued for 7 to 10 days.
• Urine culture is repeated 1–2 weeks after antimicrobial therapy is completed.
questions.learning: Discharge if afebrile for 72 hrs; Continue antibiotics for 5 days The incorrect statement regarding the management of acute pyelonephritis in pregnancy is option D.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Full form of JSSK is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram

JSSK stands for Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram, a flagship maternal and child health initiative under the National Health Mission. The program ensures free and cashless services to pregnant women and sick newborns, including drugs, diagnostics, transport, and diet.

The main goals are to:

• Promote institutional deliveries
• Reduce maternal mortality
• Reduce neonatal mortality
• Remove out-of-pocket expenditure for pregnant women

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the absolute contraindication for the device depicted in the image below?
questions.explanation: The device shown is an intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD) such as a Copper-T. The question asks for an absolute contraindication to its use. Undiagnosed vaginal bleeding is an absolute contraindication for IUCD insertion. This is because abnormal bleeding may be due to serious underlying conditions such as endometrial cancer, cervical cancer, or pregnancy-related complications, which must be evaluated before inserting any intrauterine device. Inserting an IUCD without diagnosis may worsen the condition or delay proper treatment. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Anemia : Not an absolute contraindication (though Cu-T may worsen bleeding, caution is needed) (C) Uterine malformations : Relative/functional contraindication depending on severity, not always absolute (D) Uterine fibroids : Not absolute unless they significantly distort the uterine cavity
questions.learning: The device shown is an intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD) such as a Copper-T. The question asks for an absolute contraindication to its use.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A child presents with cyanosis. His chest radiograph is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)

The given clinical scenario and chest X-ray showing a "coeur en sabot" or boot-shaped heart are suggestive of tetralogy of Fallot (TOF).

TOF is a cyanotic congenital heart disease with the following four components:

• Obstruction to right ventricular outflow (pulmonary stenosis)
• Malalignment type of ventricular septal defect (VSD)
• Dextroposition of the aorta so that it overrides the ventricular septum (overriding of the aorta), and
• Right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH)

In TOF, the hypertrophied right ventricle causes the rounded apical shadow to be uptilted so that it is situated higher above the diaphragm than normal. On x-ray, this appears as a boot-shaped heart or coeur en sabot, as shown below:

Option B: Ebstein anomaly is a rare cyanotic congenital heart disease with diminished pulmonary blood flow due to abnormality of the tricuspid valve.

In the Ebstein anomaly, there is severe right-sided cardiomegaly due to an elongated and enlarged right atrium, which leads to an elevated apex giving a box-shaped heart, as shown below:

Option C: Transposition of great arteries (TGA) can present from birth to infancy with cyanosis, decreased exercise tolerance, and poor physical development TGA is the most specific heart disease in infants of diabetic mothers.

The following is a radiograph of TGA showing the egg-on-a-string appearance/egg-on-side appearance of the heart:

Option D: Total anomalous pulmonary venous return (TAPVC) occurs due to the anomalous connection of pulmonary veins instead of joining to the left atrium resulting in pulmonary venous blood reaching the right atrium.

In the supracardiac type of TAPVC, the configuration of the heart and the superior mediastinal borders resemble a snowman. It is also referred to as the figure of 8 sign, as shown below:
questions.learning: Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) — The given clinical scenario and chest X-ray showing a "coeur en sabot" or boot-shaped heart are suggestive of tetralogy of Fallot (TOF).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text:
Which of the following are the objective tests for the hearing?

1. BERA (Brainstem evoked response audiometry)
2. OAE (Otoacoustic emission)
3. PTA (Pure tone audiometry)
4. Tympanometry
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2, and 4

BERA, OAE, and tympanometry are the objective tests for hearing. PTA (pure tone audiometry) is a subjective test for hearing as it relies on patient responses to pure tone stimuli. Other examples of subjective tests include tuning fork tests and speech audiometry.

Tympanometry is an objective test of the middle ear and eustachian tube functions (conductive compartment of hearing). Here, the compliance of the TM, i.e., how much it moves to the pressure differentials applied from the external ear is measured.

The image below shows the types of tympanogram:
questions.learning: 1, 2, and 4 BERA, OAE, and tympanometry are the objective tests for hearing. PTA (pure tone audiometry) is a subjective test for hearing as it relies on patient responses to pure tone stimuli.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text:
A student was making a presentation with charts but lost titles while editing. What could be the heading for the following chart?

Parameters
Data

Mean life expectancy at birth
67.7 years

Expected years of schooling
12.6 years

Mean years of schooling
10.6 years

Gross national income per capita
USD 6951
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Human Development Index

The index that is calculated using the given indicators such as life expectancy at birth, mean and expected years of schooling, and the per capita income is the Human Developmental Index (HDI).

Human Development Index (HDI) is defined as a composite index focusing on three basic dimensions of human development. It assesses abilities

• To lead a healthy long life - measured by life expectancy at birth
• To acquire knowledge- measured by mean years of schooling
• To achieve a decent standard of living- measured by gross national income per capita

Hence the 3 dimension indices used to calculate the human development index are as follows life expectancy index, education index, and gross national index.

Other options:

Option A- Physical Quality of Life Index (PQLI) uses three indicators which include infant mortality, life expectancy at age one, and literacy rate.

Option B- Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) - It is an international measure of acute multidimensional poverty by capturing the acute deprivations in health, education, and living standards that a person faces simultaneously. It is assessed using 3 dimensions and 10 indicators which are as follows:

1. Health - Nutrition and child mortality
2. Education- Years of schooling and school attendance
3. Standard of living -

• Cooking fuel
• Sanitation
• Drinking water
• Electricity
• Housing
• Assets

Option C- Disability-adjusted life years (DALY): It is the amount of time lost due to ill health. It is expressed as the number of years lost due to ill-health, disability, or early death. The components of DALY are:

• Years of life lost due to premature death
• Years lived with disability (YLD)
• Years lived in a state less than full health
questions.learning: Human Development Index — The index that is calculated using the given indicators such as life expectancy at birth, mean and expected years of schooling, and the per capita income is the Human Developmental Index (HDI).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Which of the following findings in an 18-year- old female is characteristic of the primary stage of this disease?
questions.explanation: The image and patient age suggest Acne Vulgaris, a common inflammatory condition of the pilosebaceous unit. The "primary" or hallmark lesion of acne is the comedone (Option D). Comedones are formed when the hair follicle becomes clogged with sebum and keratin; they can be "open" (blackheads) or "closed" (whiteheads). As inflammation progresses, comedones can evolve into inflammatory lesions. Papules (Option A) are small, solid red bumps, and pustules (Option B) are small bumps containing pus, representing the next inflammatory stages. An abscess (Option C) is a deep, painful collection of pus, usually seen in severe cystic acne. Because comedones represent the initial non-inflammatory obstruction that initiates the acne cycle, they are considered the fundamental primary lesions of the disease. Recognizing them is essential for selecting appropriate early treatments like topical retinoids, which specifically target comedone formation
questions.learning: The image and patient age suggest Acne Vulgaris, a common inflammatory condition of the pilosebaceous unit. The "primary" or hallmark lesion of acne is the comedone (Option D).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following hormone acts via this pathway?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Leptin

The given image shows the JAK-STAT signaling pathway, which is associated with tyrosine kinase receptors. Among the given hormones leptin acts via this pathway.

Hormones that use receptor tyrosine kinase/ JAK-STAT signaling include the following:

• Growth hormone
• Fibroblast growth factor
• Hepatocyte growth factor
• Insulin
• Insulin-like growth factor-1
• Leptin
• Prolactin
• Vascular endothelial growth factor

Leptin is a hormone that is secreted by fat cells. The physiological effects of leptin are regulating appetite and energy balance. The leptin receptor acts via tyrosine kinase of the Janus kinase (JAK) family, JAK2. Leptin binds to the extracellular part of the leptin receptor, which causes phosphorylation (P) and activation of the intracellular JAK2. This causes phosphorylation of signal transducer and activation of transcription (STAT) proteins, which results in the transcription of target genes and the synthesis of proteins.

Phosphorylation of JAK2 also results in the activation of other intracellular enzyme pathways such as mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPK) and phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K).

Other options:

Hormones such as adrenal (Aldosterone)and gonadal steroid hormones, thyroid hormones, retinoid hormones, and vitamin D, bind with protein receptors inside the cell rather than on the cell surface. These hormones are lipid soluble and they readily cross the cell membrane and interact with receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus.

Vasopressin in the epithelial cells acts via V2 receptor. They use adenylyl cyclase as their second messenger system. Vasopressin in the vascular smooth muscles acts via V1 receptor that uses phospholipase C as the second messenger system.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primigravida at 37 weeks of gestation has been experiencing mild uterine contractions for the past 20 hours. On examination, the cervix is only 1 cm dilated with no effacement. What is the most appropriate management strategy in this situation?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario describes a primigravida in the "latent phase" of labor. Prolonged latent phase is defined in primigravidas as lasting more than 20 hours without progression to active labor (defined as 4–6 cm dilation and effacement). The cervix remaining at 1 cm indicates she has not yet reached the active stage. The preferred first-line management for a prolonged latent phase is therapeutic rest, which typically involves "sedation and waiting". This allows the patient to rest, after which she will likely either wake up in active labor or the "false labor" pains will have ceased. Augmentation with oxytocin (Option B) or amniotomy (Option D) are generally reserved for the active phase of labor. A Cesarean section (Option C) is not indicated solely for a prolonged latent phase in the absence of maternal or fetal distress. Managing maternal exhaustion and providing reassurance are key components of care during this frustrating but often benign stage of labor
questions.learning: The clinical scenario describes a primigravida in the "latent phase" of labor. Prolonged latent phase is defined in primigravidas as lasting more than 20 hours without progression to active labor (defined as 4–6 cm dilation and effacement).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old lady presented with a 1.5cm pigmented lesion on the face which is growing rapidly in size and associated with itching. The lesion is shown below. Which of the following is likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Malignant melanoma

The given clinical scenario of a >6mm pigmented lesion on the face which is asymmetrical, with an irregular border, made of black and brown pigments, and increasing rapidly in size, points towards a diagnosis of malignant melanoma.

Types of melanoma:

* Lentigo maligna

* Superficial spreading

* Acral lentiginous

* Nodular

Histopathology of melanoma:

* Individual melanoma cells are larger than normal melanocytes

* They have large nuclei with irregular contours, chromatin is characteristically clumped at the periphery of the nuclear membrane with prominent red eosinophilic nucleoli

* All tumors have a vertical and radial phase of growth. The appearance of melanocytes is similar in both phases. The vertical growth has is often heralded by the appearance of a nodule.

* The possibility of metastasis correlates with the depth of invasion which is called the Breslow thickness.

Type
Clinical features
Spread

Basal cell carcinoma

Nodule

Central ulceration with a pearly surface,

telangiectasia

local

Squamous cell carcinoma

Ulcer with thickened margins, keratosis

Papillomatous

Local,

lymph nodes

Malignant melanoma

>6 mm pigmented,

vascularization

inflammation

Local

Other options:

Acquired melanocytic nevus (common mole) is rarely more than 1cm in size. It also does not show atypical network

Congenital melanocytic nevus may be small, medium or large size(>20cm). A large-sized mole may show an atypical network and have a risk of melanoma growth. But a history of being present since birth or infancy needs to be present.

A dysplastic nevus is formed at the dermo-epidermal junction. They are usually smaller in size than melanoma, have a fuzzy border, and more likely to show brown-tan pigmentation. Any blue-black pigmentation should raise suspicion of melanoma. The majority of them regress on their own

Pearl PF0159: Clinical findings suggestive of melanoma

The ABCDE of Melanoma consists of the rules for the examination of a nevus to assess its malignant potential:

A : Asymmetry

* Melanoma lesions are irregular, or not symmetrical, in shape.

B : Border irregular

* Melanoma lesions usually have irregular borders that are ill defined.

C : Color variegation

* The presence of multiple colors (blue, black, brown, tan, etc.) or the uneven distribution of color.

D : Diameter >6 mm

* Melanoma lesions are often greater than 6 millimeters in diameter (approximately the size of a pencil eraser).

E : Evolution

* There is a change in the size, shape, symptoms (such as itching or tenderness), surface (especially bleeding), or color of a mole.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4-year-old child has a mid–upper arm circumference of 105 mm and eagerly consumes the entire amount of therapeutic food provided. Under which category is this child most appropriately classified?
questions.explanation: Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) in children aged 6 to 59 months is diagnosed when the Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) is less than 115 mm. This child's MUAC of 105 mm confirms SAM. SAM is further classified as "uncomplicated" or "complicated" based on the presence of medical issues or the "appetite test". Because the child eagerly completed the therapeutic food, they have passed the appetite test. In the absence of severe edema or other danger signs, these patients can be managed at home with therapeutic feeding. Complicated SAM (Option B) would be diagnosed if the child had failed the appetite test, had severe pitting edema, or required immediate inpatient stabilization. Acute malnutrition (Option C) is too broad a term, and "normal nutrition" (Option D) is ruled out by the low MUAC. Thus, the child fits the criteria for Uncomplicated SAM
questions.learning: Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) in children aged 6 to 59 months is diagnosed when the Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) is less than 115 mm. This child's MUAC of 105 mm confirms SAM.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is the gold standard for measuring intraocular pressure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Goldmann applanation tonometer

Goldmann applanation tonometer is used to measure intraocular pressure (IOP).

The concept behind the procedure was introduced by Goldmann. It is based on Imbert-Fick law, which states that the pressure inside a sphere(P) is equal to the force (W) required to flatten its surface divided by the area of flattening (A).

P = W/A

The different types are Goldmann tonometer, Perkin’s tonometer, pneumatic tonometer, pulse air tonometer, tono-pen.

The image of a Goldmann applanation tonometer is given below:

Other options:

Gonioscope is used to visualize the angle of the anterior chamber (gonioscopy).

Hertel's exophthalmometer measures protrusion of the apex of the cornea from the outer orbital margin (with the eyes looking straight ahead).

Tonopen is a hand-held electronic contact tonometer which is used for measuring intraocular pressure (IOP) in a scarred cornea.
questions.learning: Goldmann applanation tonometer Goldmann applanation tonometer is used to measure intraocular pressure (IOP). The concept behind the procedure was introduced by Goldmann.

This calculation helps clinicians assess whether a child’s growth pattern is consistent with familial height or requires further evaluation

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Edematous villi with chromosome XY was found. What will be the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A complete hydatidiform mole is characterized by a diploid karyotype, most commonly 46,XX but also 46,XY (Option A). It results from the fertilization of an "empty" ovum by one or two sperm, meaning the genetic material is entirely paternal. Histopathology classically shows diffuse hydropic swelling (edematous villi) and a complete absence of fetal tissue. In contrast, a partial mole (Option B) is usually triploid (e.g., 69,XXY) and contains identifiable fetal parts alongside both normal and edematous villi. A simple cyst (Option C) would not show placental villous architecture or specific chromosomal anomalies. An ectopic pregnancy (Option D) involves a normal embryo implanted outside the uterus and does not exhibit the diffuse trophoblastic hyperplasia seen in molar pregnancies. Thus, the specific findings of edematous villi and an XY diploid karyotype confirm a complete molar pregnancy
questions.learning: A complete hydatidiform mole is characterized by a diploid karyotype, most commonly 46,XX but also 46,XY (Option A). It results from the fertilization of an "empty" ovum by one or two sperm, meaning the genetic material is entirely paternal.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 7-year-old male child weighing 40 kg presents with thermal burns involving 22% of the total body surface area. What is the approximate amount of fluid that should be administered in the first 8 hours of resuscitation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1,320 mL

The amount of fluid that needs to be administered in the first 8 hours in this case is 1,320 mL

Hartmann’s solution or Ringer’s lactate is the crystalloid most commonly used for burn resuscitation, as it closely matches the osmolality of plasma. It is cheaper compared to colloid solutions and is effective in maintaining intravascular volume.

The modified Parkland formula is the standard method for fluid calculation, expressed as:

* TBSA% burn × weight (kg) × 3 = Volume in mL.

* substituiting the given values, 22 ✖️ 3 ✖️ 40 = 2,640 mL.

To complete 24-hour resuscitation, half (1,320 mL) of this is given in the first 8 hours and the other half over the remaining 16 hours. Urine output serves as a reliable endpoint to guide resuscitation and should be maintained at 0.5–1.0 mL/kg/hour in children. Urine output greater than 2 mL/kg/hour indicates the need to reduce the infusion rate.

Resuscitation fluids in burn patients must always be commenced from the time of burn injury, and if there is any delay, the deficit should be compensated. Intravenous fluid therapy is indicated for adults with burns exceeding 15% of total body surface area (TBSA) and for children with burns exceeding 10% TBSA.

In children, maintenance fluids are required in addition to resuscitation fluids, usually in the form of dextrose–saline. The regimen is weight-based:

* 100 mL/kg for 24 hours for the first 10 kg

* 50 mL/kg for the next 10 kg

* 20 mL/kg for each kilogram above 20 kg body weight

Pearl PF2125: Burns – Formulae for Fluid Calculation(Updated according to ATLS 10th edition 2018 guidelines)

Parkland’s formula gives the total fluid requirement for 24hours. Half of this volume is infused in the first 8 hours, and the remaining half is infused in the next 16 hours.

This formula is recommended for those who have sustained large deep partial-thickness or full-thickness burns that cover more than 20% of the TBSA in adults and more than 10% in children.

Formulas provide a starting target rate; Subsequently, the amount of fluid provided should be adjusted based on urine output.

Dextrose maintenance:

* 100 ml/ kg in 24 hours for 10 kg

* 50 ml/kg for next 10 kg

* 20 ml/kg for every kg after 20 kg

Evan’s formula is used for normal saline.

For the first 24 hours:

* Amount of NS administered = weight in kgs x % TBSA

* Amount of colloid administered = weight in kgs x % TBSA

* 5% Dextrose administered= 2000 ml

After 24 hours, the amount of NS and colloid administered is half. 2000 ml of dextrose is maintained.

Muir and Barclay’s formula for colloids:

* 1 portion of colloid = (weight in kgs x % TBSA)/2

* 6 portions of colloid are administered over 36 hours

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following correctly represents “late expanding”, i.e. the third stage in the demographic cycle?
options: High birthrates and high death rates
Decline in death rates and decline in birthrates
Decline in death rates and rising birthrates
Low death rates and low birthrates
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Decline in death rates and decline in birthrates

The demographic cycle (demographic transition) is classically divided into four stages:

1. High stationary: High birth rate + high death rate
2. Early expanding: High birth rate + declining death rate
3. Late expanding: Declining birth rate + low/declining death rate
4. Low stationary: Low birth rate + low death rate

Therefore, the third stage (late expanding) is characterized by declining death rates and declining birth rates.

questions.text: A case of urinary bladder stone with a history of Proteus infection is likely to be?

Why other options are wrong

Oxalate stones

• Most common stones
• Associated with hypercalciuria, not infection.

Uric acid stones

• Occur in acidic urine
