questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 29-year-old male diagnosed with schizophrenia has been stable on risperidone for the past few months. Recently, he began experiencing dystonia, for which he was started on benztropine 2 mg twice daily by his psychiatrist. A week later, he presents to the emergency department with complaints of dry mouth, blurred vision, confusion and urinary retention. On examination, he is disoriented, tachycardic, and febrile. Pupils are dilated and bowel sounds are absent. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
options: Discontinue risperidone and initiate lorazepam for possible neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS)
Administer intravenous dantrolene and initiate cooling measures for suspected serotonin syndrome
Start physostigmine with continuous cardiac monitoring for anticholinergic toxicity due to benztropine overdose
Administer activated charcoal and IV fluids; observe the patient as symptoms are likely self-limiting
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Start physostigmine with continuous cardiac monitoring for anticholinergic toxicity due to benztropine overdose

Key clues:

• Dry mouth
• Blurred vision
• Confusion
• Urinary retention
• Dilated pupils
• Absent bowel sounds
• Tachycardia

This is classic ANTICHOLINERGIC TOXICITY

Drug added: Benztropine

• Used for:

• Drug-induced dystonia (from antipsychotics)

Mechanism:

• Central + peripheral muscarinic receptor blockade

Benztropine → muscarinic blockade

↓

Anticholinergic toxicity

↓

Give physostigmine

↓

↑ Acetylcholine

↓

Restores parasympathetic activity

Dry mouth, mydriasis, confusion, urinary retention, tachycardia, and absent bowel sounds indicate severe anticholinergic toxicity from benztropine. Physostigmine is a centrally acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that reverses both CNS and peripheral effects. It must be given with cardiac monitoring due to arrhythmia risk. This is the antidote for life-threatening anticholinergic delirium.

| Feature | Anticholinergic | NMS | Serotonin syndrome

| ------- | --------------- | --- | ------------------

| Skin | Dry | Sweaty | Sweaty

| Pupils | Dilated | Normal | Dilated

| Bowel sounds | ↓ | Normal | ↑

| Reflexes | Normal | ↓ | ↑ (clonus)

| CNS | Delirium | Rigidity | Agitation

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The best drug for maintenance therapy of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) during pregnancy is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hydroxychloroquine

Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is the drug of choice for maintenance therapy in pregnant women with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE). It is considered safe throughout pregnancy and should be continued because it reduces disease flares, improves maternal outcomes, and decreases the risk of adverse fetal outcomes.

Discontinuing hydroxychloroquine during pregnancy is associated with an increased risk of lupus flares. May reduce the risk of congenital heart block in anti-Ro/SSA-positive mothers

Why not the other options?

• B. Sulfasalazine: Used mainly for rheumatoid arthritis and inflammatory bowel disease, not as maintenance therapy for SLE.
• C. Tacrolimus: May be used in selected cases (e.g., lupus nephritis), but it is not the first-line maintenance drug.
• D. Progestins: Used for contraception or prevention of preterm birth in selected situations, not for treating SLE.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding anti-glomerular basement membrane disease? 1. It is a rare autoimmune disease which presents as rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. 2. Antibodies are formed against α3 chain of type IV collagen GBM. 3. The α3 chain is expressed in basement membrane of glomerulus and the retina. 4. The disease may be associated with retinal hemorrhage when it is known as Goodpasture syndrome. Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 and 2 only

Anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) disease is a rare autoimmune disorder characterized by the formation of autoantibodies against the α3 chain of type IV collagen in the glomerular basement membrane (GBM), leading to rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN).

Explanation of the statements:

• Statement 1. It is a rare autoimmune disease which presents as rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis: Correct. Anti-GBM disease is a rare autoimmune cause of crescentic (Type I) rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.
• Statement 2. Antibodies are formed against α3 chain of type IV collagen GBM: Correct. The pathogenic antibodies are directed against the non-collagenous (NC1) domain of the α3 chain of type IV collagen.
• Statement 3. The α3 chain is expressed in basement membrane of glomerulus and the retina:  Incorrect. The α3 chain is expressed in the glomerular and alveolar basement membranes, not the retina.
• Statement 4. The disease may be associated with retinal hemorrhage when it is known as Goodpasture syndrome: Incorrect. Goodpasture syndrome refers to anti-GBM disease with pulmonary involvement (diffuse alveolar hemorrhage/hemoptysis), not retinal hemorrhage.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman with a past history of rheumatic fever is found on examination to have a loud first heart sound and a mid-diastolic murmur. Which valvular heart disease is most likely present?
questions.explanation: The patient’s history of rheumatic fever combined with the auscultatory findings of a loud S1 and a mid-diastolic murmur are classic indicators of Mitral Stenosis (MS). Rheumatic heart disease is the leading cause of MS worldwide, resulting in the thickening and fusion of valve leaflets. The S1 is loud because the stiffened valves close forcefully at the start of systole. The mid-diastolic murmur occurs due to turbulent blood flow across the narrowed mitral orifice as the left ventricle fills. While Tricuspid Stenosis (TS) (Option A) also produces a mid-diastolic murmur, it typically increases with inspiration and is rarely seen in isolation. Mitral Regurgitation (MR) (Option B) presents with a pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla. Aortic Regurgitation (AR) (Option D) produces an early diastolic decrescendo murmur. Therefore, based on the specific location and nature of the murmur following rheumatic fever, Mitral Stenosis is the most accurate diagnosis for this patient
questions.learning: The patient’s history of rheumatic fever combined with the auscultatory findings of a loud S1 and a mid-diastolic murmur are classic indicators of Mitral Stenosis (MS).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Asbestosis is a chronic lung condition resulting from prolonged inhalation of asbestos fibers. Which type of cancer is most commonly linked to this disease?
questions.explanation: Asbestosis is a form of pneumoconiosis caused by the chronic inhalation of asbestos fibers, typically in occupational settings like construction or shipbuilding. While asbestos exposure significantly increases the risk of bronchogenic carcinoma, it is most uniquely and strongly associated with malignant mesothelioma. Mesothelioma is a rare and aggressive cancer that develops in the thin layer of tissue covering the lungs (pleura) or abdomen (peritoneum). Option B (Anthracosis) is not a malignancy but a benign accumulation of carbon pigment in the lungs. Option C (Hepatocellular carcinoma) and Option D (Renal cell carcinoma) are malignancies related to viral hepatitis or genetic mutations and are not linked to asbestos inhalation. The latency period between asbestos exposure and the development of mesothelioma is often 20 to 40 years. Because of this strong link, any patient with a clinical history of asbestosis must be closely monitored for pleural changes or effusions indicative of malignancy
questions.learning: Asbestosis is a form of pneumoconiosis caused by the chronic inhalation of asbestos fibers, typically in occupational settings like construction or shipbuilding.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: While performing surgery for acute appendicitis on a 2 year old child the following structure was found 2 feet proximal to ileocaecal junction and it was 2 inches long. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Meckel's diverticulum

The given clinical viignette and image is suggestive of Meckel's diverticulum which extends from the antimesenteric side of the small bowel.

The most common true diverticulum is Meckel's diverticulum, which occurs in the ileum.

A true diverticulum is a blind outpouching of the alimentary tract that communicates with the lumen and includes all three layers of the bowel wall. Meckel diverticulum occurs as a result of the failed involution of the vitelline duct, which connects the lumen of the developing gut to the yolk sac.

Meckel’s Diverticulum:

* Meckel’s diverticulum is caused by a failure of normal regression of the vitelline duct that develops during weeks 5 to 7 of gestation.

* The rule of 2s (Mnemonic for Meckel’s diverticulum) :

* 2 types of heterotopic mucosa (gastric & pancreatic)

* 2% incidence

* located within 2 feet of the ileocecal valve

* approximately 2 inches in length

* Usually symptomatic by 2 years of age

* Most common presentation is painless, massive, lower GI bleed in children younger than 5 years.

* A Meckel's can be the lead point for ileoileal or ileocolic intussusception.

* The bleeding Meckel's diverticulum may be confirmed by a 99 mTc-pertechnetate isotope scan to detect gastric mucosa.

* Surgical treatment is the definitive therapy for Meckel’s diverticulum. A simple V-shaped diverticulectomy with transverse closure of the ileum is the ideal surgical approach.

Pearl PF0287: Rule of two’s in Meckel's diverticulum

* 2% prevalence

* 2:1 male predominance

* Location 2 feet (60 cm) proximal to the ileocecal valve in adults

* 2 inches in length

* Half of those who are symptomatic are under 2 years of age.

Pearl PF0326: Zenker’s Diverticulum

* Hypopharyngeal diverticulum

* False diverticulum

* Pulsion diverticulum

* Acquired diverticulum, seen in the elderly (>60 years)

* Herniation is through the Killian’s triangle (a weak area between two parts of the inferior constrictor) in the posterior pharyngeal wall

* Clinical features:

* Dysphagia

* Regurgitation

* Halitosis

* Aspiration

* Gurgling sound during swallowing

* Investigation of choice: Barium swallow (Lateral X rays)

* Treatment

* Cricopharyngeal myotomy

* Surgical diverticulectomy

* Marsupialization

* Dohlman’s procedure

Zenker’s diverticulum

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following modalities is not used for hearing assessment in an infant?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pure tone audiometry

Assessment of hearing in infants requires objective or behavioral methods because they are unable to cooperate with subjective tests. Early detection of hearing loss is essential for speech and language development.

Methods used in infants:

• Brainstem Evoked Response Audiometry (BERA/ABR): Objective, evaluates auditory pathway up to brainstem
• Otoacoustic Emissions (OAE): Screens cochlear (outer hair cell) function
• Free-field audiometry (Behavioral observation audiometry): Uses sound stimuli and observes infant response

Why pure tone audiometry is not used:

• Requires active participation and subjective response from the patient
• Infants cannot understand or respond reliably to tones
questions.learning: Pure tone audiometry Assessment of hearing in infants requires objective or behavioral methods because they are unable to cooperate with subjective tests.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 34-year-old cattle handler presents with gradual onset fever, malaise, weight loss, drenching night sweats, low back pain, and mild hepatosplenomegaly. He frequently assists in animal delivery. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Brucellosis

Brucellosis is a zoonotic infection caused by Brucella species (most commonly Brucella melitensis). It is transmitted through direct contact with infected livestock (cattle, sheep, goats, pigs), exposure to animal placental tissue, or ingestion of unpasteurized milk and dairy products. The disease presents with undulating fever, drenching night sweats, malaise, weight loss, arthralgia, low back pain, and hepatosplenomegaly.

Why not the other options?

• A. Leptospirosis: Acquired through water contaminated with animal urine; presents with fever, conjunctival suffusion, jaundice (Weil disease), and renal failure.
• C. Anthrax: Caused by Bacillus anthracis; presents with a painless black eschar (cutaneous anthrax), inhalational disease, or gastrointestinal anthrax.
• D. Rabies: Transmitted by bites from infected mammals; presents with hydrophobia, aerophobia, and encephalitis, not chronic fever with hepatosplenomegaly.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: CIostridium difficile associated diarrhea occurs maximally due to:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lincosamides

Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea is mostly due to lincosamides such as clindamycin

Antibiotic-associated colitis is caused by Clostridium difficile infection due to the destruction of the normal gut microbial flora by the use of antibiotics. The antibiotics most frequently implicated include clindamycin, fluoroquinolones and broad-spectrum penicillins, and cephalosporins

Clostridium difficile infection occurs frequently in hospitals and nursing homes where antimicrobial use is high and the environment is contaminated by C. difficile spores.

Although all antibiotics can cause the condition, the most commonly implicated are:

• Clindamycin
• Third-generation cephalosporins (cefotaxime, ceftriaxone, cefuroxime, and ceftazidime)
• Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, and moxifloxacin)
• Broad-spectrum penicillins

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Insulin-independent glucose transporter is present in all of the following except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adipose tissue

Insulin-dependent (not independent) glucose transporter is found in the adipose tissue.

Glucose uptake by skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle and adipose tissues is via GLUT-4 which is insulin-dependent.

In the cytoplasm of insulin-sensitive cells, the vesicles contain a pool of GLUT-4 molecules. When the insulin receptors of these cells are activated, the vesicles move rapidly to the cell membrane and fuse with it, inserting the transporters into the cell membrane.

The membrane patches containing transporters are endocytosed when insulin action stops, preparing the vesicles for subsequent insulin exposure. Phosphoinositol 3-kinase is activated by the insulin receptor, which causes the vesicles to migrate to the cell membrane

Most of the other GLUT transporters are not insulin-sensitive and are constitutively expressed in the cell membrane. Ex: GLUT-1 in RBC's and brain, GLUT-2 in the beta cells of the pancreas and GLUT-3 present in the brain and kidneys.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman, who is 5 days postpartum, presented with tearfulness, mood swings, and occasional insomnia. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Postpartum blues

Postpartum blues is the most likely diagnosis in a postpartum woman with tearfulness, mood swings, and insomnia from day 4.

Postpartum blues, also known as baby blues, is a transient mood disorder characterized by sadness, tearfulness, confusion, and dysphoria. There are no suicidal thoughts or thoughts of harming the baby. These symptoms typically develop 3-5 days after delivery. They are thought to be due to hormonal changes, the stress of giving birth, and the responsibilities of motherhood. They resolve spontaneously within 10-14 days.

Management involves reassurance, education, and support. The patient must be followed-up and assessed if symptoms persist for >2 weeks to evaluate postpartum depression.

Other options:

Option A: Postpartum depression is when the symptoms of depressed mood, anxiety, insomnia, and weight changes persist for >4 weeks as per DSM 5 or >6 weeks as per ICD 11. The onset is within 4-6 weeks post-delivery. The patient may have occasional thoughts of harming the baby and suicidal thoughts. It can persist for months to years when untreated.

Option C: Postpartum psychosis is a psychiatric emergency that usually occurs within 4 weeks after delivery (DSM 5) or 6 weeks after delivery (ICD 11). The predominant symptoms are hallucinations, delusions, suicidal thoughts, and thoughts of harming the baby. Psychotic symptoms such as insomnia, restlessness, labile mood, and agitation are seen. Lithium, antipsychotics, and an antidepressant is the treatment of choice.

Option D: Postpartum anxiety is not defined by DSM-5. However, some platforms might describe postpartum anxiety as excessive or severe worry after childbirth.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Optic nerve glioma is seen in?
questions.explanation: Optic nerve glioma is a low-grade pilocytic astrocytoma that is highly characteristic of Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF-1). Up to 15-20% of children with NF-1 will develop an optic pathway glioma, often presenting as a painless, progressive proptosis and vision loss. NF-2 (Option C) is characteristically associated with bilateral vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuromas) and meningiomas but not typically optic gliomas. Tuberous sclerosis (Option B) is associated with retinal hamartomas (phakomas) and subependymal giant cell astrocytomas. Schwannoma (Option D) refers to a nerve sheath tumor; while NF-2 patients develop multiple schwannomas, the specific optic nerve lesion in NF-1 is a glioma. NF-1 is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a mutation on chromosome 17. Because these gliomas can be indolent, management often involves careful observation with regular MRI and ophthalmological check-ups, reserving chemotherapy or surgery for cases with documented progression that threatens vision or reaches the optic chiasm

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 32-year-old female presented with a 5-day history of increased vaginal discharge and intense vulvar pruritus. On speculum examination, the vaginal mucosa was erythematous with profuse frothy greenish discharge. A “Whiff Test” (addition of 10% KOH) was negative. What is the microscopic finding seen in this clinical scenario?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Motile flagellate organisms

Trichomonas vaginalis is a flagellated protozoan that causes trichomoniasis, characterized by profuse frothy yellow-green vaginal discharge, vulvar pruritus, vaginal erythema, Negative Whiff (amine) test and a “strawberry cervix.” Diagnosis is made by saline wet mount, which demonstrates motile, pear-shaped flagellated trophozoites.

Why is A correct?

• Frothy greenish discharge
• Intense vulvar pruritus
• Vaginal erythema
• Wet mount shows motile flagellated organisms, diagnostic of Trichomonas vaginalis.

Why not the other options?

• B. Presence of clue cells: Seen in bacterial vaginosis (Gardnerella vaginalis); Whiff test is positive.
• C. Gram-negative diplococci: Suggestive of Neisseria gonorrhoeae, causing cervicitis rather than frothy vaginitis.
• D. Pseudohyphae and spores: Seen in Candida albicans infection, which presents with thick curdy white discharge, intense itching, and normal vaginal pH.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with a neck swelling and laboratory results showing elevated T4 levels with suppressed TSH. He has a prior history of treatment with radioactive iodine (I-131) ablation. Which of the following is a likely adverse effect of this therapy?
questions.explanation: Radioactive iodine (I-131) ablation therapy is used to treat conditions like Graves' disease or toxic nodules by destroying thyroid tissue. The most common long-term side effect of this destruction is a progressive decline in thyroid hormone production, eventually resulting in hypothyroidism. Most patients who undergo this therapy will eventually require lifelong levothyroxine replacement. Acute Thyroiditis (Option A) is a transient inflammatory reaction that can occur early after treatment but is not a permanent side effect. Hyperthyroidism (Option C) might occur briefly during a "flare" phase as damaged cells release stored hormones, but it is not the intended long-term outcome. Thyroid Storm (Option D) is a rare, life-threatening crisis usually seen in untreated patients, not as a direct consequence of ablation therapy. Therefore, the destruction of the thyroid gland essentially trades hyperthyroidism for easily managed hypothyroidism

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The stroke volume depends on end-diastolic volume. This is best represented as
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Length-tension relationship

The relationship between end-diastolic volume and stroke volume is best represented by length-tension relationship.

This is explained by the ‘Frank-Starling law of heart’ which states that ‘ the volume of blood ejected by the ventricle depends on the volume present in the ventricle at the end of the diastole’. The length of the myocytes depend on the volume (and hence tension) present at the end of the diastole, which in turn, depends on the volume returned to the heart, or the venous return.

• The Frank-Starling law governs the normal ventricular function and ensures that the cardiac output equals venous return, within physiological limits.
• There is a curvilinear relationship between stroke volume or cardiac output and the ventricular end-diastolic volume.
• Agents that increase the contractility of the cardiac muscle have a positive inotropic effect and produce increased stroke volume and thereby increased cardiac output for a given end-diastolic volume. (Eg: Digoxin)
• Agents that decrease the contractility of the cardiac muscle have a negative inotropic effect and produce decreased stroke volume (and cardiac output) for a given end-diastolic volume.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient complains of a chronic morning cough with production of yellow sputum that becomes more pronounced when changing posture from the left side to the right. Based on this positional variation and symptom profile, what is the most likely underlying lung condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a chronic morning cough with copious "yellow" (purulent) sputum and postural variation (symptoms triggered or worsened by changing body positions) is highly suggestive of Bronchiectasis. In bronchiectasis, permanent dilation of the bronchi allows for the accumulation of large volumes of infected mucus. When the patient shifts positions, this pool of secretions moves and irritates different parts of the airway, triggering forceful coughing to clear the material. Lung cancer (Option A) usually presents with hemoptysis and weight loss. Bronchial asthma (Option C) is characterized by wheezing and reversible airway obstruction, usually worse at night rather than specifically tied to postural changes in sputum production. Pulmonary embolism (Option D) presents with acute pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea, not chronic purulent morning cough. Therefore, the mechanical pooling of secretions that move with gravity makes bronchiectasis the most probable diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a chronic morning cough with copious "yellow" (purulent) sputum and postural variation (symptoms triggered or worsened by changing body positions) is highly suggestive of Bronchiectasis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 32-year-old female presents with progressive bilateral hearing loss, in the right ear more than left. After the initial evaluation, a stapedotomy of the right ear was planned. What might've been the tuning fork test results of the patient?
options: Bilateral Rinne's negative, Weber's lateralized to the right
Bilateral Rinne's negative, Weber's lateralized to the left
Bilateral Rinne's positive, Weber's lateralized to the right
Bilateral Rinne's positive, Weber's lateralized to the left
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bilateral Rinne's negative, Weber's lateralized to the right

In the given clinical scenario, a female with progressive bilateral hearing loss, in the right ear more than the left, and a stapedotomy of the right ear was planned. Stapedotomy surgery is done for otosclerosis. Otosclerosis results in conductive hearing loss so, the tuning fork test results of the patient will be Bilateral Rinne's negative, Weber's lateralized to the right.

As there is conductive hearing loss in both ears, like that associated with otosclerosis (which may require a stapedotomy), the bilateral Rinne test will be negative. In Weber's test, the sound lateralizes to the affected ear, which, in this case, is the right ear with more significant hearing loss.

Tuning fork tests are performed commonly with tuning forks of frequencies such as 128, 256, 512, 1024, etc. The tuning fork of 512 Hz is considered ideal as forks of lower frequencies produce a sense of bone vibration, while those of higher frequencies have a shorter decay time.

Rinne’s test is done by placing a vibrating tuning fork on the patient’s mastoid and when he stops hearing, it is brought beside the external auditory meatus (EAC). If he still hears the sound, air conduction (AC) is better than bone conduction (BC) i.e. AC>BC. The inferences are as follows:

• Rinne's test is considered positive (normal) when the air conduction AC>BC is seen in normal people and people with sensorineural deafness.
• It is considered negative when the BC>AC, and is seen in patients with conductive deafness.

Weber test is done by placing a vibrating tuning in the middle of the forehead or the vertex and the patient is asked in which ear the sound is heard. The inferences are as follows:

• Normal result is achieved when the sound heard equally in both ears
• In conductive deafness, it is lateralized to the worse ear
• In sensorineural deafness, it is lateralized to the better ear.
questions.learning: Bilateral Rinne's negative, Weber's lateralized to the right In the given clinical scenario, a female with progressive bilateral hearing loss, in the right ear more than the left, and a stapedotomy of the right ear was planned.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn presented with chest retractions, dyspnea, and lethargy. The pediatrician diagnosed the baby with respiratory distress syndrome. This occurs due to the deficiency of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lecithin

Respiratory distress syndrome in a neonate is likely due to the deficiency of lecithin.

Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), also known as hyaline membrane disease, is due to the decreased production and secretion of the lung surfactant. Surfactant is a lipoprotein primarily made of phospholipids such as lecithin (otherwise known as dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine). The other minor components are phosphatidylglycerol, apoproteins, and cholesterol. It is synthesized in type II pneumocytes/granular pneumocytes in the endoplasmic reticulum (shown below).

RDS is commonly seen in preterm babies less than 34 weeks of gestation. Surfactant deficiency leads to an increase in the surface tension over the alveoli, causing the alveoli to collapse easily during expiration. Therefore, the baby has to put more effort to expand the lungs. Tachypnea, cyanosis, nasal flaring, prominent expiratory grunting, and intercostal and subcostal retractions are some of the common findings seen in this condition.

Chest x-ray shows features such as reticulogranular pattern, ground-glass opacity, and air bronchogram. White-out lungs can be seen on chest x-ray in severe diseases.

Management in mild to moderate RDS is with continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), where the positive pressure keeps the alveoli open in a spontaneously breathing baby. Severe cases will require mechanical ventilation. Steroids increase the production of the surfactant, and therefore, steroids are administered antenatally to mothers with preterm labor.

Other options -

Option A: Dipalmitoyl inositol, or phosphatidylinositol, acts as a precursor for the secondary messenger system. It also helps in cell signaling and membrane trafficking.

Option C: Sphingomyelin is a dominant sphingolipid in the plasma membrane. The lecithin/sphingomyelin ratio in amniotic fluid helps in determining fetal lung maturity.

Option D: Dipalmitoyl ethanolamine is present in the cell membrane.
questions.learning: Lecithin Respiratory distress syndrome in a neonate is likely due to the deficiency of lecithin. Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), also known as hyaline membrane disease, is due to the decreased production and secretion of the lung surfactant.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: At which stage of clinical trials is a newly developed drug usually approved for marketing and made available to the public?
questions.explanation: Phase III is the stage at which a newly developed drug is evaluated for regulatory approval and subsequently marketed and made available to the general public. Phase III trials are large-scale randomized controlled trials (RCTs) conducted on thousands of patients (typically 1,000–3,000) across multiple centers. These trials compare the new drug against existing standard treatments or placebo, establishing definitive evidence of efficacy, safety, optimal dosage, and side effect profile. Upon successful completion of Phase III, the pharmaceutical company submits a New Drug Application (NDA) to regulatory authorities like the FDA or CDSCO, after which the drug receives marketing approval. Why other options are wrong: (A) Phase I is incorrect because Phase I trials are conducted on a small group of healthy volunteers (20–80 people) primarily to assess safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics. No efficacy data is established here and marketing is nowhere near consideration at this stage. (B) Phase II is incorrect because Phase II trials involve moderate number of patients (100–300) with the target disease, primarily evaluating therapeutic efficacy, optimal dosing, and short-term side effects. While promising results emerge here, this data is insufficient for regulatory marketing approval. (D) Phase IV is incorrect because Phase IV trials occur after marketing approval, representing post-marketing surveillance. They monitor long-term safety, rare adverse effects, and new indications in the general population — the drug is already available to the public at this point
questions.learning: Phase III is the stage at which a newly developed drug is evaluated for regulatory approval and subsequently marketed and made available to the general public.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following patterns of visual field loss is seen in right optic tract lesion?
options: Right temporal and Left nasal vision loss
Right nasal and Left temporal vision loss
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Right nasal and Left temporal vision loss

A lesion of the right optic tract (as shown) causes left homonymous hemianopia, i.e., loss of the left visual field of both eyes.

• Right eye: Loss of the nasal visual field
• Left eye: Loss of the temporal visual field

Hence, the visual field defect is right nasal + left temporal vision loss.

Why not the other options?

• A. Right temporal and Left nasal vision loss: Represents right homonymous hemianopia.
• C. Bilateral temporal vision loss: Bitemporal hemianopia, caused by optic chiasm lesions (e.g., pituitary adenoma).
• D. Bilateral nasal vision loss: Binasal hemianopia, rare; due to bilateral lateral optic chiasm compression.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following nerves is not involved in olfaction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hypoglossal nerve

The hypoglossal nerve is purely motor cranial nerve and is not involved in olfaction.

The other three cranial nerves—trigeminal, glossopharyngeal, and vagus nerves are mixed cranial nerves and contribute to olfaction.

Vagal nerve stimulation modifies the electrical activity of the olfactory bulb.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following statements is correct for subcutaneous nodules in Rheumatic fever?
options: They are present over flexor aspect of forearm
The usual size of these nodules is 3–5 cm
They typically appear more than 3 weeks after onset of other clinical manifestations
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. They typically appear more than 3 weeks after onset of other clinical manifestations

Subcutaneous nodules are one of the major Jones criteria for the diagnosis of acute rheumatic fever (ARF). They are a late manifestation, typically appearing more than 3 weeks after the onset of other clinical features such as arthritis or carditis, and are strongly associated with severe rheumatic carditis.

Subcutaneous nodules:

• Appear weeks after the onset of rheumatic fever (usually >3 weeks). ⭐
• Often coexist with carditis.
• Tend to resolve spontaneously over weeks.

Why not the other options?

• A. They are present over flexor aspect of forearm: Incorrect. They occur over extensor surfaces and bony prominences, such as the elbows, knees, ankles, spine, and occiput.
• B. They are painful tender nodules: Incorrect. They are painless, firm, and non-tender.
• C. The usual size of these nodules is 3–5 cm: Incorrect. They are usually small (0.5–2 cm) in diameter.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 10-month-old child presents with diarrhea, hypokalemia, and muscle weakness. Despite ongoing treatment, these symptoms persist. What is the most likely reason for the treatment’s ineffectiveness?
questions.explanation: In clinical practice, refractory hypokalemia (low potassium that does not respond to supplementation) is most frequently caused by concurrent hypomagnesemia (Option A). Magnesium is a critical cofactor for the renal ROMK channels; when magnesium is low, these channels become overactive, leading to excessive and continuous urinary potassium wasting. In a 10-month-old child with chronic diarrhea, both potassium and magnesium are lost through the stool. If only potassium is replaced, the kidneys will continue to excrete it until the magnesium deficit is corrected. Options B (Hyponatremia), C (Hypermagnesemia), and D (Hypernatremia) do not interfere with potassium homeostasis in this specific inhibitory manner. Therefore, the failure of potassium levels to normalize despite treatment is a pathognomonic clinical clue for underlying magnesium deficiency. Clinicians must measure and replace magnesium to successfully treat the patient’s muscular weakness and hypokalemia. Consequently, hypomagnesemia is the definitive physiological reason for the treatment failure
questions.learning: In clinical practice, refractory hypokalemia (low potassium that does not respond to supplementation) is most frequently caused by concurrent hypomagnesemia (Option A).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with disorientation following a road traffic accident. CT scan shows no hemorrhage but reveals cerebral edema and raised intracranial pressure. Which drug is appropriate for the initial management of increased intracranial pressure?
questions.explanation: In the emergency management of raised intracranial pressure (ICP) due to cerebral edema following trauma, Mannitol is the gold-standard, first-line pharmacological intervention (Option B). Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic that works by creating an osmotic gradient, drawing fluid from the brain tissue into the vascular space, thereby rapidly reducing brain volume and ICP. Furosemide (Option A) is a loop diuretic that can be used as an adjunct but is not the primary agent for ICP. Acetazolamide (Option C) is used for chronic conditions like idiopathic intracranial hypertension but is ineffective for acute post-traumatic edema. Glycerol (Option D) is an older oral osmotic agent with a slower onset and higher risk of metabolic side effects. Therefore, because of its rapid onset and proven efficacy in trauma settings, Mannitol is the definitive initial choice. It must be administered carefully while monitoring serum osmolality and renal function
questions.learning: In the emergency management of raised intracranial pressure (ICP) due to cerebral edema following trauma, Mannitol is the gold-standard, first-line pharmacological intervention (Option B).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: While collecting blood for samples, you have spilled some on the floor. What would be the immediate next step?
options: Call the infection control team of the hospital
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Clean with absorbable material

The immediate next step in this scenario is to clean the spilled blood with absorbable material.

This absorbable material is then discarded in the yellow bin. Following this, sodium hypochlorite solution is used to decontaminate the surface. The concentrations of sodium hypochlorite used are:

• < 10 mL blood spill - 1:100 dilution to decontaminate non-porous surfaces
• > 10 mL blood spill or culture spill - 1:10 dilution for the first application, followed by 1:100 dilution

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An elderly male with a history of chronic smoking is diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma of the lower lip stage. Further investigations revealed that the lymph nodes are not involved. What is the treatment of choice in this patient?
options: Wide local excision with negative margins
Wide local excision with frozen borders
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Wide local excision with negative margins

This pateint has an early stage squamous cell carcinoma. Wide local excision with negative margins is the preferred treatment for this type of cancer.

Lip cancer most commonly occurs in men from 50 to 70 years but can be seen in younger patients. Risk factors include sunlight exposure, smoking, and tobacco use. Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common type of lip cancer. But commonly occurring cancer in the upper lip is basal cell carcinoma.

Surgical resection (wide local excision with negative margins) is the preferred treatment modality. The typical lip length is 6 to 7 cm. For defects of <1/3rd of the lip, resection with primary closure is the preferred treatment.

For defects of more than 1/3rd of the lip, require local flaps for reconstruction after resection:

* Johansen step technique- local flap for large central defects

* Lip-switch (Abbe-Estlander) flap- based on the sublabial or superior labial artery. When the defect involves only the commissure, the Estlander flap is used, and the Abbé flap is used for midline defects. Abbe-Estlander Flap is used for mixed defects. The markings of the Abbe-Estlander flap are shown below.

* Karapandzic flap - circumoral advancement flap. It is a neuromuscular flap that includes the remaining orbicularis oris muscle with its innervation.

In the presence of neck metastasis, neck dissection is indicated. Postoperative radiation is administered to patients with positive margins, lymph node metastases, tumor thickness >4mm, or perineural invasion. If the mandible is involved, mandibulectomy and free flap reconstruction is required.
questions.learning: Wide local excision with negative margins — This pateint has an early stage squamous cell carcinoma. Wide local excision with negative margins is the preferred treatment for this type of cancer.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following enzymes are active in the dephosphorylated state during glucose metabolism? 1. Glycogen synthase 2. Glycogen phosphorylase 3. Phosphofructokinase-2 4. Pyruvate dehydrogenase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 3, 4

Many enzymes involved in glucose metabolism are regulated by reversible phosphorylation. In the fed state (high insulin), protein phosphatases dephosphorylate key enzymes, promoting glycogen synthesis and glycolysis.

Enzymes active in the dephosphorylated state:

• 1. Glycogen synthase ✓: Dephosphorylation activates glycogen synthesis.
• 3. Phosphofructokinase-2 (PFK-2\, liver isoform) ✓: Dephosphorylation activates PFK-2, increasing fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, which stimulates glycolysis.
• 4. Pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) ✓: Dephosphorylation activates PDH, promoting conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA.

Why is 2 incorrect?

• 2. Glycogen phosphorylase ✗: Active in the phosphorylated state, promoting glycogen breakdown during fasting.
questions.learning: 1, 3, 4 Many enzymes involved in glucose metabolism are regulated by reversible phosphorylation. In the fed state (high insulin), protein phosphatases dephosphorylate key enzymes, promoting glycogen synthesis and glycolysis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is not required for calculation of creatinine clearance?
options: Volume of serum passing through kidney in 24 hours
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Volume of serum passing through kidney in 24 hours

The volume of plasma passing through the kidney in 24 hours is not used in the calculation of creatinine clearance.

The parameters used to calculate creatinine clearance (CCr) are:

• Urine creatinine
• Serum creatinine
• 24hr urine output

The formula used to calculate creatinine clearance (CCr) is:

UCr × V ⁄ PCr  where,

UCr - Urine creatinine(mg/dl)

PCr - Serum creatinine(mg/dl)

V - Urine volume(ml/24 hrs)

Creatinine is a metabolite of muscle metabolism and is cleared from the body mostly by glomerular filtration. Therefore, the clearance of creatinine is used to assess GFR.

Urine collection for the measurement of creatinine clearance may be subject to practical constraints. Therefore, approximate changes in GFR can be obtained by measuring the serum creatinine concentration, which is inversely proportional to GFR.
questions.learning: Volume of serum passing through kidney in 24 hours — The volume of plasma passing through the kidney in 24 hours is not used in the calculation of creatinine clearance.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A primigravida woman at 12 weeks of gestation comes to the antenatal clinic for nutritional advice. Which of the following will you recommend?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Additional 300kcal in 2nd trimester

For a pregnant woman, an additional 300kcal in the 2nd trimester is recommended.

According to Williams Obstetrics, in the first trimester, energy requirements are generally the same as non-pregnant women. In the second trimester, it increases by 340 kcal and in the third, it increases by 452 kcal per day. According to ICMR (Indian Council of Medical Research), an additional intake of 300 Kcal during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy is recommended. Therefore, option A would be a better answer in this case.

Pregnancy is a period where a mother will require additional nutritional requirements to support the healthy growth and development of the fetus. According to the National Institute of Nutrition,

• Protein intake should increase by 23g per day compared to non-pregnant women
• Fat intake should be 30g per day
• Calcium intake should be 1200mg per day
• Iron intake should be 35mg per day

During lactation, ICMR recommends increasing 550 Kcal during the first six months of lactation and 400 Kcal during 7- 12 months of lactation.
questions.learning: Additional 300kcal in 2nd trimester For a pregnant woman, an additional 300kcal in the 2nd trimester is recommended. According to Williams Obstetrics, in the first trimester, energy requirements are generally the same as non-pregnant women.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A man was brought to the ER after being involved in a fistfight with a bartender, presenting with severe chest pain, dyspnea, distended neck veins, and hypotension (80/50 mmHg). He subsequently collapsed. On examination, percussion revealed hyper resonance in the infraclavicular region with absent breath sounds on the left. A chest X-ray showed a tracheal shift to the right. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tension pneumothorax

The given X-ray features showing a well-demarcated area devoid of lung markings on the left side with tracheal deviation and the mediastinal shift to the right side, along with the clinical scenario is suggestive of tension pneumothorax.

Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis, and treatment should never be delayed while waiting for radiological confirmation. Imaging modalities used are ultrasound–extended focused assessment with sonar for trauma (eFAST), chest x-ray, and spiral CT.

A tension pneumothorax develops when there is a tear either in the parietal or visceral pleura. This tear acts as a one-way valve i.e., air enters from the lung or chest wall through it during inspiration but has no way to escape during expiration. This ultimately leads to the collapse of the affected lung.

It usually occurs following penetrating or blunt chest trauma, iatrogenic lung injury, or mechanical positive pressure ventilation.

It is characterized by:

* Chest pain

* Tachypnea and acute dyspnea

* Sudden onset hemodynamic compromise (tachycardia, hypotension, low O2 saturation, loss of consciousness)

* Neck vein distention

* Tracheal deviation away from the side of the injury

* Decreased chest movements on the affected side

* Hyper-resonance on percussion on the affected side

* Absence or decreased breath sounds on the affected side

The X-ray below shows a left-sided tension pneumothorax. There is a large, well-demarcated area devoid of lung markings on the left side. The yellow arrows are pointing towards the tracheal deviation and the mediastinal shift to the right side.

Management of tension pneumothorax:

* Immediate management- needle decompression or needle thoracostomy i.e. insertion of a wide-bore needle in the 5th ICS anterior to the midaxillary line

* Definitive management- tube thoracostomy or chest tube insertion in the 5th ICS in the triangle of safety, identified as a triangle that lies anterior to the midaxillary line above the nipple, below, and lateral to the pectoralis major muscle.

Other Options:

Option B: Pleural effusion may present with dyspnea, pleuritic pain, dry cough, and associated symptoms like fever, weight loss, oedema, and ascites depending on the aetiology. On examination, there may be tachypnea, dullness on percussion and decreased/absent breath sounds at the base(s).

Option C: Constrictive pericarditis symptoms may include swelling in the legs, fatigue, and discomfort, but it's not directly associated with reduced breath sounds or hyperresonance.

Option D: Pneumomediastinum presents with clinical features include severe substernal chest pain (may or may not radiate to the neck and arms) and subcutaneous emphysema over the suprasternal notch.
questions.learning: Tension pneumothorax — The given X-ray features showing a well-demarcated area devoid of lung markings on the left side with tracheal deviation and the mediastinal shift to the right side, along with the clinical scenario is suggestive of tension pneumothorax.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: An electrician sustains electrical burns while at work. On arrival at the ED, he was hemodynamically stable. ECG monitoring and initial fluid resuscitation are started. His urine is collected for routine lab examination and is positive for myoglobin. On histopathology of the kidneys, which of the following will be observed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Metastatic calcification

The most likely diagnosis based on the clinical vignette given is a case of rhabdomyolysis leading to endogenous intrinsic acute kidney injury (AKI). In rhabdomyolysis with AKI, calcium-phosphate imbalance leads to metastatic calcification in normal renal tissue, especially interstitium.

* Metastatic calcification can occur in normal tissues whenever there is hypercalcemia.

* The major causes of hypercalcemia are

* Secretion of parathyroid hormone -related protein (PTHRP), due to malignant tumors

* Paget's disease, immobilization, or tumors (increased bone catabolism associated with multiple myeloma, leukemia, or skeletal metastases)

* Vitamin D intoxication and sarcoidosis

* Renal failure

* Metastatic calcification can occur throughout the body but mainly affects the interstitial tissues of the vasculature, kidneys, lungs, and gastric mucosa.

AKI is defined as a decline in kidney function within 7 days, resulting in the accumulation of nitrogenous waste and other toxic metabolites usually excreted in the urine. It includes a variety of conditions that share some common features, such as elevated creatinine levels and reduced urine output. It is broadly divided into three categories:

* Renal/intrinsic parenchymal

* Prerenal

* Postrenal

Other options:

Option A: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in conditions like vasculitis(immune mediated), malignant hypertension.

Option B: Caseous necrosis - characteristic of granulomatous infections like tuberculosis.

Option C: Dystrophic calcification:

* It is encountered in areas of necrosis, whether they are of coagulative, caseous, or liquefactive type, and in foci of enzymatic necrosis of fat.

* Calcification is almost always present in the atheromas of advanced atherosclerosis. It also commonly develops in ageing or damaged heart valves, further hampering their function

* Calcium salts appear macroscopically as fine, white granules or clumps, often felt as gritty deposits

* Tuberculous lymph nodes can be affected by this

* Although dystrophic calcification may simply be a telltale sign of previous cell injury, it is often a cause of organ dysfunction.

* Serum calcium is normal in dystrophic calcification.

Pearl PF0841: Types of calcifications

Dystrophic calcification
Metastatic calcification

Location
Dead and dying tissues
Normal interstitial tissues of the vasculature, kidneys, lungs, and gastric mucosa.

Calcium metabolism
Normal
deranged causing hypercalcemia

Examples

Calcific valvular stenosis

Advanced Atheromatous plaque

Monckeberg medial sclerosis

Parathyroid tumors

Hypercalcemia of malignancy

Paget disease

vitamin D intoxication

Sarcoidosis

Renal failure
questions.learning: Metastatic calcification — The most likely diagnosis based on the clinical vignette given is a case of rhabdomyolysis leading to endogenous intrinsic acute kidney injury (AKI).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
A 40-year-old man presents to the ER with severe abdominal pain. On examination, his HR is 110bpm, BP- 88/60mmHg. On per abdomen examination, guarding is present. The erect abdominal X-ray is shown below. Which of the following would you proceed with, for the management of this case?

1. USG abdomen
2. IV fluids
3. Exploratory laparotomy
4. Elective surgery
5. Conservative management
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2 & 3

The given clinical scenario and erect X-ray abdomen showing gas under the diaphragm are suggestive of pneumoperitoneum, which is managed by initial resuscitation with IV fluids followed by exploratory laparotomy.

Pneumoperitoneum is the presence of air or gas in the peritoneal cavity. The most common cause of pneumoperitoneum is a perforation of a hollow viscus.  Other causes of pneumoperitoneum in adults include peritoneal dialysis, and mechanical ventilation, after procedures like colonoscopy and endoscopy. In children, it can be caused by necrotizing enterocolitis, hirschsprung's disease, meconium ileus and mechanical ventilation.

The patient presents with abdominal pain and distension, vomiting, fever, constipation, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, and reduced urine output. Per-abdomen examination can show guarding and rigidity.

An erect X-ray abdomen is highly sensitive for the detection of free intraperitoneal gas. Some of the signs seen in the X-ray include:

• Cupola sign is the presence of air underneath the diaphragm, giving a dome-like appearance.
• Rigler's sign is where both bowel surfaces are seen together as a sharp margin.
• Falciform ligament sign is the outlining of the falciform ligament with free abdominal gas.
• Liver/gallbladder edge sign is where the sharp margins of the liver/gallbladder are visible due to the collection of air.

Management includes,

• Adequate preoperative resuscitation with intravenous fluids followed by correction of electrolyte imbalance, instituting broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and
• Early surgical intervention/laparotomy to address the cause of pneumoperitoneum and prevent further contamination of the peritoneal cavity.
questions.learning: 2 & 3 The given clinical scenario and erect X-ray abdomen showing gas under the diaphragm are suggestive of pneumoperitoneum, which is managed by initial resuscitation with IV fluids followed by exploratory laparotomy.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: identify the true statement about the given dose-response curve:
options: Drug B is the most potent
Drug B is the most efficacious
Drug C is more efficacious than drug D
Drug B is more efficacious than drug A
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Drug B is the most potent

The more the curve is to the left, the more its potency. Hence drug B is the most potent on the given dose-response curve (DRC).

Potency

* It is defined as the amount of drug needed to produce a given response.

* The more the curve is on the left side, the more its potency.

* Hence in the given DRC drug B is the most potent and drug D is the least potent.

Efficacy

* It is defined as the maximum effect produced by the drug and is determined by the peak of the curve.

* Hence in the given DRC, drug B has the least efficacy, and drugs A, C & D are equally efficacious.
questions.learning: Drug B is the most potent — The more the curve is to the left, the more its potency. Hence drug B is the most potent on the given dose-response curve (DRC).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the hormonal check for pregnancy at home?
questions.explanation: Home pregnancy tests function by detecting the beta subunit of human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) in the urine. This hormone is secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast shortly after implantation, which typically occurs about 5–6 days post-ovulation. It is generally detectable in the urine by 10 days after ovulation. β-hCG is critical for maintaining the corpus luteum to ensure continued progesterone production until the placenta is fully functional. Estrogen (Option B) and Progesterone (Option C) are essential for maintaining pregnancy but are not used as diagnostic markers for initial detection. Human Placental Lactogen (hPL) (Option D) is secreted by the placenta to regulate maternal metabolism and ensure glucose availability for the fetus, but it appears much later in pregnancy than hCG. Therefore, β-hCG remains the earliest and most reliable biochemical marker for confirming pregnancy at home
questions.learning: Home pregnancy tests function by detecting the beta subunit of human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) in the urine. This hormone is secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast shortly after implantation, which typically occurs about 5–6 days post-ovulation.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: If a wide range of values are present in a community, what is the best measure of central tendency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Median

The best measure of central tendency if there are a wide range of values is median.

If we take an example of a dataset of (1, 1, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 11, 41), we can see that 41 seems to be well away from the mean of 7.45 of the dataset.  If we eliminate this outlier, we can get a new dataset of (1, 1, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 11) with a median of 4.5 and a mean of 4.1. We see that the median only changed by 10% (went down to 4.5 from 5), while the mean decreased by 45%. Therefore, the median is less affected by outliers or extreme values.

The median is not sensitive to extreme values or outliers and thus it is the preferred measure of central tendency in a distribution with a wide range of values.

* The median is the central element in a distribution when all the elements are arranged in order.

* In a distribution that has an odd number of elements, the median is the middle value.

* In a distribution that has an even number of elements, the median is the average of the middle values, i.e., the arithmetic mean of the two middle values.

* The drawback of the median is that it doesn’t respond to the actual values of the elements but only to the number of values above or below it.

* The median is the same as the 50th centile.

* It is sometimes symbolized by Mdn.

* The median can be arrived at in ordinal, interval and ratio data scales.
questions.learning: Median — The best measure of central tendency if there are a wide range of values is median. If we take an example of a dataset of (1, 1, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 11, 41), we can see that 41 seems to be well away from the mean of 7.45 of the dataset.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presents to the medicine OPD with acute vomiting shortly after consuming fried rice. Based on this clinical presentation and food history, which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: The association between consuming "fried rice" and subsequent rapid-onset vomiting is a classic clinical clue for food poisoning caused by Bacillus cereus. B. cereus is a spore-forming bacterium often found in rice. If rice is cooked and then left at room temperature, the spores can germinate and produce a heat-stable emetic toxin. Reheating (frying) the rice does not inactivate this toxin, leading to vomiting within 1 to 6 hours of ingestion. Clostridium perfringens (Option A) and the diarrheal form of B. cereus typically present with diarrhea and a longer incubation period. Staphylococcus aureus (Option C) also causes rapid-onset vomiting but is usually linked to dairy products or meats. Bacillus anthracis (Option D) causes anthrax and is not a common cause of standard food poisoning. Therefore, Bacillus cereus is the most likely pathogen given the specific rice-based history
questions.learning: The association between consuming "fried rice" and subsequent rapid-onset vomiting is a classic clinical clue for food poisoning caused by Bacillus cereus.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following factors is least likely to predispose an individual to mucormycosis?
questions.explanation: Mucormycosis is a serious opportunistic fungal infection caused by mucormycetes, commonly present in the environment. It primarily affects individuals with impaired immunity or metabolic abnormalities. Neutropenia, uncontrolled diabetes (even without DKA), and prolonged steroid use are well-established risk factors. Neutropenia reduces the body’s ability to destroy fungal spores. Diabetes impairs immune function and increases susceptibility, while steroids cause immunosuppression and hyperglycemia. In contrast, broad-spectrum antibiotics are least likely to predispose to mucormycosis. These drugs mainly disturb normal bacterial flora and are more commonly associated with Candida infections, rather than invasive mould infections like mucormycosis. Why Other Options Are Not Correct (A) Neutropenia: Strong risk factor (C) Uncontrolled diabetes (without DKA): Still predisposes (D) Steroids: Major immunosuppressive risk
questions.learning: Mucormycosis is a serious opportunistic fungal infection caused by mucormycetes, commonly present in the environment. It primarily affects individuals with impaired immunity or metabolic abnormalities.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: A 64-year-old with inferior STEMI becomes hypotensive. JVP is raised. Lungs are clear. What is the most appropriate immediate management for the likely complication?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Isotonic fluid bolus

This patient has right ventricular infarction (RVI) complicating an inferior wall STEMI, suggested by the triad of:

• Hypotension
• Elevated JVP
• Clear lung fields

Right ventricular dysfunction reduces blood flow to the left ventricle, causing preload-dependent hypotension. Therefore, the immediate treatment is volume expansion with an isotonic fluid bolus to improve right ventricular filling and cardiac output.

Why not the others?

• A. IV nitrates → Reduce preload and can precipitate profound hypotension in RV infarction.
• B. IV furosemide → Decreases preload and worsens hemodynamics.
• D. ACE inhibitor → May further lower blood pressure in the acute setting.
