questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A USG can detect lymph node metastases in a patient with breast cancer and clinically negative lymph nodes by what percentage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 50 – 60%

A USG can detect lymph node metastasis in a patient with clinically negative lymph nodes by 50-60%.

The clinical determination of axillary lymph node metastases has an accuracy of only 33%.

Ultrasound (USG) is more sensitive than physical examination alone in determining axillary lymph node involvement during the preliminary staging of breast carcinoma.

Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) or core biopsy of sonographically indeterminate or suspicious lymph nodes can provide a more definitive diagnosis than USG alone.

Ultrasonography can also be utilized to image the regional lymph nodes in patients with breast cancer. The sensitivity for the status of axillary nodes ranges from 35% to 82% and specificity ranges from 73% to 97%.

The features of a lymph node involved with cancer on USG include:

• Cortical thickening
• Change in shape of the node to a more circular appearance
• Size larger than 10 mm
• Absence of a fatty hilum
• Hypoechoic internal echoes
questions.learning: 50 – 60% A USG can detect lymph node metastasis in a patient with clinically negative lymph nodes by 50-60%. The clinical determination of axillary lymph node metastases has an accuracy of only 33%.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Which of the following agents does not elicit pain on injection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ketamine

Ketamine does not elicit pain on injection, instead produces profound analgesia.

Propofol is formulated as a lipid emulsion, which causes pain on injection. A new aqueous prodrug, fospropofol is associated with less pain on injection.

Etomidate, although it causes pain on injection, the lipid formulation of etomidate is associated with a much less frequent incidence of pain.

Thiopentone at a concentration greater than 2.5% can produce pain on injection and venous thrombosis.
questions.learning: Ketamine Ketamine does not elicit pain on injection, instead produces profound analgesia. Propofol is formulated as a lipid emulsion, which causes pain on injection.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The most common ocular manifestation of COVID-19 is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Follicular conjunctivitis

The most common ocular manifestation of COVID-19 is follicular conjunctivitis.

It has been observed that SARS-CoV-2 needs the ACE-2 receptors for cell invasion. The ACE-2 receptors are found not only in human type 2 alveolar epithelial cells but also in the cornea and conjunctiva. This suggests that ocular surface tissue may be a potential target tissue for SARS-CoV-2.

The ocular manifestations of COVID-19 vary greatly. The most prevalent ocular symptoms were dry eye or foreign body sensation, redness, tearing, itching, eye pain, and discharge.

The most common ocular complication of COVID-19 is mild follicular conjunctivitis. Hemorrhagic conjunctivitis, dry eye disease, episcleritis, chemosis, and photophobia can also occur, but less frequently. Intraocular complications include retinal artery occlusions, hemorrhages, and cotton wool spots caused by complement-mediated thrombotic angiopathy.

Sometimes, conjunctivitis may appear as the only sign and symptom of COVID-19. Patients should therefore undergo a nasopharyngeal RT-PCR test.

All physicians and ophthalmologists should be cautious when addressing a patient with conjunctivitis and should wear eye-protective gear in addition to face masks and other protective devices during clinical examination of these patients.
questions.learning: Follicular conjunctivitis — The most common ocular manifestation of COVID-19 is follicular conjunctivitis. It has been observed that SARS-CoV-2 needs the ACE-2 receptors for cell invasion.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The joint between the attachment of the 8th and 9th rib to the 7th rib is a:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Synovial joint

The interchondral joint between the attachment of the 8th and 9th rib with the 7th rib is a synovial joint.

Joints in the thoracic cavity are of the following types:

• Synarthrosis - structures are connected by a fibrous band of tissue. E.g, 1st sternocostal joint
• Synchondrosis - primary cartilaginous joints. E.g., costochondral joints
• Symphysis - secondary cartilaginous joints. E.g. manubriosternal and xiphisternal joints
• Synovial joints - the presence of these help the thoracic cavity expand during inspiration. E.g.:

• Interchondral joint
• Sternocostal joint
• Costovertebral joint
• Costotransverse joint

Note:

The interchondral joint between the 9th and 10th cartilages is never synovial and sometimes absent.
questions.learning: Synovial joint — The interchondral joint between the attachment of the 8th and 9th rib with the 7th rib is a synovial joint. Joints in the thoracic cavity are of the following types: • Synarthrosis - structures are connected by a fibrous band of tissue.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 56-year-old man with a known history of diabetes presents to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain and vomiting. On examination, he has rapid breathing, a fruity (acetone) odor on his breath, and hypotension. Laboratory investigations show markedly elevated blood glucose levels, and urine testing is positive for ketones. What is the most appropriate initial step in management for this patient?
options: IV fluids and check potassium levels
questions.explanation: The patient presents with the classic clinical triad of Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA): hyperglycemia (≥250 mg/dL), ketonuria, and metabolic acidosis, suggested by the fruity breath odor and Kussmaul (rapid) breathing. While insulin is essential to stop ketogenesis, the absolute priority in initial management is aggressive fluid resuscitation with isotonic saline to restore circulatory volume and stabilize blood pressure. Concurrently, potassium levels must be verified before starting insulin, as insulin drives potassium intracellularly and can cause fatal hypokalemia. Option A is secondary to stabilization; insulin should only begin if potassium is . Option B is reserved for extreme acidosis (pH ). Option C provides confirmation but does not alter the immediate life-saving steps of rehydration and electrolyte checking. Therefore, intravenous fluids and potassium monitoring constitute the most appropriate first-line clinical intervention for this emergency
questions.learning: The patient presents with the classic clinical triad of Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA): hyperglycemia (≥250 mg/dL), ketonuria, and metabolic acidosis, suggested by the fruity breath odor and Kussmaul (rapid) breathing.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient presents with swelling and severe pain in the right leg that has not subsided with analgesics. On examination, the pulse is feeble in the affected limb. Acute compartment syndrome is diagnosed, and intracompartmental pressure is 40 mmHg. On repeat examination, the pulse becomes absent. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fasciotomy

Acute compartment syndrome (ACS) is a limb-threatening surgical emergency caused by increased pressure within a closed fascial compartment, resulting in reduced tissue perfusion, muscle ischemia, and nerve injury. Urgent fasciotomy is the definitive treatment and should be performed without delay once the diagnosis is established.

• The patient has classic features of acute compartment syndrome:

• Severe pain out of proportion to the injury
• Pain not relieved by analgesics
• Feeble progressing to absent pulse
• Intracompartmental pressure of 90 mmHg (markedly elevated)

• These findings mandate emergency fasciotomy to decompress all involved compartments and restore tissue perfusion.

Why not the other options?

• A. Hot fomentation of the leg: Contraindicated; delays definitive treatment and may worsen edema.
• B. Cold fomentation of the leg: Does not relieve compartment pressure and delays life- and limb-saving surgery.
• D. Reassurance and send home: Dangerous and inappropriate; untreated ACS can lead to irreversible muscle necrosis, nerve damage, and limb loss.
questions.learning: Fasciotomy Acute compartment syndrome (ACS) is a limb-threatening surgical emergency caused by increased pressure within a closed fascial compartment, resulting in reduced tissue perfusion, muscle ischemia, and nerve injury.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which hormone is primarily produced during starvation to regulate and maintain blood glucose levels?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Glucagon

Glucagon produced during starvation helps regulate and maintain blood glucose levels.

Role of insulin and glucagon:

When blood glucose falls during fasting, there is increased secretion of glucagon and decreased release of insulin.

Effects of increased glucagon: insulin ratio on enzymes of glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis:

* It activates glycogen phosphorylase, the key enzyme of glycogenolysis, and deactivates glycogen synthase. This causes a rapid mobilization of liver glycogen stores to be utilized as fuel.

* It favors the synthesis of glucose-6-phosphatase which converts glucose-6-phosphate to glucose. The resulting glucose is used by red blood cells (lack mitochondria) and the brain as they are largely dependent on glucose in the fasting state.

* Phosphoenol pyruvate carboxykinase and fructose-1, 6-bisphosphatase are induced, leading to increased gluconeogenesis.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Identify the type of homicide caused by smothering and traumatic asphyxia.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Burking

Burking is a type of homicidal asphyxial death comprising of smothering and traumatic asphyxia. In burking, the assaulter throws the victim to the ground and kneels or sits on the chest of the victim preventing chest movements. He/she then covers the nose and mouth of the victim with his/her hands.

Other options:

Option A: Mugging is a type of strangulation caused by holding the neck of the victim in the crook of the elbow.  Pressure is then exerted either on the front of the larynx or at one or both sides by the forearm and upper arm. In mugging, the attack is usually made from behind. Death occurs due to reflex cardiac arrest or asphyxia.

The below image show strangulation by mugging.

Option B: Garrotting involves attacking the victim from behind using a ligature. The ligature is thrown around the unaware victim’s neck and then tightened by twisting it with a lever such as a rod or stick within the ligature. Earlier in Spain, garroting was an official method of judicial execution.

Option D: In bansdola, one strong bamboo or stick is placed across the back of the neck and another across the front. The victim is squeezed to death by tieing both ends of the stick with rope.

On examination, a bruise can be seen in the centre of the neck across the windpipe corresponding to the width of the stick or the substance used. A similar mark can be seen on the back of the neck if two sticks are used.

Sometimes two sticks are used across the back and front of the upper part of the chest and squeezed forcibly. This causes laceration of the muscles, and rib fractures and interferes with respiration.
questions.learning: Burking Burking is a type of homicidal asphyxial death comprising of smothering and traumatic asphyxia. In burking, the assaulter throws the victim to the ground and kneels or sits on the chest of the victim preventing chest movements.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: An 11-month-old infant previously noted to have left-sided ptosis shows abnormal eyelid movements in which the left upper eyelid elevates and depresses during feeding. The ptosis disappears when the child opens his mouth or sucks his thumb. What is this condition called?
questions.explanation: Marcus-Gunn jaw-winking phenomenon is a congenital synkinetic ptosis caused by an abnormal "miswiring" of the cranial nerves during development. Specifically, the levator palpebrae superioris muscle (supplied by CN III) is abnormally innervated by a branch of the trigeminal nerve (CN V) that normally supplies the muscles of mastication. Consequently, when the infant engages in jaw movements like sucking or mouth opening, the eyelid involuntarily retracts or "winks". Option A (Symblepharon) is an adhesion between the eyelid and the eyeball. Option B (Blepharophimosis syndrome) is a complex of ptosis, shortened palpebral fissures, and epicanthus inversus. Option C (Lagophthalmos) is the inability to close the eyelids completely. Marcus-Gunn phenomenon is usually unilateral. It does not typically resolve on its own, but patients often learn to mask the movement. Surgical correction is indicated if the ptosis is severe or causing amblyopia, usually involving levator excision and a frontalis suspension

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 34-year-old man with a known history of G6PD deficiency undergoes a minor dermatological procedure. A topical anesthetic cream containing lidocaine and prilocaine is applied under occlusion for a prolonged duration. Soon after, he develops acute dyspnea, cyanosis, and headache. Pulse oximetry shows oxygen saturation of 85% that does not improve despite administration of 100% oxygen. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Intravenous vitamin C

This patient has methemoglobinemia due to topical lidocaine/prilocaine, which oxidize hemoglobin iron to the ferric (Fe³⁺) state, impairing oxygen delivery. Clues include cyanosis, dyspnea, headache, and low pulse oximetry unresponsive to 100% oxygen. Although methylene blue is standard therapy, it is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency because it can precipitate hemolysis and worsen oxidative stress. Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is a safe alternative that reduces methemoglobin nonenzymatically.

A. Hemodialysis: Ineffective, as methemoglobin is intracellular.

C. Corticosteroids: No role in treating methemoglobinemia.

D. Methylene blue: Contraindicated in G6PD deficiency.
questions.learning: Intravenous vitamin C — This patient has methemoglobinemia due to topical lidocaine/prilocaine, which oxidize hemoglobin iron to the ferric (Fe³⁺) state, impairing oxygen delivery.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which anticancer drug is used in the treatment of both Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors (GIST) and Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML)?
questions.explanation: Imatinib is a breakthrough targeted therapy that works as a tyrosine kinase inhibitor. It was specifically designed to inhibit the BCR-ABL fusion protein found in Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML), which is created by the "Philadelphia chromosome" translocation. Additionally, Imatinib is the standard treatment for Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors (GIST) because it inhibits the c-KIT and PDGF receptor tyrosine kinases that drive these tumors. This drug revolutionized the treatment of CML, turning what was once a fatal disease into a manageable chronic condition. Methotrexate (Option B) is an antimetabolite used for many cancers and autoimmune diseases. Doxorubicin (Option C) is an anthracycline that works by DNA intercalation. Cisplatin (Option D) is a platinum-based alkylating agent. Imatinib's success paved the way for the development of many other targeted "small molecule" inhibitors, which focus on specific genetic mutations in cancer cells while sparing normal tissue, significantly reducing side effects compared to traditional chemotherapy
questions.learning: Imatinib is a breakthrough targeted therapy that works as a tyrosine kinase inhibitor. It was specifically designed to inhibit the BCR-ABL fusion protein found in Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML), which is created by the "Philadelphia chromosome" translocation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the use of the Mallampati classification?
options: To evaluate the risk of surgery
To evaluate the pros and cons of surgery
To evaluate the fitness of the patient
questions.explanation: The Mallampati classification is a standard clinical tool used by anesthesiologists during the preoperative assessment to predict the ease of endotracheal intubation. By asking the patient to open their mouth and protrude their tongue without phonating, the physician assesses how much of the soft palate, fauces, and uvula are visible. There are four classes; Class I (complete visibility) suggests an easy intubation, while Class IV (only the hard palate is visible) predicts a "difficult airway". It does not evaluate the overall risk of surgery (Option B), the pros and cons of the procedure (Option C), or the patient's general fitness (Option D). The American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical status classification is used for overall surgical risk and fitness assessment. Correctly identifying a difficult airway using Mallampati is essential for the anesthetic team to prepare appropriate equipment, such as a video laryngoscope or fiberoptic scope, to ensure patient safety during the induction of anesthesia
questions.learning: The Mallampati classification is a standard clinical tool used by anesthesiologists during the preoperative assessment to predict the ease of endotracheal intubation.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: An oncologist evaluates a patient with advanced breast cancer and determines that the prognosis is poor. The family is informed that further chemotherapy or radiotherapy will not improve survival. The patient is conscious but appears anxious. Her daughter insists on pursuing all possible interventions, including ICU admission. What is the next best step in management?
options: Discharge patient saying that there is nothing more to be done. Send to hospice for palliative care
Listen to daughter and be aggressive
Convene family and discuss patient's priority
Give placebo to reduce anxiety of patient
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Convene family and discuss patient's priority

This scenario involves end-of-life decision-making in a conscious patient with poor prognosis. When treatment becomes futile (no survival benefit), the physician should focus on:

• Patient autonomy
• Shared decision making
• Goals of care discussion

The patient is conscious, so her preferences must be central to the decision.

Core ethical principles apply:

• Autonomy: The patient is conscious and capable of expressing her wishes. Her preferences must take priority over family demands.
• Beneficence & Non-maleficence: Avoid futile, burdensome interventions that offer no survival benefit.
• Shared decision-making: Requires a family meeting to discuss prognosis, goals of care, and patient values (comfort vs life-prolongation).

The correct step is to convene a family meeting, clarify the patient’s goals, address anxiety, and then decide on palliative or hospice care with informed consent.

A. Discharge patient saying nothing more can be done- This is abandonment of care and unethical.

B. Listen to daughter and be aggressive- Aggressive treatment that provides no benefit is medically futile. Patient autonomy must be respected.

D. Give placebo to reduce anxiety- Giving placebo without disclosure is unethical and deceptive.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding nikshay poshan yojana?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Rs 500 is given per month

Under nikshay poshan yojana, a financial incentive of Rs.500 per month is provided for nutritional support to each notified TB patient for the duration of anti-TB treatment.

For pediatric TB patients who do not have bank accounts, the money shall be deposited in parent's/guardian's accounts whose details are to be sought and entered in nikshay against the patient’s records.

The processing of payment is on the 7th of every month.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following fungal infection is most commonly seen in the maxillary sinus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Aspergillosis

Aspergillosis and mucormycosis are the most common fungal infections that involve the maxillary sinuses.

The most common sinus affected by a fungal infection is the maxillary sinus (fungal balls), accounting for approximately 94% of the cases.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The pretracheal layer of deep cervical fascia encloses all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sternocleidomastoid

All the above structures are enclosed by the pretracheal layer of deep cervical fascia except sternocleidomastoid. It is enclosed by the investing layer of deep cervical fascia.

The deep cervical fascia of the neck is organized into the following layers:

• The investing layer, which surrounds all structures in the neck
• The prevertebral layer, which surrounds the vertebral column and the deep muscles associated with the back.
• The pretracheal layer, which encloses the viscera of the neck
• The carotid sheath, which receives a contribution from the other three fascial layers

In the neck, the pretracheal fascia covers the strap muscles i.e sternohyoid, omohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid. It splits to enclose the thyroid gland. It also surrounds the trachea and the esophagus including the recurrent laryngeal nerve present in the groove between them.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following bones is most accurate for sex determination?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pelvis

The whole pelvis is the most reliable bone for sex determination.

Krogman’s degree of accuracy in sex determination from adult skeletal remains:

* Entire skeleton – 100%

* Pelvis alone – 95%

* Skull alone – 90%

* Pelvis plus skull – 98%

* Long bones alone – 80-90%

* Long bones and skull - 90-95%

* Long bones and pelvis - >95%

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Consider the following statements with regard to jaundice: 1. Presence of scleral icterus indicates a serum bilirubin level of at least 3 mg/dL. 2. If the examiner suspects scleral icterus, second site to examine is underneath the tongue. 3. In long-standing jaundice, skin may become green due to reduction of bilirubin to biliverdin. 4. Sclerae have a particular affinity for bilirubin due to its high elastin content. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2 and 4 only

Jaundice becomes clinically apparent when serum bilirubin exceeds approximately 2–3 mg/dL. Scleral icterus is the earliest clinical sign because the sclera is rich in elastin, which has a high affinity for bilirubin. If scleral icterus is doubtful, the undersurface of the tongue (sublingual mucosa) should be examined, as it is another early site of bilirubin deposition.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• 1. Presence of scleral icterus indicates a serum bilirubin level of at least 3 mg/dL ✔️: Clinically, scleral icterus is usually evident when bilirubin is \~2–3 mg/dL.
• 2. If scleral icterus is suspected\, examine underneath the tongue ✔️: The sublingual mucosa is an early site for detecting jaundice.
• 3. In long-standing jaundice\, skin may become green due to reduction of bilirubin to biliverdin ❌: The green discoloration is due to oxidation of bilirubin to biliverdin, not reduction.
• 4. Sclerae have a particular affinity for bilirubin due to high elastin content ✔️: Correct.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 4 only Jaundice becomes clinically apparent when serum bilirubin exceeds approximately 2–3 mg/dL. Scleral icterus is the earliest clinical sign because the sclera is rich in elastin, which has a high affinity for bilirubin.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following types of amino acids are present in the transmembranous part of the membrane receptor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hydrophobic

The transmembranous part of the membrane receptor consists of hydrophobic amino acids.

A membrane protein can be either integral protein (spans the thickness of the cell membrane) or peripheral protein (attached to the peripheral side of the membrane). The membrane-spanning segment of integral proteins are usually hydrophobic alpha-helices.

The central core of the cell membrane is hydrophobic. Integral proteins have their hydrophobic portions usually in the interior of the membrane and the hydrophilic portions towards the surfaces. The presence of these hydrophobic amino acids in the interior is a special adaptation that allows the protein to remain stable in the hydrophobic milieu of the cell membrane.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old lady presents with body pain, easy fatigability and problems while standing. Neurological examination revealed loss of vibration sense and proprioception. Investigations revealed a hemoglobin level of 7 gm/dL. Which of the following should be administered for the patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vit B12

The given scenario describes megaloblastic anaemia due to vitamin B12 deficiency. Vitamin B12 deficiency may lead to subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord  and the patient needs to be given Vit B12.

It presents with symmetrical paraesthesia and progresses to weakness, ataxia and spasticity. It can be treated by administration of vitamin B12.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30-year-old man presents with a history of a fall on the posterior aspect of the shoulder. He has lacerations over the posterior shoulder and has sustained a fracture of the shaft of the humerus as shown in the X-ray below. Which nerve is most likely to be affected in this injury?

Correct answer: C. Radial nerve

In the above clinical scenario, the history and radiograph suggest a closed fracture of the shaft of the humerus. The radial nerve is commonly damaged in this condition.

It manifests as an inability to dorsiflex the wrist and digits (wrist drop and finger drop). Numbness occurs on the dorsoradial aspect of the hand and the dorsal aspect of the radial 31/2 digits.

Management of humerus shaft fractures:

* Conservative management using a hanging cast or U-slab for 2-3 weeks, followed by functional bracing

* Surgical fixation by compression plating, interlocking intramedullary nail, semi-flexible pins, or an external fixator is indicated in:

* Open fractures

* Pathological fractures

* Unstable humeral and forearm fractures (floating elbow)

* Radial nerve palsy

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: 30,000 women were followed up for 10 years for the development of breast cancer. 1200 women developed cancer and were given a questionnaire to assess possible risk factors. Additionally, 2000 women from the same study were used as controls and were also given the questionnaire. What is this type of study called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Nested case control

The type of study described in the question is a nested case-control study.

A nested case-control study is essentially a case-control study that is present inside a cohort study. The cases are all the cohort members who developed the disease being studied at a given point in time during the follow-up period. However, each case is matched to one or more controls — individuals who did not develop the disease but are otherwise comparable to cases in terms of age and gender. Cases and controls are then compared in terms of their respective exposures to the risk factor. Nested case-control studies thus represent an interim analysis of the exposure and outcome data of a cohort study.

A case-cohort study (option A) involves selecting a subset of the entire cohort at the beginning of the study. This sub-cohort acts as the control group for making comparisons with multiple case groups. For example, if a cohort study is being done to assess smoking as a risk factor for ischemic heart disease and lung cancer, the same sub-cohort can be used as the control group for both outcomes. If it was a nested case-control study, it would require two separate control groups. Case-cohort studies are more efficient than nested case-control studies when multiple outcomes are being studied.

In a retrospective cohort study (option B), the outcomes have already occurred before the study begins. The investigator has to analyze the history of prior exposures and the duration of such exposures. Even though the exposure and the outcome have already occurred, the investigator goes from the exposure → outcome in a retrospective cohort study. This is in contrast to case-control studies, where the investigator goes from outcome → exposure.

Cross control cohort (option D) is not a type of study design.
questions.learning: Nested case control — The type of study described in the question is a nested case-control study. A nested case-control study is essentially a case-control study that is present inside a cohort study.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Modified Robson's classification class 1 includes:
options: Multiparous without previous CS, spontaneous labour
Multiparous without previous CS, induced/CS before labour
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nulliparous, singleton, cephalic, spontaneous labour

Class 1 of modified Robson's classification includes nullipara, equal to or >37 weeks, single, cephalic, spontaneous labor.

It is the most widely accepted classification system available for analyzing characteristics of delivering women worldwide. It consists of 10 patient population categories. The basis for these categories include:

• Parity
• Onset of labor and mode of delivery
• Gestational age
• Fetal presentation
• No. of fetuses

The modified Robson system classification is as follows:

Class 1
Nullipara, equal to or >37 weeks, single, cephalic, spontaneous labor

Class 2

Nullipara, equal to or >37 weeks, single, cephalic

2a: induced labor  2b: CS before labor

Class 3
Multipara, equal to or >37 weeks, single, cephalic, spontaneous labor (excludes previous CS)

Class 4
Multipara, equal to or >37 weeks, single, cephalic   4a: induced labor 4b: CS before labor

Class 5
Multipara, previous CS, equal to or >37 weeks, single, cephalic

Class 6
Nullipara, single, breech

Class 7
Multipara, single, breech (including previous CS)

Class 8
Multiple pregnancies (with or without previous CS)

Class 9
Singleton pregnancy, oblique/transverse lie (with or without previous CS)

Class 10
Single, cephalic <37 weeks (including previous CS)
questions.learning: Nulliparous, singleton, cephalic, spontaneous labour Class 1 of modified Robson's classification includes nullipara, equal to or >37 weeks, single, cephalic, spontaneous labor.

questions.text:
Match the following organisms with their association :

1) H. pylori
a)Cutaneous MALT

2) C.psittaci
b)Alpha heavy chain disease

3) Borrelia burgdorferi
c)Gastric MALT

4) Campylobacter jejuni
d)Ocular MALT
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 - c ; 2 -d ; 3 - a ; 4 - b

The correct answer is option B: 1 - c  ; 2 -d ; 3 - a ; 4 - b.

1) H. pylori
c)Gastric MALT

2) C.psittaci
d)Ocular MALT

3) Borrelia burgdorferi
a)Cutaneous MALT

4) Campylobacter jejuni
b)Alpha heavy chain disease

MALT (mucosa-associated lymphoid tumor) lymphoma is an extranodal marginal zone lymphoma, most commonly seen in the stomach, but other common sites include the skin, salivary glands, small bowel, ocular adnexa, and synovium. It is associated with states of chronic inflammation due to either autoimmune diseases (Sjögren’s syndrome or Hashimoto’s thyroiditis) or chronic infections with organisms like H. pylori (gastric), Borrelia burgdorferi (skin), C. psittaci (conjunctiva), C. jejuni (intestines), and hepatitis C virus.

The essential pathologic feature of MALT lymphoma is the presence of lymphoepithelial lesions, which result from the invasion of mucosal glands and crypts by the neoplastic lymphocytes. These cells are positive for CD19, CD20, and CD79a and negative for CD5 and CD10. Recurrent cytogenetic abnormalities include t(11;18), t(14;18), t(1;14), t(3;14), and trisomy 8. The t(11;18) is most common, occurring in up to 50% of MALT lymphomas.

Unlike other indolent B-cell lymphomas, MALT lymphomas present most commonly with stage I or II disease. In these cases, radiation therapy may be curative. Alternatively, patients may respond to antibiotics for the associated underlying infection.

Alpha heavy chain disease / immunoproliferative small intestinal disease (IPSID) is recognized as an infectious pathogen-associated human lymphoma associated with Campylobacter jejuni. It involves mainly the proximal small intestine, resulting in malabsorption, diarrhea, and abdominal pain. IPSID is associated with excessive plasma cell differentiation and produces truncated alpha heavy chain proteins lacking the light chains. Early-stage IPSID responds to antibiotics (30–70% complete remission). Most untreated IPSID patients progress to lymphoplasmacytic and immunoblastic lymphoma.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following nerve can be injured, when a fracture is sustained at the area marked with the red arrow in the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ulnar nerve

In the given image the arrow points to the medial epicondyle. Fracture at the medial epicondyle damages the ulnar nerve.

The nerves related to the humerus are:

* Axillary nerve is at the surgical neck

* Ulnar nerve is at the medial epicondyle

* Radial nerve is at the spiral groove of the shaft of the humerus.

Ulnar Nerve: Branches and Innervation

* Superficial branch:

Innervates palmaris brevis. Provides sensory supply to the skin on the palmar side of the medial 1½ fingers.

* Deep branch:

Travels through the concavity of the deep palmar arch.

Supplies all intrinsic hand muscles except:

* The first two lumbricals

* The thenar muscles

Injury to the ulnar nerve can be as follows:

High lesion
(Elbow)
Low lesion
(Wrist)

Site of injury

• Fracture/dislocation of the medial epicondyle
• Cubital tunnel syndrome
• Compression between the two heads of FCU
• Tardy ulnar nerve palsy (Valgus deformity)

• Wrist laceration/ slashing
• Guyon's canal syndrome

Motor loss

• Claw-hand deformity
• Hypothenar & interosseous wasting
• Loss of:

• Abduction & adduction of fingers
(Card test - Positive)
• Adduction of thumb
(Froment sign- Positive)
• Flexion of MCP joints

• Weakness of wrist flexion (radial deviation)

• Claw-hand deformity
(more pronounced)
• Hypothenar & interosseous wasting
• Loss of:

• Abduction & adduction of fingers
(Card test - Positive)
• Adduction of thumb
(Froment sign- Positive)

Sensory loss

• Over palmar & dorsal aspect of the medial third of the hand
• Over palmar & dorsal aspect of the medial 1 1/2 fingers

• No sensory loss over palmar & dorsal aspect of the medial third of the hand
• Over palmar & dorsal aspect of the medial 1 1/2 fingers

Other tests seen in ulnar nerve lesions are as follows:

* Claw hand deformity

* Froment's sign positive

* Wartenberg sign

* Palmaris brevis sign

The image below shows a positive card test:

Wartenberg's sign: (Weakness of palmar interossei), Sensory loss of palmar and dorsal surface of the medial third of hand and medial 1 and a half fingers.
